"ComE and have a quiet game of tennis," said Johnson. "Impossible," replied Thompson; "how can I play tennis without a racket I" "THIS is a sad and bitter world," remarked a gentleman of Irish extraction. "We never strew flowers on a man's grave until after he is dead." HE—" What would you think, dear, if I should say you were a harp of a thousand strings l" She—" I should think, love, that you were a lyre. A HEALTH journal is telling people "how to lie when asleep." If it could persuade them to tell the truth when awake it would be doing real service. "WELL, Mary, how do you like yclur new place 7" "I can't tell yet, positively; you know, the first day the ladies are always politeness itself." AN old bachelor says—" It is all nonsense to pretend that love is blind. I never knew a man in love who did not see ten times as much in his sweetheart as I did." "Do you have damp sheets 1" said the fussy old man at the hotel, securing a room. "No," said the clerk, who wanted to be obliging; "bit we can sprinkle 'em for you if you like them that way." M. FEATHEItLY—"You seem to have a nice, rich colour this evening, Bobby." "Yes, sister had to step around to the dressmaker's a moment before supper and I got hold of some of hers." THE chiropodist is a humble individual. In the professions he begins and is content to remain at the foot. The barber, on the other hand, is ambi- tious. He begins at the head and stays there. "I HOPE you appreciate the fact, sir, that in marrying my daughter you marry a large-hearted, generous girl." "I do, sir," with emotion, "and I hope she inherits those qualities from her father." MOSES JUNIOR—" Fader, a shentleman in de shop vants to know if dat all-vool nonshrinkable shirt Till shrink 7" Moses senior—" Does it fid him ?" Moses junior—" No; id is too big." Moses senior —" Yah, id viii shrink !" LADY—" You know sir, I wish my portrait to be a total surprise for my husband." Artist, "Yes, madam, I understand." Lady—" And you will try not to have too strong a likeness, as I would not wish him to recognise it at the first glance. "WRY cannot a woman become a successful lawyer, I should like to know ?" asked a lady; of a cynical old judge. "Because, madam," he answered, "she's too fond of giving her opinion without pay." "PROFESSOR, what are your views concerning the schools of medicine and theology I" Professor— "That depends upon circumstances. When lam slightly ill, I am a hommopathist and a Unitarian; but when I am very sick, I am an allopathist and a Calvinist." DuitlNG a ball, a lady discovered, sitting with a dreamy, far away gaze. To her a gentleman from whom she has long received marked advances You must surely be thinking of your future husband? Lady—Ah, Mr. N., you seem to have a good opinion of yourself! OLD LADY, locking over art-student copying at South Kensington from the old masters—" Now, that's uncommon bright and pretty; ain't it, John? Something like a picture, I calls that I" Old gentle- man—" Yes my dear. I wonder," ruminatively, "what they're going to do with the old ones I" LADY, in registry office—" I am afraid that little girl won't do for a nurse; she is too small. I should hesitate to trust her with the baby." Clerk—" Her size madam, we look upon as her greatest recom- mendation. You should remember that when she drops a baby it doesn't have very far to fall." JACK wanted to convince his old-fashioned :mole that a bicycle was a practical and useful machine, and to that end offered to carry a basket of eggs borne for him. Poor Jack met with a "header," but was consoled by his uncle, who said, "It ain't a success fur carrying eggs, Jack, but it makes an omelette fast rate." POND MAMMA (showing the baby to visitor)— " Sh-h—he's asleep. The little darling! Isn't he the sweetest you ever saw ?" Visitor (in awe-struck whisper)—" Decidedly. Can he talk ?" Fond mom- ma—" Talk? I should think he could talk I Why, he can say 'goo' and 'ga' and gown.' Picked them up himself, too." "WHAT if I was one of those husbands, my dear, who get up in the morning and bang things around, and kick like everything, just because the coffee is cold ? " "John," responded his wife, "I would make it hot for you." As her words admitted of more than one interpretation, John said nothing more about the coffee. A LADY, whose portrait Opie was painting, was mustering all her smiles to look charming, till at length the artist could endure the constrained and affected features no longer • starting up, and throw- ing down his brush, he exclaimed, in his broad style, "I tell ye what it is, ma'am, if ye grin so, I canna draw you at all." "No, sin," said a pompous little merchant, "I Can't be trifled with. I know the world; I've been through it." "Yes, I suppose so," said the man to whom these remarks were addressed. " I'm a self- pade man—entirely self-made. What do you think ttat, sir ?" " Well, it strikes me you might have ,doni cleat better to let out the contract." "WE had for dinner," writes Mr. IL B. Cater in his " Memoir of Henry Compton," "among other things, a ham which was not well-flavoured; and Mrs. Frederick Mackenzie, whe was annoyed about it, began apologising, and said that Ellerton, the local grocer, had said it to her as something very excellent, and as a genuine Westphalia. • Ah,' said Compton, I cannot determine precisely whether it is East or West, but it is a iailure ef some sort.'" Miss Many., innocently—" Here are two kinds of cigars: one papa calls his friends' cigars,' the other he calls his Own cigars;' but I don't know which are the best." Capt. Corkscrew, who does know which are the best, carefully selecting one from " papa's " own box—" As it w,..uld be almost presumptuous to call myself one of your dear papa's friends, Miss Mary, I think that I had pettcr try one of what he so appi okrigttely olvn cigars."

In spite of the fact that the glass is below zero, my right foot rejoices in more than normal warmth, whereas the left is quite rigid and stiff, and cold as ice." Upon the advice of the family doctor, who was sent for without delay, the professor was put te bed, when it was discovere4 he „ . n am .is right foot, while his left was .I..rsy upon entirety tlnpro.ecteu. THE late Baron Rothschild, dining once at his -club in Paris, heard some one say, "Horrible bore; lent X —lO,OOO francs; have not even got an acknowledgment, and he's gose to Constantinople." "Write to-him," said the Baron. "Have done so, and it don't answer.' " Then, my dear sir, write to him thus Dear Monsieur X--, when the Turks and Turkesses leave you a little leisure time send me the 20,000 francs I lent you." "But he only owes me 10,000." " Precisely ;he will write and say so, and then there's your acknowledgment." THE late Mr. Neil M.Vicar, minister of St. Cuth- bert's, Edinburgh, was taking a walk one afternoon, when he discovered a woman, one of his parishioners sitting by the roadside in a state of intoxication, while her burden lay in the mud before her. "Oh, will ye help me up wi my bundle I" said she to the minister, as he approached. "Fie! fie! Janet," said he, "to see the like o' you in such a plight. Do you know where all drinkers go to 7" "Help me up wr my bundle, sir, and I'll tell ye." "Well, well," said the clergyman, "I shall. Now, answer my question." " Weel, to tell you the truth, sir, just whaur the drap o' gude drink is to be gotten!" WON OR LOST 7—Mrs. Grigsby (who has been reading a newspaper), "Here is a strange story, Mr. Grigsby, and I don't know whether to believe it or not'—Mr. Grigsby (crossly), " Humph I If it's any.. thing against one of your sex you'll believe it easy enough. What is it 7"—Mrs. Grigsby (not regarding the slur, being used to them), "It's about a man who courted a woman persistently for more than forty years. Every time he asked her to marry him she said No,' but he persisted, and when they finally married he was 72 years old and she 61. How much that man lost (sighing)."—Mr. Grigsby, " Lost! Why, that man was way ahead.—Mrs. Grigsby, "How do you make that out."—Mr. Grigsby, " Forty years less of domestic turmoil, see 7"—"Oh, you brute," exclaimed Mrs. Grigsby, as she went out of the room and slammed the door. div.head: "CAPITAL CHAT."
div.p: "CAPITAL CHAT."
TV.

Mr. Isaac Holden, M.P., has forwarded to 4r. P. Byles, of Bradford, treasurer of the movement, a cheque for £l,OOO in aid of the English Fund for Ireland. In an accompanying letter he says: "I hope the Liberal party will take it up heartily and thus assist the Irish patriotic party in effecting their peaceful revolution."

The generosity of Dr. Wordsworth might be copied by some of his colleagues with excellent effect. Not content with building technical schools at Salisbury. and contributing £2,000 to the new parochial schools, he had just guaranteed £5OO towards a much-needed church, and subscribed £lOO per annum to the Bournemouth church fund.

The service of reconciliation in connection with the recent suicide at St. Paul's Cathedral is the result of a consultation of musty precedents of pre- Reformation date, and has caused considerable dis- may in church circles, by whom such a revival, under the present regime at St. Paul's, was not anticipated. This is by no means the first suicide in the Cathedral, and it was only a few years back that a madman jumped from the whispering gallery into the Dome area, but no such service was then even talked of, much less held.

The "Labour World " is the property of a limited company, of which Mr. Davitt is the managing director and secretary, as well as the chief share- holder, and the great success of the venture has led the proprietors to double the original capital of the concern, which is now £lO,OOO. When this was first decided upon one Of the shareholders offered to take up the total amount, but to this Mr. Davitt was not agreeable, so the whole of the new shares have been equally distributed among the original subscribers.

Mr. W. H. Smith's appearance has delighted his colleagues, and dispels any fears of his being unable to continue the leadership of the House of Com- mons. He is looking well; the eczema has entirely disappeared, and his complexion is bronzed and ruddy. Lord Salisbury is also wonderfully better for his stay at Royat, and has lost over a stone in weight ; he has at last begun to take exercise, walk- ing a considerable distance every day. Mr. Ritchie looks as well as ever. Only the Chancellor of the Exchequer retains the pallid complexion he never loses.

I hear that General Booth will not have much difficulty in finding the money necessary to start his great scheme for the social regeneraaion of the country. There are already many rich contributors to the funds of the Salvation Army, and the publi- cation of General Booth's scheme will interest philanthropists all over the country. He needs £lOO,OOO to start with, and a sum of £30,000 annually afterwards. It is believed that the 100,000 will be provided by a few hunilreds of wealthy philanthropists, and once this sum is obtained there will not be much difficulty in raising the £30,000 a year.

A German contemporary is responsible for the following :—The peasantry of the village of Radnitz, in Crossen, are a thrifty class. While a little party of them were on their way to work it occurred to a woman that in her cottage were some 1,200 marks in bank notes. She returned, tied up the notes in a handkerchief, and rejoined her friends. While at work, the woman saw a crow hovering about her things, and hastened to beat it off. She arrived in time to see the bird soaring off with the handkerchief. She shouted lustily as she saw the crow in the air. The bird perched on the topmost branch of a tree, and presently the notes fluttered to earth. All the treasure was recovered.

One of the " Spectator's" natural history corres- pondents has discovered that cockatoos have a sense of humour. Here is the correspondent's story "A very tame sulphur-crested white cockatoo hap- pened one day to be on his perch near a lawn-tennis ground. The day was damp, and the ground slip- pery. In the course of the game several falls occurred. Each tumble gave rise to much laughter and merriment amongst both players and onlookers, which seemed to attract the especial attention of the bird. When the set' was finished, and the per- formers were talking together on one side of the court, 'Cocky' quietly descended from his stand, walked on to the lawn-tennis ground, rolled over and over two or three times on the grass, and then, picking himself up, laughed long and loud in exact imitation of the players."

The American invasion of England continues apace, and in the next generation half the English peerage will boast American blood. The latest con- quest is that of the Ron. Dudley Leigh, Lord Leigh's eldest son, who is engaged to Miss Beck- with, of New York, but now resident in England. Mr. Leigh is brother to Lady Jersey, and nephew maternally of the Duke of Westminster. Lord Leigh's house, Stoneleigh Abbey, near Leamington, is one of the show places of the Midlands, and the historic ruins of Kenilworth stand on the estate, which extends over some 20,000 acres. Lord Leigh's father was raised to the peerage in recognition of his services to the popular cause at the time of the first Reform Bill. The family are steady and con- sistent Liberals in spite of their Whiggish associa- tions, and the present Lord Leigh is one of the very few peers who follows Lord Granville's lead in the Rouse of Lords.

Dr. Parker's challenge to the public to declare their opinion on the modern sermon appears to have been freely accepted. He is reported to have said on Sunday in what he calls his one-minute sermon at the City Temple—" I have made inquiries upon this subject through the newspapers; and the , arlsWerS, very abl.:; Written, have simply appalled me. Preachers are in many instances living in a fool's paradise. The evidence is to the effect that preachers do not concern themselves about the everyday life of the people, but drivel in meta- physics and theology, about which the people know nothing and care nothing. There is a solemn demand for practical preaching, and for preaching that touches sympathetically the sorrow and the need of daily life. I heartily adopt this view. Yet I cannot acquit the pew of all blame. The pew has called for old phrases and old references, and when these have been absent the pew has thought that the Gospel has not been preached. The pew must be sensible if ever the pulpit is to become wise."

Nine of the few survivors of the famous charge of the Light Brigade are paupers, to the disgrace of the War Office. One of them, Charles Carrott, has been receiving out-door relief from the Horncastle Union for some time. Ile was discharged after the terrible Crimean campaign with good character and a ruined constitution, but without a pension. Dr.. Aubrey, the Liberal candidate for the Horncastle Division, has repeatedly called attention to this scandal, and he had it brought under the notice of the House of Commons last Session, but the invari- able official reply was that nothing could be done. Mr. Stanhope,the War Secretary,added that political capital was being made out of it by the other side. As Dr. Aubrey continued to refer to it at his public meetings in the district, Mr. Stanhope, in a speech last week, challenged him to bear half the cost of making suitable provision for the old soldier. The challenge was at once accepted, and the man now ceases to be a recipient of parochial relief. But the injustice remains that the military system, as at present administered, too often leaves the common soldiers to starve when their term of service expires, while titled officers are lavishly rewarded. Six hundred retired and half-pay generals and admirals draw nearly half a million annually. Ten times that number of officers, all told, received in half-pay and pensions, more than two millions and a half, while alike sum has to suffice for 116.000 common soldiers and sailors, and many get nothing.

• THE LATE PROFESSOR ROGERS. tar" says :—The late Professor Thorold Rogers was one of the most prominent members of the first English Liberal deputation to Ireland in 1886. Everywhere throughout the country the am- bassadors of the new policy of peace and goodwill were hailed with acclaim, and even in the city of Belfast the horses were unyoked from the carriages, and the English delegates drawn through the streetsin the midst of cheering thousands. During his Belfast visit, Mr. Rogers was asked by an admirer to sign his name in an autograph book, which he did, prefixing to his autograph the coup- let :

"We came up here to plead for poor old Erin, And none but Orangemen are hard of hearinl." The poetical example was contagious, for Mr. Richard Eve, well known to our readers as a staunch Liberal, wrote as follows : " Normans of old to Ireland came to thieve, But nobler motives now bring Richard Eve." Mr. John Pinkerton, M.P., the Protestant representa- tive of Catholic Galway, could not resist the temptation to follow their example, and thereupon he produced the following couplet:— "These Englishmen are very jolly 'codgers.' I I like them all, both Hobson, Eve, and Rogers." Mr. Rogers use to relate an amusing incident of his experiences during the 1885 elections. Some of the replies he received during the canvass were more expressive than polite, and upon one occasion, in response to the stereotyped requests voter answered indignantly, "No, I won't: I would see you in h-- first !" The Professor received the outburst in a very resigned spirit, and meekly replied, "Well my friend, in case I do get there, I should say that you will be pretty sure to see me." Equally amusing was his reply to the elector who frankly assured him that he would "vote for the devil first" "Very good, sir, very good," said the stoical Professor; but in case your friend does not come to the poll, may I hope to be favoured with your support ?" The retort was both happy and effective, for from that day the voter to whom it was addressed was amongst his most enthusiastic supporters.

enquiry held by the chief constable into his conduct la February, 1887. We desire it to be understood that we express this opinion as the result of the investigation we have now made, in which further and additional evidence has been placed before us, which was not at that time before the chief constable."

As to the neglect of their beats by the police in order to aid gamekeepers at night, the Committee say, It was alleged by several ex-police officers that they had been engaged frequently, and sometimes for several consecu- tive nights (in one instance to the extent of a month), in assisting gamekeepers in watching at night on private lands. But in our opinion much of the evidence has I been seriously discredited. The number of occasions on which police officers have joined keepers has been exag- gerated, but there can be no doubt that it has happen,ed that police officers have gone out with or met keepers, and on various occasions on private lands, and it doubt- less was the case that although the beats of these officers in some cases were patrolled by the officers of adjoining beats, they were in other cases left unpatrolled for such time. These occasions were distinct breaches of duty and disobedience of orders on the part of these indivi- dual constables, in so far as they occurred on private land not in the immediate neighbourhood of a public i road or footpath, and were not n conformity with the law.

The Committee cite the general order placed on the instruction-book of every constable in carrying out the Act for the Prevention of Poaching, and proceed to say that the" assistance to gamekeepers given by the police at night on the occasions establishedrwith one exception on the Addington estate, was without the knowledge of the owners of the lands. While therefore we find that the statements made by the ex-police- officers who were called to substantiate these charges cannot be entirely relied upon, and while we hold that there has not been, except on the unauthorised occasions-referred to, any in- fringement of the law in this respect, we cannot avoid expressing our regret that there should have been, on the part of the constables implicated, a departure from a strict compliance with the letter and spirit of the chief constable's order." With reference to the allegation "That it is part of the police system generally to conceal the fact of so doing by entries in their journals mis- leading the Government Inspector of Police," the Com- mittee find tha* the allegation is not proved. As to the charge that the Runcorn police on the 24th September, 1889, left the town between IT. p.m. and 4 a.m. without any protection, whatever, in order to aid Sir Stopford Brooke's keepers at Norton, the' Committee find that' it is not proved. They add, however, that "there can be no doubt that the town was deprived to a considerable extent of its ordinary police protection dur- ing a large part of the night. On the other hand, it is to be observed that'the mission of the police toNortou on that night was clearly a legal one, and, as far as we can , judge by the evidence 'before us, was lawfully and pro- perly carried out." With reference to the allegation that "Constables in and about the district of Macclesfield did formerly, if not now, receive gratuities for every conviction of poachers obtained by them in the police courts from some fund believed to be established by game preservers in or about that district, some of whom were justices of the peace,' we have (say' the Committee) to report that there is, evi- dence of money having been paid for some years past to police officers on conviction of poachers in the Maccles- field district, and it appears that in January, 1890, Colonel Hamersley's attention having been called to the alleged existence of such a fund,„ he applied to Superintendent Downes, of Macclesfield, and received from him the-lot- lowing letter :

-No. 9,-Macclesfield Division, Cheshkre Constabuiary, Superintendent's Office, 19th .I:binary, 1899; Sir —I have thehonourito report for your information, inre- ference to your mernorindum dated lgth January, that there. is a fond existing here from which constables receive £l. for the convictivni of a poacher, which is paid bythe Eev.—DPx, of Parkside. Before he took it in hand, one cfghe Brocklehursts- paid it to a superintendent for him to give iti to the constable. I believe this has been done for years. I de not know who. the fund is maintained by, only that Mr. Dix told me that the magistrates and landowners subscribed and he acted, as, secretary.--I have the honour to be, sir, your obedient ser- van t ,

JOSEPH DOWNES. Supt. Chief Constable of Cheshire, Chester. Upon receipt of this letter the Chief Constable at once- wrote as follows:,--- The receipt of such rewards by county constables musat.7 once be discontinued =less specially sanctioned by me. In.. form Mr. Dix to this eftect, and warn the constObles,

Chester, 21st 'Tannery, 1890. LH. H., C.C. Note and return and report you have carried but above. Superintendent Downes reports on 29th January, 189 N that" the above order has been carried out' Under these circumstances (continue the Committee) we applied to Mr. Dix, and he has informed us, "that this fund originated abont four years ago, after a discussion at a- social gathering as.th whether some legitimate scheme could not be adapted to intercept the spoils of poachers on the way to thssmarket. That he was thenasked to be secretary, and that there were 15 subscribers, five of them being jtisticesof the peace." It is reported to us in answer to our inquiries that there were no rules or regu- lationsand no books of account, beyond a memorandum of the balance left' in the hands of Mr. Dix when the Chief Constable issued his-order in January, 1890?•'..and that- since that time the fund has practically ceased to exist We cannot but express our-opinion that the existence of a system of offering rewards in connection with game rases, when the earning of the reward depend on the obtaining of a conviction, ia objectionable and calculated to impede the due-and equitable administrationefjtistice. "We find that this allegation has been proved." - i We have now dealt with each speci9c chargenantained in the memorandurrrof accusations, and as a4result of bur investigations., we thinktit right to place on record our sense of the ability and devotion to duty which have characterised Colbnel Harnmersley's tenure of ' the oflii3e- of chief constable. It is gratifying to us to' find the *eneral discipline and management of the forceron a satis- factory basis, and that in so-large a body of men a high) percentage of good conduct is maintained. In conclusion the Committee recommend thnto all

div.head: IIS THIS BEACON LIGHTED FOR YOU?
div.p: IIS THIS BEACON LIGHTED FOR YOU?

"I think the Government should at once erect a new lighthouse on the spot I have named on the coast of Florida. It is a dangerous place, and ships are liable to be driven ashore there, and wrecked." So writes a sea captain to the Government of the United States. He alludes to a locality on the coast of America. No doubt he is right. There can hardly,be too many warnings of peril. The following letter, which is here printed in the writer's very words,:may prove a sort of beacon light to hundreds of our readers. The writer is Mrs. Plowright, wife of Mr. William Plowright, of the Lincolnshire Bakery, 23, Cheetham-st., North- at., Cheetham, Manchester. The lady says :—" In the spring of 1889 I suffered from heart disease and general debility, and was ailing from April to September. At kirst my illness came upon me almost imperceptibly. I had a feeling of lassitude, and was tired with little or no exertion, and was troubled with shqrtness of breath anctfaintness. J could not eat and my sleep was disturbed: I had previously been of a cheerful, llvely disposition, but achange came over me, and I easily became tired (flagged), dull, and depressed. I had great paid in the region of the heart and chest, and could not eat anything without distress. Even the swallowing of a few drops of water gave me intense pain.

"I went on in this way for several weeks, still going about my work in the house and shop, but I felt miser- able and dejected. I tried our simple medicines (I am very averse to taking physic) but felt 'that I must do something to relieve me. Getting no better, I consulted our family doctor, a gentleman who has a large practice and is considered very skilful. After a careful examina- tion he informed me that I .was suffering from conges- tion of the liver, heart disease, and debility. I was un- der his treatment for some months. He gave me medi- cine that relieved me a little for a time, and then I re- I lapsed into my former condition. Once in a while my heart would stop beating, and I had all the appearance of being in q dying state. This alarmed me very much, but in a little while I would revive and be somewhat better. "This I was told was the so-called incurable complaint known as Angina Pectoris—or breast pang. Well,l went on in this way until the end of August, when my hus- band and some friends persuaded me to try Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, my husband had already taken a potion of a bottle of this medicine, and I myself had read about it in a book which had been left at the shop. Still I did not think it would do much for me. I began by taking fifteen drops, but as this had no gocd effect I took thirty drops and followed the directions. This dose seemed to suit me, for, after taking a bottle I felt gradu- ally getting stronger. The pain in my chest and side gradually disappeared, and, after taking two bottles I was completely restored to health. lam now in the en- joyment of good health, and have never bad any of the heart trouble since."

This is Mrs. Plowright'S calm and dispassionate state- ment. We have added nothing to it—taken nothing from it. Yet the reader will ask how a person who more than once "had all the appearance and feeling of being in a dying state" cotdd be so quickly restored to health by a single medicine after the trettntent of a skilful-and able physician had faded. To this question we are bound to furnish a reasonable and satisfactory reply.—These are not the days of magic or miracle.• The Creator works by means of his own laws and leaves to men to learn what they are by experiment and observa- tion. Mrs. Plowright's real malady was indigestien and dyspepsia, brought on, no doubt, by overwork, and, possibly, want of caution as to eating and sleep. fa this common, yet dangerous, disease, the stomach is 4 eon- stantly more or less inflated by a gas which is generated' by the decaying and fermenting food. This causes the ' stomach to press upon the heart, which lies just above-it, and so produces the irregular beating palpitation, step-- page, and faintness. The remedy used--Blother Seigeref Curative Syrup-- abrogated this alarming state of things by curing the real' disease from which it arose, indigestion, constipa- tion,.and dyspepsia. This case should serve as a warn.

ing ar,ainst the tendency to mistake symptoms for their cause: Mrs. Plowright was fortunatein baring usedtlar only existing remedi before her situation became even moreserious than it was at the time.

The deceased was pulling dOwn Some coal in.his working place when a piece of rock fell from the rocf.• It dropped an Lewis, who was knocked down. another miner (Royes) went to ,his assistance, and it was. found that he was badly crushed. He was taken up the shaft and; removed to his- home,..where he was attended by. Dr. Gaskell, but death, ensued shortly before oneo'cloclt next morning.—Akr inquest•on the body of the deceased was. held before lktr. Nr. T. Husband, deputy coroner, at the Vulcan Inn,..St. Helens Junction, on Monday:: after-.- Mr. Jackson,. certfficated manager of thomine... r represented the firm—Catherine Lew*,widow. gave ' evidence ofldentifination,. and said her-husband. did nce blame any ace for what had occurred.---James Mayes' . a ( drawer, sa:sl he worked with the deceased, and witnessed the accident. There were sufficient props and spnags about the place, and there was no fault to findl,with the management of the mine. —The Deputy, Coroner-remarked that he hald received a letter from Mr. Hall, the govern- ment inspector, stating that he had examined the-scene of the accident, and thund that the place- was well timbereck—The jury returned a verdict of "'Accidintal , death."

div.head: WARRINGTONIANS IN AMERICA.
div.p: WARRINGTONIANS IN AMERICA.
LETTERS FROM MR. JAMES WINSTANLEY.

We have been favoured by Mr. John Gandy, of Church-st., with the following extracts from letters sent to him by Mr. James Winstanley, who left Warrington about two years ago, and is now in Salem, Oregon, United States. On July 13th, Mr. Winetanley writes :—" I have just been thinking over the past a little. Two years ago to-day we were on the wild waves on the good ship 'Parisian,' spending our first Sunday on the sea, anxiously wondering where we should locate and in what kind of country. Well, here we are, with just as pretty a home as you ever did see, and in as fair a land as ever the sun shone on. I have also been taking stock, mentally of course, not like I you—weighing and pricing the stock. Well, I must say lam well satisfied with it all. I have been making another addition to our barn 36ft. by 131 t., two stories high, to put away a lot of hay. I guess I should be able to run you round with a spanking team if you were coming to see your old friend. We would make the dust fly along these roads. I am sure you would enjoy it. I have just had a walk round our oat field to look at the crops. 1 think we shall have quite as many as we had last year, but only half as much wheat. We cannot help it—we can only try and do better another year. lam sure you would have enjoyed the walk round, if only to eat the wild raspberries. They are far better than the cultivated red ones to my taste, and they make splendid jam:' On July 27th, Mr. Winstanley writes :—" My son John is growing finely. He is stout but not very tall ; he is very hearty and strong, and he goes swimming four or five times every week. Next Sunday he starts for the mountains to spend his vacation. He has been busy looking up all kinds of fishing tackle. I hope he will have a good time; he is a good boy and deserves it. Little Barry is grow- ing tall and thin, and he is very sunburnt through constant exposure. He runs barefooted to school all through the summer as do most of the boys and girls over here. He is having nearly three months. Poor boy he has no playmates, and has to amuse himself as best he can ; but now the fruit is ripe he goes in for a Tot of that. My nephew, who is living with us, is a fine youug fellow, and is 'ruddier than the cherry.' Our place is looking very nice ; we have hops and flowers growing round the porch, and we have some fine cactus flowering, besides a lot of other flowers, some as large as a dinner plate. I don't know their names; I know more about melons and squashes, I wish could give you some. We have some beauties, and they make a fine dish; after peas and beans these come as a very agreeable change. We shall have to-feed a lot to the cows after a while. You speak of your walks. My memory often carries ma over some of them with you at my side. We do not walk far here—we drive. I have bought a wild horse, and an having him broken in for me. I went to see him last night; he is a noble animal about sixteen hands high, but, how wild he is! He distemis his nostrils and snorts if you approach him. I shall have him home next week. What a difference! our old horse will let my little lad Harry do just what he likes- with her. He puts his arms round her neck, and rides about on her without the slightest fear; butt guess it will be a long time before he dared° that with our new one. lam still working at the foundry, pattern making. It is a nice shop, and not hard work.. On September 8, Mr. Winstaialey writes This is the first time I have misse& writing to you on Sunday since we arranged to write to, each other every two weeks_ And what a 9unday we had! I guess people in the good old town of Warrington would be horrified if they had seen us working away, thrashing the grain. I tell you I' kicked just as hard as I could against it, but it was no,use. The thrashing crews were breaking-. up and going to their homes, and the crew that had promised to thrash for me finished up about four miles from here, and it would not pay the boas to keep ,26, men and an engine to thrash my bit and that era farmer across the road. He had only about 410 bashels*and mine only ran about 320—just about half what it was last year. About half-past fomr in the morning the engine came stalling through the fenge we had Itaken down, and then the rush commenced to get ' through before dark. The sun sets about half-past six, and then it soon gets dark. I fixed a table out- side for the feeding baeiness, and I tell you it Ma treat to see threshers. feed. They breakfast soon after five in the morning, run until twelve,,arndthert until sundown. Long hours theset ' English har- vesters would require-a lunch, but they do-not stop for one here. The boa& thresher is paid by- the 'bus- hel, and he runs it through just as last as possible. Somebody stole two-sacks of oats whilst standing under the shed, but I will Int things-under-lock and key. I have already sold my wheatt—that is,. what I had to sell. I have- got about shay bushels for seed and other- purposes. Sixty-seven, cents is the price I got for it last year. I field it at tlie ware- house for six months, and eventually. had to, sell for five rents less-than I could have got at first„so this time I sold it straight off. I had a close shave-of losing all my took} last week. I only moved my chest from. the- sash and door factory a few weeks back, and last week the factory was burned clean out. The men got some of their tools out„but most of them, were- burned. I am glad L moved my chest out, as owing to the position it was in in the shoo it would most cer- tainly hays been burned. Last week we turned out at the foundry two electric cars,, the. first cars ever built at Salem, as the cars used by the Com- pany had all been brought from the, East. I built this car, and the car was photographed as well as I the shop group.. A gold medal was- struck in honour of the first Salem-built car,,and given to the. lady who first got seated in the can Allow me tn. tell you there was a slight scramble for places., About thirty ladies passed the starter, and he told i me he was dumbfounded at the way they went for the car. There were ladies of all ages and all sizes, so you may guess what a rustle there would be, and finally a young girt was the winner of the medal.. I made all the patterns for the ironwork, and SCAlle of the drawings for them, and I had the entire con- struction of the whole thing. I wish we had some more to build ; it would make things look better. My wife has plenty. to do with fruit drying and canning, and one thing and another keeps her con- stantly busy. /am happy to say we are all well.

div.head: : WM-MAKER OF MOSCOW
div.p: : WM-MAKER OF MOSCOW
OR, VALDIMIR THE MONK. BY SYLVA.NI7B COBB, ht.
CHAPTER I. /WE GUN-MAR AND THE MONK.

The time at which we open,our story is mid- winter, and towards the close of the seventeenth century. Russia had Passed through the long and bitter ordeal of national night. The Tartar yoke had been worn till the very bones of the nation were galled ; and when this was thrown off civil dissensions and insurrections commenced. The Poles and Swedes plundered the country, and amid general tumult and confusion some half dozen men were clamoring for the throne. At length a few patriotic citizens, pledging everything they held dear on earth to the souse of freedom from this curse of anarchy, and beaded by a noble prince and an humble, patriotic butcher, made a bolds'stand to save the country. Moscow was retaken. and Michael Romanoff was chosen Czar ;—and this il- lustrious family still occupies the Imperial throne. And no.vr the day of Russian greatness dawned; but the sun was not fairly up—and the broad light opened not upon the empire—until Peter came-to the throne, • •

In the department of the Skiboda—the suburbs. of Moscow—and very near therriver Moskwa, stoat an humble cot, the exterior bf which betrayed SP neatness of arrangement and show of taste that more than made up for its smallness of size. Nor was it so very small, in fact, but only in contrast ;' for near at hand abOut it stood many large, shabby, dirtyAlooking structures that overlooked the prim cot, as bleak mountains may look down upon a ver- dant hill. And within this cot was as neat as without. The two apartments in front, one of which was only used in winter, were furnished not only with neatness, but with a fair show of orna- ment and luxury.- Back of these were &large cook- ing and dining room, and two small bedrooms ; and back still from these was an artisaurs shop, and other out-buildings. This shop was 'devoted prin- cipally to the manufacture of fire-arras. Some swords, and other edged weapons, were raade here upon special application. • The gun-maker now stood by his forge. watching the white smoke as, it curled up towards the throat of the chimney. He was a young man,. not over three-and-tfrenty, and possessed a frame of more than ordinary symmetry and muscular development He was not large—not above the medium size— but a single glance at the swelling chest, the broad shoulders, and the sinewy ridges of the bare arms, told at once that he was master of great physical power. His features, were regular, yet strongly marked, and eminently handsome; his brow, which was full and high, was half covered by the-light brown curls that, waved over it; while his eyes, which were of a brightOorilliant, deep grayrineolor, lent a cast of genius to the intellect of , the- brow.. His name was RuricNevel. His father had been kit:, led in the then late war with the Turks,and the son, leaving his mother properly cared for,went 'bpain soon after the bereayement.. There he found work in the most noted armories-; and now, welilversed in the trade, he had returned to his native city to 'follow his calling, and support his mother. Near by stood a boy4=Pael Peepoff—a bright,. in- ' telligent lad, some fifteen years of age, who had ;bound himself to the gan.rmaker for the purpose of ,learning the art. His hair and his eyes were darker than his master's, and if he possessed not so-much :sound intellect, he certainly possessed an un- wonted degree of keen, quick wit, and unswerving integrity. The sun had been some time-below the horizon, and the only light of .amy consequence that made thingsuartially visible within the shop cams-from ,the duir blaze of the coals-on.the forge, as Paulever and anon bore down uporithe brake that moved the , bellow& Suddenly Rutin.- started back from the forge as his mind broke from, the deep reverisinto which he, had fallen, and having bade his boy to see ,that matters were properik disposed for the night, he turned towards the doer,:and was soon is the kitchen,where his mother-hack supper all prepared and so out

Mud%) Nevel was a noble • looking woman, inhe impress of a noble, generous soul can be called Such, ,andthelight of her still handsome countenance-was never brighter than when, gfusing upon lies dooy. Slre.had seen the snows ofififty winters, and if,they had left some silver upon her bead, and soms•age- usarkeupon her face, the sunshine of full as many summers had left her with a,thankful, loving :lE)art, ,and a prayerful, loving soul.. "It- is snowing again fasterthan ever," remarked Paul,.as he took his seat at the table. "AV' returned Rurieir resting his knife a few moments. while he bent his ear to listen to the-voice of the storm. "I had hoped 'twould snow no more for the, present. The. snow' iis deep enouglVnow. And how it blows !" 4 "Never mind," spoke the dame, in a trustffit easy tone, "-it must storm.when it; listeth, and we can only thank God that we have^shelter, and pray for those-who have none- ' "lemen !" responded Mirth-, fervently. , Afterthis the trio remained some minutes silent, seeming. to be busy in listening to the storm.notes that came pealing about the. cot. The wind was high, and the snow was now dashing upon the win- ' dows-with a dreary,melancholy sound. The meal 'was- at length eaten, and the table set bark, and shortly afterwards Paul retired-to his bed. it was hismont to retire early4.forbe rose early tn build the fires and prepare for the labours of the day. Rbriedrew his chair clOse Up to the fireplace, and loaning against the jambedte bowed his head and !pondered again. This bad' become a habit with him elate: Sometimes he would sit thus d'uring a wholshour without speaking, or even moving, and Ilia mother did not interrept him, as she supposed he might be solving some-meehanical problem that lliad' arisen to bother him. Rut these fits of thought' had become too frequent. too lengthy 4 and too moody, for such a conclusion, and the good woman was-forced to believe that they were caused by something more remote • than the business of the forge or the lathe. The youth now sat with his brow- resting upon his hand, and his eyes bent upon the hearth. For half an hour he had not moved, and his face wore an anxious, troubled look. Rurie, my son," spoke the mother at length, in, a lbw, kind 'sone, " what is it that occupies your• thoughts so much The young man started and turned his gaze upon- his mother: "Did you speak to me, my motherr he asked,' after having recalled his mind to things about him., "Yes," nay boy,:' she. said, " I did, speak to you. ;/ asked you what it was that, occupied you thoughts. "Oh—nothing--nothing," Rurie answered, after- some moments of 'hesitation. " Dwa.s only thinking, —that was all. "I know you' were thinking'-and I know that. was allot the tune; but of what; Rorie? Come— hide no secrets_froin your mother.. / have noticed'

" Tell me, my boy," she added, in o low, persuasive I tone, " What it in that dwells thus, upon your mind." Runic reached out and took his mother's hand; and having gazed for some moments into her face, he said : "Surely, my mother, I have nothing in my soul that I would hide from thee. If I have kept my thoughts to myself with unseeming silence, it has been because I feared you would laugh at me if I told you of them.' " Ah, no, my son," the mother replied, almost reprovingly; "nothing that could claim such deep and absorbing consideration from a mind like yours would move me to derisicn. Speak plainly and be sure of ray sympathy? A few moments more the youth gazed silently upon his mother, and then he answered : "All this thought has been of one person—of— Rosalind Valdai." Claudia Nevel started as she heard that name, and for the while,the color forsook her cheeks.

" Whab, my dear boy—what of her have yott thought?" she asked, tremulously. "What, but of one thing, could I think, my mother? You have seen her?" "Yes, Runic." "And you have marked the grace, ibe loveliness, the soul-given beauty of the noble girl ?" "I know she is beautiful, my son; and also that she is good—at least so .1 think.'' "Then what but love could move me with deep thought of her? 01r, my mother, I- do love her: I.love her with the whole strength of my heart and ' soTti." . • " Alas, my Ruric, she will never dare love thee.' "" You know not that," the youth quickl3r replied his eyes burning deeply, and his open brow flushing-, ", Did I not know she loved me be sure I vapid neverhave allowed my thoughts such range. We were children together, and even then we loved. Fate hae dealt differently by us in the years that, have passed since those childhood times;' but yet r am sure-that her love for me is not , changed, save as increasing age must change-all the emotions of our nature into deeper, stronger lights and' shades." . "But think, my boy; you, a mere artisan—she' the offspring of nobility- and the ward of a duke— a stern, cokli proud aristocrat, who looks upon our station onlyas harsh masters look upon their beasts Of burden. llfear you will find liftle else but nais-- ery in such a,oourse of thought." "At least, ray mother. I will see Rosalind ; and if She loves me us*Move her—and if she would accept my hand—" . • Hugh, my boy. Do not cherish such hopes. Why should she-mate with thee when the richest ,nobles of the land would kneel for her h and ?" , "Hold!" cried Rune, starting to his feet. his ,handsome face flashed and his bright eyes burning.; s"Speak not thus—at least, not now, I flatter not 'myself ; but I claim•a soul as pure, and a heart as noble, as any man- in the land. 34- mind is an• 'clear, my hopes as high.; my ambition as true to real greatness, and my will as firm, as any of them. Ifll?..osalind seeks the love of a true her.rt„ and the protection of stout arms and determined success, then I fear not to place myself by the side of any suitor in the land. The youth caught up the candle, and hastenedny the door. He opened it, but the-blast came roaring in, whirling a cloud of snow-into Bei— rie's face,-and extinguishing-the light at once:. - "Is there anyone here ? ' the gun-maker asked, • bowing his head and shielding his eyes from the driving snow with one hand. " Yesrieturned a voice from the Stygian,dark- ness. "In God's name let use in, or L shall perish." The youth found the thickly gloved hancl-,—gloved with the softest fur —and having led the invisible applicant into, the hall he closed the door, and then led the way to the kitchen. An soon as-the candle was relighted Runic turned audgazed uponthe-new- comer. It, was a monk—and habited something like one ef'tbe Black monks of St. Michael.. He was - of mediumsheight, and possessed a rotundity of per- son which-was comical to behold. • THE POPE AND THE TEXPORAL POWER., correspondent telegraphs from Rome—The Fel),e‘ has issued an encyclical to the Italian bishops, in whie" he. declares that the existing r6gime is a mere instru. moot (.1 Freemasonr3r, and is tending: to the unchristian" ixing of Italy. His Holiness enumerates the measurea hostile to the Church that have been passed during the last few years„ and advises the Italian people to guard scrupuamsly its religious faith. He adds that withouo 'religion a people declines morally, politically, and socially. He. then draivs attention to the growth of Socialist ideas in Italy which have been fostered by the war against religion, and enumerates the evils and Wile that have been caused to Italy by the conflict with the Vatican. The country has, he declares, been compelled to sustain serious economic burdens for the purpose of retaining Rome as the capital, and has in reture only drawn down upon it the enmity of the Catholic. world. The Pope then again insists upon the right of the PapaeY to the exclusive possession et Rome, which, he declares, canzaot be divided between two Powers. The encYclioll is, in some quarters, regarded as a reply to Signor Crispi a recent speech at Florence.

div.head: FLOODS IN SOUTH. AMERICA.
div.p: FLOODS IN SOUTH. AMERICA.

GREAT LOSS OD LIFE. Advices received at Queenstown last night from South ,America report that the river Orinoco, and its affluents . overflowed their banks on.the 16th and 17th ult„ c ausing terrible loss of life and property in the province of Apure. Twenty square miles of land were covered with water to a depth of 61 t. Fifty personswere drowned, 15,000 head of cattle were destroyed, and 200 houses swept away. On Ciudad Bolivar, 2,000 of the inhabitants are destitute. The loss is estimated at 2,000,000 dols. Tile Government is taking prompt measures to relieve the sufferers.

div.head: TERRIBLE DOMESTIC TRAGEDY.
div.p: TERRIBLE DOMESTIC TRAGEDY.

TRIPLE MURDER AND SUICIDE. BERLIN, Trmusnix.—Another terrible domestic:tragedy has occurred here. Hofmand :Gast, a retired -farmer, having mixed poison with some sweetmeats, gave them to his five children—three girls and two boys—varying in. age from two-and-a-half to thirteen years, and then ate some himself. When his wife came home .he found her husband, two of the ghils, and one boy -dead, and the-other children vomiting violently and ia great pain. TheAemnants of the sweetmeat have been saved for analysis. Gast was of respectable family, but had be- come seriously involved in debt.

div.head: PLUMSTEAD MURDER.
div.p: THE PLUMSTEAD MURDER.

Walter James Lyons, 20, dekrithed as a labourer, was -indicted at the Old Bailey, on Thursday, for the wilful murder of Quartermaster John Stuart, at Ptumstead. Prisoner pleaded not guilty. Mr. C. Mathews opened the case for the Crown, and briefly', reviewed the facts.— Edwin Phillimore, who lodged at the house ,cyf the pri- soner's mother, deposed that on the night of September 12th he was awakened by quarrelling,and hearcbprisoner say, "If you do not go out of the room, I will dash your brains out." A further altercation followed, and de- ceased said he was a soldier, and had been in battles,and could kill the prisoner at one blow. After the murder 'prisoner said what he saw between the deceasecland his mother drove him mad. The jury, after an absence of 25 minutes, found the prisoner guilty of manslaughter, but recommended him to mercy on account of his-youth. The announcement was received with cheers, and the Judge said if anyone interrupted in that way he would commit them to prison. He added that he would pass sentence net morning.

div.head: MR. MORLEY AT NEWCASTLE.
div.p: MR. MORLEY AT NEWCASTLE.

Speaking at a great Liberal meeting at Newcastle on 'Monday night, and replying to Mr. BaHour's speech, Mr. Morley said it was absolutely untrue that duricg the six months he was Chief Secretary for Irelandile was only in Ireland five days. The occasion of his last offioial Visit extended over five. days. As to Mr. Balfour's state- ment that the Liberll Government used resident magis- trates to try the Belfast rioters, he deferred reply until he had time to -inquire into the circumstances. He c iaimed that he had proposed a commission to inquire into the conduct of the police, which was more than Mr. .Balfour had done regarding Mitchelstown„ He denied Mr. Balfour's allegation that he was prejudiced against the police, contended that Mr. Balfour had blundered in his statements regarding the Tipperarytincident, justi- -fied his statement that Colonel Caddell said that the road was" nearly blocked" by reference to the letter which appeared in the newspapers, and adhered to his etatement that the police used excessive force. He de- clined to reply to Mr. Balfour's invitation to express an opinion as to the innocence or guilt of the prisoners un- til they had been tried before a judge and jury. Earl Oranville, who was one of the speakers at the meeting and at a luncheon during the day, strongly condemned the aspersions which Mr. Balfour had cast upon Mr.
Morley.

div.head: TIPPER&RY PROSECUTIONS.
div.p: THE TIPPER&RY PROSECUTIONS.

CONTEMPT OF COURT. The Crimes Act Court sat again on Saturday and on Monday Mr. Irwin and Mr. Shannon, R.M.'s, presided. Mr. Ronan, Q.C., and Mr. Hart prosecuted on behalf of the Crown. Mr, Redmond. M.P., and Mr. V. B. Dillon (solictor) appeared for the defence. Further evidence was given for the prosecution. At the sitting of the Crimes Act Court, at Tipperary on Tuesday morning, Mr. Redmond appealed to the Bench to use their influ- ence with the authorities to prevent the system of shadowing which had been adopted in reference to him- self and his clients. Mr. Irwin, the presiding magistrate, said the Bench had no power to take any steps in the matter, and they judicially refrained from giving an expression of opinion. Sergeant Hobson was further examined by Mr. Redmond. Thomas Butler, a tenant of Mr. Stafford O'Brien's next gave evidence. During the examination of this witness, there were several scenes in court, in the course of which the Bench again intimated that if the proceedings were continually interrupted in this manner, they would take extreme measures. Ulti- mately, Mr. Sheehy, M.P., was committed to Clonmel prison for one week for contempt of court. The case was further adjourned until Friday. SUMMONSES WITHDRAWN. Mr. V. B. Dillon, the solicitor engaged to defend a number of persons charged along with Mr. Harrison, M.P., in connection with the Tipperary riots, received formal notice from the Crown solicitor, on Wednesday, • that the summonses would not be proceeded with, but that ether proceedings would be instituted. Mr. Dillon, acknowledging the intimation, says he regards it as an admission by Mr. Balfour of the truth of his contention, that after the Chief Secretary's speech at Newcattle it would be impossible to obtain even the semblance of a fair trial before any two of his resident magistrates.

MR. GLADSTONE IN SCOT- LAND. - THE JOURNEY NORTH. -Jr. Gladstone left the neighbourhood of Liveneleol for Edinburgh, on Monday morning; beginning his railway journey from the Broad Green Station'of the Lendon and North-Western Railway, to which he drove in a closed carriage, amid a drizzling rain, from Conn Hey, the residence of his nephews. The scene at Broad Green Station was one of great animation and enthusiasm. A large contingent of Liverpool Liberals had previouply travelledfrom the Litne-st. terminus to Broad Green to wish Mr. Gladstone a good journey. They were joined by a large body of Broad Green residents and others. During the watt for the araival of the team by which Mr. Gladstone was to travel, two young eadies presented a. handsome bouquet to Mrs. Gladstone ;and Mr. E. Evans, jun., on behalf of the Liverpool Liberal Federal Council, and Mr. Lynskey, on behalf of the lhsh people of Liver- poet, expressed hopes thatlVlr. Gladstone's health would enable him to go successfully through the present Mid- lothian campaign, and that he might be spared to see a settlement of the drish question. Mr. Gladstone, in reply, acknowledged that to undertake a new campaign was a violent act it his time of life, but he felt it to be called fer by a duty to the public altogether great,specialeand-separate. Amid enthusiastic cheers the eight . hon. gentleman mad Mrs. Gladstone were concluded to a -saloon carriagaeand the cheering was renewed and-con- tinued till the trail steamed-wt.:if the station. :The arrival of the train was awaited at St. Helens station by a crowd of several hundreds of persons, who thronged the 'Liverpool and Wigan platform. Arrange- ments had been made by the ',leaders of the St. Helens Liberal Association to present an address to the eight honourable gentleman, mad the officers of the St. Relene Women's Literal Association decided to accord a-sinfilar testimony if esteem to Mrs. Gladstone. The addresses were on patehment in bookform. Whenthe train, which 'was received with cheers, had come to .a standstill, CouncilkeJohn Forster, wko was supported by the pro- minent members of the iLiberal party, handed to Mr, , Gladstone an address, which expressed the heartiest wishes for the success of the Midlothian campaign. It was signed on behalf ece the Associaeion by Thomas Cook, etesident ; John Forster, chairman of the Executive Committee; 'Henry Martin, honorary trea-1 surer; and John :P. Mearns, 'honorary secre- tary. -Mr. Gladstone, who seemed to appreciate ' the pementation of the address, said—Gentlemen, I ; thank you for your address. I hope youwill return Mr. Kennedy at the next election. He deserves to be sup- ported, and will be •tveyaluable addition to the Liberal partyrin the House cif Commons. (Cheers.)—The train was then moving omits way to Wigan, and Mrs. J. P. Meaxets, president -di the St. Helens Women's Liberal Asseciation, handed-to Mrs Gladstone au address on be- half of that Associate:tn.—Mrs. Gladstone had only time to say "I have much pleasure in receiving in" as the train left the etation amid the parting cheers of the crowd. At Wigan there was a stoppage of ten minutes, but the proceedings there 'were confined to a conversation at the carriage window -with Mr. Worthington, the Liberal leader, who expressed a preference;that Mr. Gladstone should reserve his -voice for the Midlothian campaign. At Preston similar consideration was-shown and Mr. Glad- stone was not &eked to speak. He thanked the local Liberals for that-evidence of their kindness and care for his health arid strength. At Lancaster, Carnforth, Oxen- Penrith, and Carlisle, Mr. Gladstone received cordial greetings, but made no speeches. Short stoppages were made at Lockerbie, Carstairsoand Mid-Calder, and addresses which were presented at the two places last named were briefly acknowledged. Edinburgh was reached at ten minutes past six. The gathering of the public at Princess-st. Station was very great, and the right hole gentleman was received by his host, Mr. J. B. Balfour (the Dean of Fecuftye, Mr. Arnold Morley. and Mr. Mar)eribanks. There was loud and continuous cheering from the crowds Who threnged the streets in the neighbourhood as Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone left the station for Mr. Balfouf's residence. SPEECH ON TRISH AFFAIRS. Mr. Gladstone addressed a greet Liberal meeting in the Corn Exchange, at Edinburgh, on Tuesday after- noon. The Earl of Rosebery presided, and there were about 5,000 persons present. Mr. Gladstone, who was received witheumultuous enthusiasm, commenced his remarks by indicating the 'course in which, during his present campaign, he should clealewith the various topics of greatest public interest. First he proposed to deal with the work of the present ParTrament, how, where; and why it has failed. Next he should refer to foreign affairs, and the question of public economy, and then to that of the difference between labour and capital. He should postpone for .some days dealing with Scottish' questions, until he had time to consider the various corn- mqnications he had received on the subject. The q ues- don , however, which overshadowed and anticipated and, absorbed into itself every other questice i of the present day was that of Ireland; and it must ct netinue to block the way until removed by an effectual settlement. Refer- ing next to the position of the Liberal party in 1886, he denied that the step which led to the se were defeat eus- teined in that year by the party was one for which they were greetly to blame. If the demand for Home Rule was a just and safe demand—an he maintained that it was—the acknowledgment of its justice and safety ought not to be postponed. The post- ponement of the just claims of Ireland had been the disgrace as well as the calamity of Great Britain ever since the commencement of the century. Until 1885, however, the demand had always been made by the minority only of the Irish representatives, and had . sometimes been made in alarming terms. But in 1885 eve-sixths of the representatives of Ireland detnatded Home Rule, and limited their definition in such a way as to satisfy every reasonable man. The magnitude and cruelty of the subject was such that he was not greatly surprised at, nor could he presumt to censure, that con- siderable fraction of the Liberal party which hesitated to vote at the election of 1886. Another cause of the defeat, however, was the way in which the electorate were hood- winked and deluded by the promises given by his oppo- nents. They denourmed coercion, promised local govern- ment, and repudiated the idea of making a large advance of British money for the purpose of buying out the Irish landlords. But coercion had been thesrst, the favourite, and the greatest measure of the Government, the promises of local government had Vanished into thin air, and dur- ing the present year they had had a proposal to advance £40,000,000 of British money to buy out the Irish land- lords and bring the tenantry of Ireland as debtors face to face with the British Government as creditors. He claimed that the improvement in the condition of Ireland was due not to " resolute" government, but to the inter- vention of Parliament on behalf of the Irish occupiers. The agricultural returns shoWed that inspite of coercion, I derelict farms had not ceased to be unlet, and large 'quantities of Irish land were going out of cultivation altogether. Referring at some length to the state lof affairs in Tipperary, Mr. Gladstone denounced the manner in which the law had been administered there, and denied the right of the police or of the magistrates to exclude the populace from a public court of law. He did not defend law-breaking, but contended that the acts of the administrators of the law had been such as to con- 'saute a continual provocation to breakers of the law, and it was perfectly wonderful that breaches of the law were not infinitely more frequent than they are., The Government itself was, in fact, the greatest master and most perfect pattern of illegality. The manner in which the practice of " shadowing" was carried on was placed beyond doubt or dispute by means of photography, an agency which had also been very useful in revealing the truth as to the shooting at Mitchelstown, and also in corroborating Mr. Morley's estimate of the crowd at Tip- perary. The behaviour of the police on the latter occa- sion was an instance of gross illegality. In another case, that of Father Kennedy, a priest, had recovered £lOO damages from the superior courts against a peliceman who forced his way into his house. Having alluded to the packing of juries, the speaker went on to deal with the appointment of Mr. Shannon to try Messrs. Dillon and O'Brien, maintaining that the case differed entirely from that of the Belfast riots, ju which Mr. Morley selected to try the rioters before the resident magistrates who had previously led the police against them. If such tricks and pranks were played in the wantonness of power on this side of the Channel, the people would soon find a way out of it. Having once again recounted the circumstances of the riot at Mitchels- town, which, he asserted, had evidently taken great hold on the public mind, and having mentioned further instances in which the police had interfered with public meetings, Mr. Gladstone censured the absenteeism of Mr. Balfour, attributing to it in no small measure the outrageous conduct of, his subordinates. Referring to the disparity between the numbers of police in Great Britain and in Ireland, he declared that in the latter country the police were maintained for the purpsse of collecting the rents of the landlords, whom he declared to have received relatively more for their land than the landlords of England and Scotland. Reverting once more to the question of elections, he said the Liberals had only won a seat here and there because there had only been an election here and there ; but when a genera election took place they would win seats here, there, and everywhere. In conclusion, Mr. Gladstone pointed to the advantages which followed in the lonian Islands, in Canada, and at the Cape, from entrusting the people with self-government, and appealed to his hearers to aid in removing the stain of our past relations with Ireland by a similar concession on a question with the satisfac- tory settlement of which the welfare and prosperity of the whole empire was bound up. (Cheers.) VISIT TO THE FORTH BRIDGE. Mr. Gladstone was on Wednesday no worse for the feat of endurance which was involved in his oratorical effort of Tuesday. At the Music Hall, on Tuesday night, Mr. Gladstone as an attraction rivalled Madame Patti.of whose auditors he was the of the most enthusiastic. The great orator and the great singer afterwards chatted together in Italian behind the platform. In the after- noon of Wednesday, Mrs. Gladstone was presented with an address from the Women's Liberal Association, but Mr. Gladstone, whose presence had been half expected, stayed away, and sent a genial letter. He hoped, how- ever, and believed, that the ladies would be formidable rivals in this happy competition. Mrs. Gladstone, who had a splendid reception, spoke on the text supplied by her husband, and gave her view of the methodsby which women might make themselves useful in theefiald of

div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 25, 1890.

Duting part of the fore" noo- "n, Mr.igedstone was engaged in conference with Mr.Ca mpbell-Bannerman, Mr. Childers, Mr. A. Morley, and Mr. E. Majoribanks, and in the afternoon, the weather having improved, he drove out to the worth Bridge. ' Accompanied by Mr. Gilmour Lord Resebery's secretary, he walked across the bridge. Every four minutes, it is calculi bid, a train rushes over the estuary. One of these now cam 3 up at a great speed. Mr. Gladstone squeezed himself against a girder. The structure moved perceptibly. Such an experience is somewhat hazardous, but Mr. Gladstone' seemed to enjoy it. His first exclamation related to the extraordinary stability of the bridge. Another train passed on the opposite side, and the passengers, catch- ing sight of the unmistakable figure before them, leaned out 'of the windows and cheered. On returning, Mr. Gladstone drove to Dalmeny, where Lady Rosebery is slowly recovering from her severe illness. Later he was ioinedThere by Mrs. Gladstone.
LOSS OF SEVEN LIVES.
Lloyd's agency says a cablegram from Buffalo, on Tuesday states that the steamer Annie Young, with merchandise, has been burned near Sarnia. Seven lives were lost.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Alder- man Harrison presided, and there were also present Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. J. Houghton, A. Jolley, Davies, Heaton, T. Jones, Gill, Owen, Dobson, Auk- land, Mather, Ratcliffe,'Turton, Dignum, Clarke, W. Houtpton,Balharry, Hood-Wright, Smith, Hibbert; T. G. Sntton (clerk), S. Sutton, (assistant clerk) C. H. Ward (Workhouse master), and H. M. Mines (superintendent of Padget° Schools). A KITCHEN RANGE. The House Committee recommended that the tender of H. Halliwell, of Bewsey-rd., for a kitchen range at ' £l9 be accepted.—Adopted. PADGATE SCHCOLS• The Schools Committee reported tnat the doctor testi- fied that the health of the children had never been better. There had been four applications for the post of assist- ant schoolmaster and two of them—Evans, of the Grammar School, Lymm, and Bailey, of the police office, Hednesford, near Stafford—Were requested to 'attend the next meeting of the Committee.—Mr. W. Hounirrox in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the number of children at the schools had now been reduced to 136. He was glad to say the decrease had been gradual but sure.—The minutes were adopted. INCREASES OF SALARIES. Notices had been given of motions to increase the salaries of the master of the workhouse by £l5, of the matron by £5, of Nurse Daniels by £2, and of the portress (Miss Curry) by £3. There was also an applica- tion for an increase of salary from Mr. Harbourne, the relieving officer of No. 1 district.—Mr. RA'TCLIFFE moved that the increases be made to the master and matron, and Mr. HEATON, in seconding this proposition, said the salaries after the increases would still be £lO less than they had paid to the previous master and matron.—The CLERK here read the application which had been sent in by the master and in which he referred to economies he had made, one of which was for gas, the bill for which used to be over £BO per annum but was now only £5O.— Mr. GILL moved, as an amendment, that the increases should not be granted. He did think they should have I had some reasons for the increases given by the mover and seconder of the motion for the increases but so far they had heard nothing. He could not see why they were bound to bring the master's salary up to that of his predecessor because the circumstances were not at all the same. In the present house he should think there were not much more than half the number of inmates there were when Mr. Mackey was there. If they kept that I before them they would see where the saving of gas came in—it should be saved when they had only half the number of gases going. Then , again, though Mr. Ward would be within £lO of what the previous master got he had also the assistance of a clerk who would cost the Union in salary and rations between £4O and £5O. There was now a reduced number of lunatics in the workhouse, and altogether he did not see any reasons why those increases should be made.—Mr. DOBSON seconded the amendment, and it was supported by Mr. W. Houurcrox. The latter gentleman remarked that be was one of the overseers of the Union and he knew the difficulties people had to pay their rates, There was now not nearly so much money in the out-townships as there was when Mr. Mackey's salary was fixed at £lBO. He thought that instead of fixing a time to consider applications for increases of salaries they should fix a time to consider what decreases should be made. (Laughter.)—Mr. T. JONES thought they had an excellent master and matron, and if they did not increase their salaries there was the danger of losing them. 'He supported the motion.—Mr. HEATON said he supported the increases on the ground that if they did not pay the man what he was worth he would leave them, and as it was they were constantly pay- ing for advertisements for new officers. —On being put' to the vote the motion for the increases of salary were carried by 11 votes to 7.—The proposed increases to nurse Daniels and Miss Curry were carried without opposition.—Mr. DonsoN proposed that the in- crease to Miss Curry should be £5 instead of £3, but it was stated that there could be no increase made on the amount given notice of —Mr. HARBOURNE, in his appli- cation, pointed out, that although he had been employed by the Board 15 years, that was the first time he had ever made any application for an increase of salary, al- though his duties had been considerably increased since the new Lunacy Act came into force.—lt was stated,by the CLERK, in answer to a question, that Mr.liarbourne s salary was £l5O a year.—Mr. FIEATON moved that Mr. Harbourne have an increase of £lO a year, and this was seconded by Mr. DAVIES.—Mr. W. HOUGHTON moved, as an amendment, that there be no increase, and Mr.FLOOO. WRIGHT seconded this.—Mr. T. Jon, Mr. Hibbert, and the Chairman supported the motion, while Mr. Owen spoke in favour of the amendment. On being put to the vote, there was a tie, 10 for the increase and 10 against, the Chairman giving the casting vote in favour of the increase. The relief cases were then taken.

div.head: AT WEST CALDER.
div.p: AT WEST CALDER.

Mr. Gladstone addressed his West Calder constituents on Thursday, meeting with a reception of the most enthusiastic kind. He commenced his speech with a reference to the great political fact of the day— the Liberal victory ia the Eccles Division. He said the Liberal party were blessed with a very good candidate indeed. But the Tories had a candidate of the most extraordinary personal influence, and any other man than Mr. Egerton would, he thought, have been defeated by four times the Liberal majority. Since the close of 1886 the Liberals had gained upon a balance of contested elections no fewer than 14 seats, and if they had gained this slumber on 96 elections, how many seats were:they likely to gain on 670 elections ? It would be impossible to make any calculation which would give them:less than asnajority of 80 or 90 seats in the new Parliament, andlor his part he thought the majority was much more likely to be increased than dimin- ished. He complained that their opponents called them Separatists. To invent names of that kind was a barbarising practice; it was contrary to fair play—was "striking below the belt." There was nobody endeavouring to repeal the Act of Uni3n. It was an enactment with everyone was bound to main- tain, and -whatever it was in its origin, the Liberal party proposed to retain it. One of the aspirations of the party was torepeal the Septennial Act, and thereby to increase the people's control over their representatives. The righthon. gentleman then proceeded to speak of the relations between capital and labour, and gave the working-class portion of his audience some earnest advice about the exercise of their growing power in the State. 'When they had become in one sense the political masters of the country they should "continue to be just:" As to the eight hours movement, he did not see his way even taconsider the question in regard to labour gener- ally. The matter was on a different footing with respect to miners, but he thought it right that he should preserve an opes mind on the subject. Until they got a strong, solid, end permanent demand from the miners as a class they were hardly in a condition to press the adoption of such a-measure in a peremptory way. He advised the ,wotking classes, however, not to depend for too much on Acts of Parliament.

div.head: NORTHWICH DrVISIONAL LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: NORTHWICH DrVISIONAL LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.

A-n eeting of the executive committee of this associa- I tion, including delegates from Runcorn Windford, Middlewich, and Northwich, was held at the Gladstone Club,' Northwich, on Saturday. Mr. H. Bratt, was in the chair, and amongst those present were Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., and Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P.—Mr. Hand- ley, the Liberal agent, in presenting a return of the Liberal registration results, said he sticuld like to point out that they had done a great deal of work this year in the division which did not appear on paper. A great deal had been done through the overseers. He did not mean to say that they had used the overseers wrongly at all. But they had obtained information beforehand which had been utilised by the overseers in making their lists. The following were the results of the work done at the revision court :—Ownership claims allowed, 81 Liberal, 27 Tory; occupier claims allowed, 183 Liberal, ,84 Tory ; lodger claims allowed, 86 Liberal, 103 Tory; ownership objections sustained, S Liberal, and 10 Tory; occupier objections sustained, 34 Liberal, 13 Tory: lodger objections sustained, 2 Liberal; total Liberal claims and objections sus- tained, 391, ditto Tory, 237. Deducting the latter -from,the former gives the result, 154 Liberal gains. The Chairman congratulated the members of the association on the result of the registration work and the evident growth of the Liberal numbers throughout the district. Various communications were considered with -reference to-new work. There was an offer of assistance from the -County Voters' Defence Association, who take up cases inWhich intimidation can be proved, with a view to securing the independence of the agricultural voter, but it-was considered that, generally speaking, the secrecy and security of the ballot were generally understood, and only in a few country districts was there a slight linger- ing fear.—The Scottish Home Rule Association sub- mitted for approval a resolution that no settlement of the Home Rule question would be satisfactory Unless on federal lines, and that purely Scottish business should be inanaged and controlled by a Scottish Legislature, sub- ordinate to the Imperial Parliament. The committee considered that Irish Home Rule must first be dealt with, and did not entertain the proposition.—The Bow and Bromley Radical Association forwarded a resolution that no Government or fnunicipal employe should be required tomork more than eight hours per day, or 48 hours per -week, or receive less than a standard rate of wages • but •-tlio-I,rneeting did not see its way to applying special legis- lation to Government employes.
