div.head: FASTEST AMERICAN PASSAGE.
div.p: FASTEST AMERICAN PASSAGE.
The White Star steamer Teutonic passed the Fastnet at 8.35 on Tuesday from New York, having made the passage in five days 19 hours, the fastest eastern pass- age on record.

div.head: MEETING OF PARLIAMENT.
div.p: MEETING OF PARLIAMENT.
The Press Association is authorized to state that it was definitely decided on Monday that Parliament should be summoned to meet on the day' fixed some time ago, namely, Tuesday, November 25th.

div.head: ALLEGATIONS AGAINST_ A_ WARRING-
div.p: ALLEGATIONS AGAINST_ A_ WARRING-
TON POLICEMAN.

MAGISTERIAL STRICTURES. Ann Wade, of Jones' Buildings, was chatged at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, with hav- ing been drunk and disorderly on the 7th inst. The case was adjourned from the previous week.—P.C. Cooper deposed that on the day in queston, he met the- defendant's husband at Towns-end, and from what was said to him he proceeded to Jones' Build- ings, and then found defendant lying on the sofa in the house. Immediately he (witnesa) entered, defen- dant sprang np and said Good evening, are you come for me. Witness replied "Na, not if you will be quiet." lie afterwards persuaded her not to be disorderly, and then left the house. Defendant followed him outside, and there( acted in a shocking manner, and used bad names towards her eldest daughter.—Witness accordingly reported defendant, A summons was taken out; and she wa-s charged with the offence last week, but the case was adjourned in order that he might produce :corroborative evidence. Defendant: Wa I lying down or sitting down when you came in 2—Wit- ness: Lying down.—Defendant: I was not. k Defen- dant :then stated that she noticed beer was taken into the house whilst the constable was inside, but this the officer dented.—Ann Wade, daughter of defendant, deposed that no intoxicants were carried to the house whilst the officer was there.—The Chief Constable: It was said last week that the constable remained in the house half-an-hour,and that aquantity of drink was dur- ing that period taken in.—Witness continuing, said her father and brother had drink after the policeman had gone:—The defendant was then proceeding to speak and denounce theconduct of her daughter, when the Mayor said, "I should think you are a terrible mother to live with."—The daughter further said that once her mother was very attentive and good, but since she had resided at Jones'-buildings she had neglected the house.; and in -answer to the Bench, stated that when her mother fol- lowed the policeman outside she stood at the back door, :but did not hear her mother use abusive language.—Mr. Hunt said that the statement-of defendant's'daughter to the effect that no drink was taken in the house whilst the officer was present, cleared him of that charge. Cooper met the defendant's husband, who complained about his wife's conduct at home ; but he (Mr. Hunt) did not see what business the constable had in the house. The woman could shout as hard as she liked so long as she threatened no one, and broke no bones.—ln answer to the Chief Constable, the policeman said the husband asked him to go into the house to speak to his wife.—Mr. Hunt: But you had no power to go in; there was no murder or violence of any sort going on.—Mr. Harrison: But he was authorised to go in by the husband, who was the master of the house. If the constable had been asked to go in by the woman there might have been some impropriety. —Mr. Hunt said in this ease the man was the constable of his own house.—Mr. Harrison: I really think the officer is blameless in the matter.—TheMayor : It is cer- tainly clear that there is no charge substantiated against him.—Defendant again interrupted, when the Mayor said: "I think you are capable of ill-using anybody myself," and added "you know people who use their tongues too freely often get to blows, and if you try to master your own tongue, you will find you will have more peace at home. This morning We have had a terrible job even to do you justice, simply because you would not give us any chance. We do not wish to injure you in theleast ; and we are exceedingly sorry to see a respectable woman like yourself broxight here. Mr. Hunt said if the husband had spoken to him about the affair he should have told him that he must manage his wife himself; and he would have refused to interfere and would not have allowed a constable to do so.— &Defendant : If I was drunk and disorderly, why did he policeman not take me away ? If I was a bad women my sister-in-law would not have me.—Mr. Harrison asked defendant why she objected to live with her daughter, to which she replied because her daughter was a bad girl to her, and this everybody knew.—Mr. Harrison said if she would set her daughter a better example and conduct herself in a proper manner she would be a better daughter to her.—Defendant was then discharged.

The United Labour Council of the port of London, on Tuesday, received the following telegram from Mel- bourne :—" Champion enemy. Australia struggling on, will win with your assistance. Will repay shortly. Murphy, Trades Ball, Melbourne."
THE ALLEGED NUNNERY REVELA- TIONS.

- The Berlin" Tagblatt " returns to the late revelations in connection with the Nunnery of the Boned Alive, declaring them to be true. It further asserts that the Solicitors-General at Naples on Saturday obtained an indictment against the priests who manage the convent.
THE CHARGE AGAINST MRS. MAUDE
YATES.

At the Old Bailey on Tuesday, Maud Yates, daughter- in-law of Mr. Edmund Yates, living apart from her hus- band, pleaded guilty to forging a cheque signed by Mr. Edmund Yates, which had been left blank, and which she filled up for £lOO. The charge was not pressed, and judgment was postponed.

div.head: 10,000 CASE.
div.p: THE 10,000 CASE.

Leslie Fraser Duncan, late editor of the "Matrimonial News," and the defendant in a recent sensational breach of promise case, resulting in a verdict for £IO,OOO for the plaintiff ,was charged at Bow-st., London, on Wednesday morning, with committing various offences under the Debtors Act. It was stated in the course of the proceed- ings that the two ladies alleged to have received the gifts of £6,000 appeared to be mythical. The case was ad- journed until the 29th inst., and it was stated on behalf of the Treasury that a more serious charge might be pre- ferred.

div.head: TRAGEDY AT CARDIFF.
div.p: TRAGEDY AT CARDIFF.

A terrible tragedy took place at Cardiff on Monday I evening at the private boarding-house in Chrisdan-St., kept by Anthony Roderick and his wife. A ledger named David Harsant, a Norfolk sailor, on coming home shortly before midnight was accused of improper conduct. He immediately drew a revolver and fired three shots, one entering Mrs. Roderick's body below the heart and another piercing her husband's groin. Both ran into the street, and other lodgers, despite Harsant's threats, came down and assisted them. Mrs. ,Roderick died within an hour, and her husband was removed to the hospital. Harsant ran off when the police appeared, but he was arrested with a revolver, which he had recharged, upon him. He was brought before the magistrates qn Tuesday, charged with the murder of Mrs. Roderick, and the attempted murder Of her h'usba.nd, and was formally remanded.

div.head: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

WEDNESDAY.—Before his llonour,'Judge Foulkes. CAUSE LlST.—This comprised three default sum- monses, two adjourned plaints, 149 original plaints, and 50 judgment summonses. CLAIM BY BREWERS.—Messrs. Greenall and Whitley claimed for £3 13s. Bd., balance of account for beer sup- plied to the defendant, T. Reid, of Manchester, who oc- cupied a bar at Newton races. Mr. R. W. H. Thomas, of St. Helens, appeared on behalf of the plaintiffs. The defendant produced some papers referring to an account for bottled beer, and tha Judge suggested an adjourn- ment of the case in order that the accounts might be looked into. RELEASE OF A BANSRUPT.—Mr. Forshaw (of the firm of Messrs. Percy Davies and Forshaw) again applied for the release from Kirkdale prison of John Campkin, bankrupt, late of Dutton Hall, Cheshire. He said the re- quired bond had now been filed, the £5 to meet expens- es had been paid, and certain preliminary questions had been answered. The bankrupt now wished to do every- thing he possibly could to assist the official receiver in the realiza.tion of his affairs. The Judge ordered that the bankrupt should have his discharge. REFUSING TO Qurr.—Joseph Smith, executor for the late William Litherland, made an application through Mr. Forshaw (of the firm of Messrs. Percy Davies and Forshaw), for the ISossesion of the house, 25, Dakin's Court, which was held by John Pritchard. Notice to quit, expiring on the 29th September, had been served. The defendant said his wife was a daughter of the late Mr. Litherland, and as he believed that should had some claim to the house, be wished to know what the condi- tions of the will were before he quitted. Mr. Forshaw produced the will which said that the proceeds of the property were to be devoted to the widow during her life ' and afterwards for the children to share equally. An order to give up possession was made. THE WINALLIE CASE.—The ease in connection with the Winallie Cycle Company which we alluded to last week as down for hearing had been settled out of court. Amu:ix AGAINST A FAllMElL—Jamesilaynes, former- ly a boot and shoe manufacturer, in Horsemarket-st., Warrington, sued John Warburton, lately a farmer at Dallam, for £8 is. Bd. for boots and shoes supplied and repaired. Mr. A. Browne represented the plaintiff, and Mr. Horridge, barrister, of Liverpool, was for the defence, James Haynes, son of the plaintiff, said the previous ac- count of £9 was paid in February, 1889, by Mr. Warbur- ton personally. At that time Mr. Warburton said nothing about discontinuing the credit or of his having assigned the farm, and all the effects to his wife. The goods and repairs continued to be supplied on the orders of the children or of the servants. Mr. Horridge said that at the end of 1887 the defendant transferred his, • farm to his wife, and she had a private income 9 CPCI a year. The defendant had orlemd the ke)ectg, aii he contended he was not liable for the bill amounting to £8 is. Bd.—Llis Honour held that the defendant was not liable, and gave judgreent for him, with costs. He did not see that therc_t was any implied authority on the part of the childre'a to pledge their father's credit. The evi- dence W9:4 that the wife had an apple income in her own riet , as wall as the management of the farm.

Police Cheshire THE Sub-committee appointed to Inquiry inquire into the charges a gularities in connection with the s Ito irre- administration of the Cheshire Police presented their Report to a quarterly meeting of the Joint Committee, which was' held at Chester Castl° On Saturday. It will be remembered that the inquirY had its origin in statements made by Ex-Inspec-
tor 0' vigoro quiry v that 0' The in and as will be allegat has be warran that C( ,should magist repres( for the it wou
eig gr Pri ga rei be all ti(
I

tor O'DONNELL whose cause MT. SLATER-LEWIS vigorously championed; but the scope of the in- quiry was considerably widened when it was decided that O'DoxNELL's case was, according to law, one •solely for the discretion of the Chief Constable. The investigation occupied eight public sittings, and as many as 67 witnesses were examined. It will be seen from the Report that some of the allegations have not been proved; but sufficient has been proved to justify the investigation, and Warrant the public in coming to the conclusion that County Police,as in the case of Borough Police, ,should be subject to the control—not of irresponsible magistrates, or even a Joint Committee, but of the representatives of the ratepayers who are taxed for their maintenance. According to the Report, it would seem that drunkenness and other irregu- larities did exist amongst the police at Runcorn, "but not in excess of the ordinary proportion of 'such irregularities." With regard to Superinten- dent HoLLniciwoarn it is remarked that "enough has been proved to satisfy us that he was, on more than one occasion, under the influence of drink," and it is intimated that it would have been better if the Runcorn police had been under the direction, during the last two years, of an officer more circumspect in his conduct." But it is in the use to which the police have been put as gamekeepers' assistants that the most interest attaches, and it is not too much to say that the evidence reveals a state of things which 'the ordinary citizen, who ,is neither a poacher nor a game preserver, will regard as scandalous. There have—to quote the words of the Report— been" distinct breaches of duty and disobedience of orders' on the part of police officers who have "gone out with or met keepers on various occasions on private land." It is not denied that on the night of the 24th September, 1889, the police of ' Runcorn were employed in poacher-hunting, at Norton, on the estate of Sir RICHARD BROOKE; or that "the town was deprived to a considerable ex- tent of its ordinary police protection during a large part of the night." It is held, however, that the mission was a legal one ; and, if this be so, it is high time that the law was altered, or that it was administered with greater regard to the interests of sleeping townsfolk. The lives of citizens are surely of more value than many heads of game. But the most suggestive portion of the Report is that the allegation is proved that "Constables in and about the district of Macclesfield did formerly if not now, receive gratuities for every conviction of poachers obtained by them in the police courts, from some fund believed to be established by game preservers in or about that district, some of whom were Justices of the Peace." 'Will these gentlemen continue to remain on the Commission of therPeace now that it has been disclosed that they have been party to a system, which, to quote the mild lan- guage of the Sub-committee is " objectionable and calculated to impede the due and equitable admin- istration of justice ?" That is a question which requires to be answered ; and. if need be, followed Up in the House of Commons. It transpires that it was a clergyman—the Rev. Dix, of Parkside, Who acted as Secretary to these game-preserving squires. He was their go-between in paying the police, and it would be interesting to know what and how he was paid himself for work which few clergymen, it is to be hoped, would undertake. The Chief Constable, it should be stated, is com- mended by the Sub-Committee for his ability and devotion to duty ; but the issue is one which affects the character of a system rather than its chief ad- ministrator—a distinction which will, we do not doubt, be duly taken into account when the Report is specially considered, as it will be, at the next meeting of the Joint Committee.

div.head: "TOUCH AND GO."
div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."
A new tale—" The Gunmaker of Moscow" is commenced in the "Examiner" in the present issue. Those who read it will give themselves a treat.

Mr. Balfour has tried a fall with Mr. Morley, and, as might be expected, he has come off second best. The member for Newcastle is always cautious and careful in his statement of facts; and, in addition to that, he speaks from personal obser- vation of what happened at Tipperary; while the Irish Secretary has to take his information second- hand from the police—who are offenders. He has been led by the nose once more, and remains a spectacle for gods and men.

Mr. Gladstone went through St. Helens, on Monday, instead of Warrington, on his way to Scotland; and the Liberals of St. Helens, using their opportunity, gave him an address and a most enthusiastic reception. He had a good word to say for Mr. Kennedy, the Liberal candidate; and it usually happens that when the Liberal leader recommends a candidate that candidate heads the poll. Mr. Gladstone, at eighty, is an example to men half his age; let the Liberals of St. Helens but follow that example, and victory is assured.

It is something new to have contests in the various wards of Warrington ; and it is a healthy sign. It is not good for a community when it grows stagnant, or when compromise upon com- promise deprives the electors of an opportunity of getting in touch with those who are called upon to represent or misrepresent them. Whatever may be the result of the elections, the borough will be all the better for the ventilation of local ques- tions.

Take for Example the nuisance of the Intercept- ing Depots; it is only during a municipal contest that the sufferers can get an attentive hearing. Their complaints, at other times, are treated as something which signifies nothing. Just now, however, they are receiving every attention, and as no candidate from the north-east or south-east wards has a ghost of a chance of being returned, unless he is pledged upon the subject, there is hope of measures being taken to remedy or remove what has hitherto proved a source of danger and discomfort to the inhabitants.

There was a tug of war at the General Purposes Committee, on Monday, on the question of the assignment of the contract for the winding and repair of the Warrington Corporation clocks. Mr. Alfred Woods, Conservative candidate for White- cross Ward, found that he must either give up the contract or remain disqualified for election. He +determined to assign the contract, and the ques- tion was whether the General Purposes Committee should assist his electioneering campaign by ac- cepting the assignment. It was a nice point, and it resulted in some nice discussion.

-- It is almost a matter of course to say that the question was made a party question. When the votes were taken, it was found that there were five Tories in favour of accepting the assignment, and five Liberals against that course. This is the year of casting votes, and the casting vote was given by the Mayor in favour of accepting the assignment. The issue has still to come before the Town Coun- cil ; and it might be carried further ; but, happily, the point will cease to be a point when Mr. Woods is defeated on the first of November.

Electors who are being wheedled with the cry of 4‘ no politics in municipal elections" will do well to remember that the Tories last year opposed Councillor F. A. Roberts and Councillor Platt, two of the most useful and esteemed members of the Warrington Town Council. It ought, too, to stimulate the Liberal workers in every ward to leave no stone unturned to achieve a victory. , Working-men will not forget that the Tories, at the last Couneil meeting, walked out of the Conu-

cil Chamber rather than consider a working-man's question introduced by a representative of working- men. Not one of the Tory candidates has expressed his disapproval of such mean tactics ; and thoy have no title therefore to the confidence of working-men.

Australian workers sent their thousands of pounds to assist the English dockers out on strike; and English workmen are about to return the compliment. On Thursday evening about 120 delegates to the London Trades Council met to consider a message that had been received from Australia asking for aid to the amount of £20,000 to carry on the strike there. After dig- mission, it was unanimously resolved to appeal to all the Trade Councils and Trade Unions of the United Kingdom to assist in raising the sum named. "Each for all and all for each" is now the motto of the toilers on both sides of the globe.

There has been a deal of cheering at Eccles since one o'clock on Thursday morning, and there is no doubt the place is regarded as cheerful—that is to say by Liberals, for the Tories have suddenly become as gloomy as the weather. It is hard on them that an Egerton should be sent to the right- about; but majorities must rule, and Mr. Roby, the Liberal candidate, is returned by a majority of 205. To this must be added 292—the Tory majority in 1886, and it will then be seen that the Liberal gain is 497. This, as " Mercutio" would say, "is not so deep as a well, nor so wide as a church-door, but 'tis enough."

The Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority are finding that there is something besides tanning refuse that has to do with the pollution of Keck- wick Brook. Dr. Carter Bell describes the sample of water sent him as "pretty strong sewage," and it is neeolless to say that he does not recommend it for cattle. It is hard on the farmers that they should have such water running through their land; and the Authority are quite right in trying to get at the cause of pollution with a view to stopping it. We pay, alas! a high price for " civil- isation," when our trout streams are converted into sewers.
LOCAL NEWS.

UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice. —J . & W. DUTTON'S Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt. SWING BOAT ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN. While in a swing boat on the fair ground, on Tuesday evening, a boy named George Rutter, became giddy and was thrown out into the yard of a house adjoining. He sustained serious injuries to the head and body, but is now progressing favourably. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W. DUTTON'S Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt. FATAL ACCIDENT AT WESTON WORKS. Adam Peacock, a boy 14 years of age,whose home was at 2, Duke-st.' died on Thursday from injuries received at the Weston Chemical Works, on the 15th inst. The deceased fell from a shed into the yard, and sustained severe injuries to the head, which terminated in his death. The Coroner will hold an inquest to-day. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt. SUCCESS OF A WIDNES TRADESMAN. Mr. William Crabtree, of Nottingham, formerly of Widnes, has been promoted from assistant inspector of Weights and Measures to Inspector with a salary of £l5O a year, and extras amounting to a further £BO. Mr. Crabtree had held the position of assistant for but a few months, and his rapid promotion has given much satis- faction to his Widnes friends. LAMPS, choice designs.—Garland's Lamp Shops, Earlestown and Warrington.—Advt. FIRE AT A WIDNES CHEMICAL WORKS. An alarming fire, fortunately without serious results, occurred at the Globe Chemical Works (Messrs. Scott and Company) on Tuesday. A lorry whilst being moved in the yard broke a pipe G.,nnectin,g two boilers containing sulphide of carbon, which caught lire, and as the efforts to extinguish the flames were fruitless, the explosive liqcid was turned into the sewers by means of an exhaust pipe. An hour or two afterwards a series of explosions occurred in the sewers,and in various places "manhole':," and the roadway in the vicinity,were blown up. The damage is not heavy. OAS FITTINOS.—GarIand, Gas Fitter, 51, Bridge-st., War- rlngton.—Advt. A VIOLENT SON AT WIDNES. Owen Tansey, a young man, was brought before the Widnes Bench on Thursday, charged with having been drunk and disorderly, and further with damaging his father's house in Minor-lane to the extent of 105. by breaking windows.—The father said the prisoner was a very violent character and he could do no good with him. He had offered to pay his passage abroad, but he had re- fused to go.—The prisoner said he could get no work or money, and he had been starving. He had been sleeping out for eleven days and could get no food. It was stated that the prisoner had been before the magistrates on 14 previous occasions for drunkenness, felony, and assaults on the police. He was now fined 10s. and costs for being drunk, and 10s. and costs for the damage, or in default a month's hard labour. EWBANK CARPET SWEEPERS,—J. S. Garland, Ironmonger, 61, Bridge-st., Warrington.—Advt. BREACH OF MARKET BYE LAWS AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Parker Wood, provision dealer, Liverpool, was summoned by the Run- corn Improvement Commissioners for selling certain marketable articles, to wit, ham and cheese, he not be- ing a licensed hawker, within the prescribed limits of the Commissioners' district, on the 4th inst. Mr. F. A. Lake, law clerk to the Board who prosecuted, said the defend- ant opened a stall in Church-st. near to the Working- men's Club and there sold ham, cheese and provisions. The stall was not connected with any dwelling house. The market had been provided at great expense to the ratepayers and it would be an injustice to allow rival markets to be established in various parts of the town to the injury of the ratepayers. Another disadvantage in regard to private markets was that there was no inspec- tion of meat, and it was quite possible that inferior and unwholesome meat might be sold. Mr. E. Wynne Humphreys, who defended, said the person from whom the defendant rented the land was a resident of the town, and the land was rated to the Commissioners ; therefore he did not think they could say there was any loss to the town. The defendant would give a guarantee that there should be no repetition of the offence, and Mr. Humphreys asked the Bench to treat the matter as a technical breach of the law. A fine of 103. and costs was imposed. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. &W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—.Advt. A YOUTH DROWNED AT CADISHEA.D. At 6.20 on Thursday morning a youth named Arthur Reed, residing in Chapel-:lane, Cadishead, fell into the River Mersey at Cadishead, where dredg- ing operations are going on, and was drowned before assistance could be rendered to him. Deceased was employed on the canal. EMIGIIITION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston, Philadelphia, San Francisco. Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zaland, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the " Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Guion, American, and other lines.— John Walker, agent, "Examiner ' Office, Bewsey-et.. Warrington.—Advt. DINING WITH THE LORD MAYOR, Over a thousand guests were present on Wednes- day night at the ball given at the Mansion House by the Lord Mayor and Lady Mayoress in honour of the provincial municipalities. The Lord Mayor's invitation was accepted by the Mayors and Mayor- esses of Manchester, Blackburn, Wigan, War- rington, and Southport. Miss Ellen Terry, Mr. Gordon Craig, Mr. Beerbohm Tree, and Mr. and Mrs. Bancroft were some of the most prominent repre- sentatives of the drama present. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. 6: W. DUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. CRUELTY TO HORSES AT RUNCORN. Thomas Pilkington, contractor, Warrington, was summoned to Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, to answer a charge of causing a horse to be worked whilst in an unfit state. John Ward was summcned for working the same. Mr. Arthur Brown defended Mr. Pilkington.—P.C. Fryer proved that the animal was unfit to work. Ward was fined 10s. and costs and the summons against Mr. Pilkington was dis- missed.—Mr. Pilkington was summoned with regard to another horse,and Thomas Rathbone was charged with working the animal. In this case the horse was also suffering from wounds, and Rathbone was fined 10. s. and costs. The summons against Mr. Pilkington was dismissed.—Alfred Carter and George Simpson, both of North wich, were respectively charged with causing to be worked a horse whilst in an unfit state. Simpson was fined 10s. 6d, and costs and Carter was dismissed. Mr. Carter and a man named Morton were also sumiticned in respect to another horse which was worked on the canal bank in an unfit condition. Morton was fined 10s. 6d. and costs and the case against Mr. Carter was dismissed. Now OPEN FOR THE SEISON.—Smart and Co.'s private , Writing and Commercial Academy for ladies and gentlemen, at the Literary Institution, George-at., Altrincham. Open on Tuesdays only from sto 9 pm. Writing : Gentlemen are taught a fine, bold, rapid business hand, and ladies an elegant and flowing style. Terms for complete course, One Guinea. Book-keeping : Pupils are taught how to open. keep, balance, andelose a complete set of books by double entry ; and our certificate for proficency is given to each pupil. Arithmetic and mental calculation taught practically. Shorthand, Pit- man's system. Pupils will ne received on Tuesday next, at any hour from sto 9 p.m. No classes, the instruction is indiVidlial. Card of terms and full particulars may be had at the Literary Institution, George-st., Altrincham. or post free from our Head Academy, 2, Dreuyn-st.. Market-st., Man- chester—Add,

VIOLENT ASSAULT AT THE PRESCOT WORNHOUSE. Joseph Kelly and James Lynch, rough-looking characters,of unsettled residence, were charged at the Prescot Police Court, on Tuesday, with disorderly conduct-, in the Union Workhouse; also with assault- ing the porter, William Williams, and further with talking spirituous liquor into the institution contrary to the byelaws.—Mr. S. IL Hartley, clerk to the guardians, prosecuted. Evidence in support of the charge having been given. the prisoners were each fined 10s. and costs for taking the spirits into the building ; for the drunkenness they were each committed to prison for 14 days, and for the assault they were committed for one month. A FIGHT AT A FOOTBALL MATCH. At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Messrs. A. R. Gladstone and F. Stapleton-Bretherton, Joseph Eaton, a labourer, was charged with commit- ting a breach of the peace on Saturday, the 4th inst. Constable Dyson gave evidence that on the date named there had been a football match between the Prescot and Whiston teams, and the defendant struck one of the Whiston players named Lyon. As they were leaving the field a great crowd gathered, and the defendant again struck Lyon, who then acted in his own defence. The defendant stated that there was some quarrelling on the football field, and as he was coming off the ground he was "pitched into," and he only defended himself. Woodward and Travis, two of the players with the Prescot team, gave Corroborative testimony, and the bench—re- marking that they were not quite convinced that the defendant struck the first blow—dismissed the case. UMBRELLAS Re-COVERED at the shortest notice.—J. .4: W. DUTTON'S Sankey-t.. Warrington.—Advt.

SAD COLLIERY FATALITY AT RAINFORD. On Saturday, Frederick Plant, 31 years of age, a collier, of School-brow, Rainford, met with his death under shocking circumstances, in Victoria Colliery, Rainford. 'He was at work down the No. 5 pit, and was assisted by a drawer named Thomas Kenyon. The two men had prepared the coal for blasting, and in the forenoon the fireman (Thomas Blackledge) fired the shot. Kenyon and the de- ceased then returned to the place. and a few minutes later some stones and dirt fell from the roof, and covered the deceased. Kenyon and Blackledge at once went to his assistance, and got his head and shoulders uncovered. The unfortunate man ex- claimed, "Oh, I'm done. The Lord have mercy upon me," and at that moment another heavy fall from the roof occurred. The other two men had a very narrow escape, but deceased was completely covered by a quantity of rubbish. Over an hour elapsed be- fore he•was again reached, and it was found that death had taken place. The body was removed to deceased's late home.

RUNCORN Ii,URAI; SANITARY AUTHORITY. The fortnightiv meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Present—Colonel Ashton (in the chair), Messrs. Mclntyre, Lewis, Heywood, Hewitt, P. Hall, Parr,J. Hall, Stokes, Yarwood, H. Linaker (clerk), H. G. Linaker (deputy clerk), and Dr. Adams (medical officer). THE SHIP CANAL AND SEWERAGE. At a meetingof the Ship Canal Company on the pre- vious day, a letter was read -from Messrs Urrundy, Ker- shaw, and Co.. solicitors to the Ship Canal Company, with regard to the sewers and sewer outfalls of the Authority. The letter, which was addressed to Messrs-. Linaker and Linaker, of Runcorn,solicitors to the Autho- rity, stated that the draft agreement submitted was so. long, and had so much detail in it, that it had given con- siderable trouble, and the solicitors were not yet in a position to return it. They would have to ask the Autho- rity to make the necessary arrangements with the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners for an extension F of their agreement with them of the Bth of January,lBBs, if they required one. It was not for the Canal Company to enter into any arrangement. We have not (the letter proceeded) got any agreement with the Runcorn Im- provement Commissioners to give you an extension, and we are not sufficiently acquainted with your require- ments to enable us to negotiate one.—After a long dis- cussion, it was resolved unanimously, on the motion of Mr.Brandreth, seconded by Mr.Aaron,that the Authority insist upon their rights of sewering into the Folly Brook being protected, and a separate outfall into the Mersey provided, and that until the agreement is com- pleted the Authority objects to any further interference with any of their sewers, and that if their requirements be not agreed to by the 3rd day of November next pro- ceedings must be instituted to prevent the Manchestor Ship Canal Company interfering with any sewers or sewer outfall. On the proposal of Mr. Aaron, seconded by Mr. Heywood, the minutes were passed. FEVER IN THE DISTRICT: INSANITARY PROPERTY. The Medical Officer reported two cases of scarlet fever at Colliers Row, Weston. The infection was derived from a visit to a brother-in-law in Church-st., Runcorn, where the disease had recently attacked the children. A case of scarlet fever had occurred at Stafford Villa, Wilderspool Appleton. A case of scarlet fever had occurred at the Rock, Frodsham. It was alleged the infection came from school, but this seemeddoubtful. A case of diptheria had occurred at Kingsley, and also at The Brow, Frodsham Bridge. In the latter case the back part of the premises were in a very filthy condition, sewerage lying about and soaking into the soft soil, bad smells are much complained of, arising from the grids, and coming into the houses. The whole drainage for these cottages requires relaying. A case of erysipelas was reported from Weston. A case of typhoid fever, reported from Runcorn, had occurred ot Mersey View, Halton Road, Runcorn. A case of typhoid fever had also occurred at a cottage near the Red Bull Inn, Kingsley. The patient, James Wilding, died on the 18th inst.—The water supply was from a running spout in the garden. The sewerage arrangement at the back of the premises are most defective: the sewerage from an adjacent cottage backs up and overflows into the house. There were bad smells and at times the back of the premises are simply muddy sewerage. This all re- quired immediate attention. A case of typhoid fever had occurred at Overton Cottage, where slight sanitary defects existed, which should be remedied. There had been two deaths from typhoid fever at Oveiton.—The customary orders had been given. The report was adopted. THE ALLEGED POLLUTION, OF EECHWICK DROOL Inspector Farrington reported that he had forwarded a sample of the water of the Preston Brook, taken from just above the. junction where the refuse is discharged from the tannery. The analyst (Dr. Carterßell) certified that the water contained total solids, 274 grains per gallon, chlorine 103, oxogen required to oxidise organic matter 230;. parts per million of free ammonia 1-0; of albuminoid ammonia -48. This water is what I should call pretty strong sewerage, and I certainly do not think sewage is fit for cattle to drink. In his letter to the Inspector the Analyst says: You ask me is No. 5 fit for cattle to drink. I have had some instances of cattle dying from drinking sewage water, and therefore I could not recommend any farmer to give hia cattle sewage water. (Laughter.) Mr. Mclntyre: It would appear that there is more than one source of pollution to Keckwick Brook.

div.head: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MRS.
div.p: DEATH AND FUNERAL OF MRS.

RAVE NSCROFT. Our readers will learn with regret of the death of Mrs. Elizabeth Ravenscroft, wife of Mr. Samuel Ravenscroft, sailmaker, Waterloo-road. The de- ceased lady who had attained the advanced age of 70 years, had been an invalid for several years and she bore her severe sufferings with a patience and resignation that was the admiration of her many friends, and aquaintances. he died on Sunday last, and her remains were interred in Run- corn cemetery on Wednesday afternoon. A highly respected member of the Wesleyan Society, many mem- bers of that religious body followed the deceased lady to the grave, and joined together in singing two of her favoulite hymns "Jesus lover of my soul," and " Rock of Ages." The burial service was conducted by the Rev. H. Burson, assisted by the Rev. J. Kendrew. In the funeral procession preceding the hearse walked the following gentlemen :—Rev. H. Burson, Rev. J. Ken- drew Mr. G. Millington, M. C. Littler, Mr. Jno. Davies, Mr. Le Couteur, Capt. A. Anderson, Capt. A. Millinger, Mr. J. Gregory, Mr. J. Unsworth, Mr. Lunt, Mr. W. Rowlands, Mr. Simister, Mr. Jos. Littler, Mr. Boot°, Mr. D. 13isbrown, Mr. Jno. Arrowsmith, Mr. Bottomley, Mr. R. Hampson, Mr. Molyneaux, Capt. Jno. Ellis, Capt. K. Janion, Mr. S. Taylor, Mr. J. W. Woodland, Mr. It. Norman, Mr. J. 9. Harrison,Mr. Jos. Williams, Mr. Cay- gill, Mr. F. Hayes, Mr. R. Morris, Mr. D. H. Jones. Then came the hearse escorted by the bearers, Messrs. E. Pritchard, T. Millings, F. Couth and F. Groome, employees of Mr. Ravenscroft. Bringing up the rear were the following mourners :—Mr. Samuel Ravenscroft, Mr. John Ravenscroft, Mr. A. Ravenscroft, Mr. S. Blair, Mr. E. Marston, Mr. Treacy, Mr. S. Smith, Master Geo. Treacy and Dr. Robinson. The coffin was made by Mrs. Cavgill and the funeral arrangements were carried out by Mr. R. Morris.

RUNCORN .BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday, Colonel Ashton presiding present :—Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. Mclntyre. Taylor, Lewis, Aaron, Heywood. Brandreth, J. W. Baguley, Parr, Yar wood, llewitt, P. Hall, Bretherton, Forster, Mounttleld, Harrison, J. Stokes, J. Hall, H. Linaker (clerk) and H. G. Linaker (deputy clerk.)

LUNATICPAUPERS. The Rey. J. W. A. Tanner reported that the Commit- tee appointed by the Board had visited the county asylum at Chester. There were 38 patients from Run - corn Union,at a cost per head per week of 6s sd, of which 45. per week was being repaid to the Guardians. Nine- teen were males, and nineteen females ; being a decrease of two from last year. FINANCE EXTRA FEES. Mr. Brandreth presented the report of the Finance Committee, who recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £96 lie 9d. The balance in the treasurers hands was £941 Is. 11d. There was one account from Dr. McDougall, for extras—a fractured leg £3, and in- strumental labour £2. The doctor signed that this was a case of instrumental labour and they ought to have some one besides the man who received the money to say that was the case. It seemed in this case the woman came into Runcorn and the relieving officer gave her an order and the doctor attended her, and she was away in a week afterwards with another man. (Laughter.) Mr. Stokes : And we have to pay £2 for it.—The Clerk said he did not see any remedy. The relieving officer gave an order to the Medical Officer, and he said it was an instrumental case.—Mr. Brandreth said they ought not to be so handy in giving these orders.—Mr. Lewis What could the relieving officer do if the woman was in labour.—Mr. Brandreth moved the adoption of the re- port. Mr. Heywood seconded; carried. POOR LAW CONFERENCE. The Chairman reported that Dr. Gastaldi, Mr. P. ' Speakman, Mr. Brandreth, and himself had attended the Poor Law Conference at Crewe. The speeches tended to show that indoor relief should be given in preference to outdoor relief, on the ground that it would have a ten- dency to save the rates, and that it would make poor people try to save for their old age.—Dr. Gastaldi said he did not agree with the extreme views propounded by the majority of those present at the conference who tried to prove that outdoor relief tended to increase the rates. He contended that the contrary would be the case.—Mr. Brandreth thought the Board could not have a better plan than that pursued—of taking each case on its merits. DR. MCDOUGALL AND PETER PATIENTS. Dr. Gastaldi presented the report of the Visiting Committee which stated that two cases of typhoid fever had been admitted into the House. One was sent from Runcorn on the previous day, and the Committee wished ' to know why the patient was sent from Runcorn in an ordinary carriage instead of the ambulance, a distance of seven miles.—The hospital was pretty well filled now and if fever cases were to be admitted from outside another nurse would be required.—The Master (Mr. Cunnah) said the order admitting the man whose name was Ashley, stated he was suffering from gastric fever. He Naas admitted at 4 o'clock in the afternoon and died that morning. He had received a letter from Dr. Robinson stating there was a hospital at Run- corn where these cases could be treated. He believed the fever wards at the Workhouse were only erected for cases arising within the House and if other fever cases were admitted they would have to provide a trained nurse.—The Clerk said the fever wards were intended for case tht might be brought into the House.—The Deputy Clerk said the Board had an arrange- ment with the Runcorn Commissioners by which pauper patients were admitted to the Runcorn Fever Hospital on payment of a guinea per week.—Mr. Ward, the re- lieving officer, was called in, and explained that he sent the man to the Workhouse according to the instructions of Dr. McDougall. The order stated he was suffering from gastritis ; if it had stated typhoid fever he should have sent for the ambulance.—Mr. Brandreth : Did you see the man ?—Mr. %Nord : Brandreth : You ought to have segn the man before you took the doctor's order.—Mr. Heywood: Surely he must take the doctor's order.—Mr. Ward : The doctor's certi- ficatc ought to be good enough.—The Chairman asked in cases of fever at Runcorn did he order them to the Runcorn Hospital or where.—Mr. Ward said he under- stood that there was some misunderstanding, or he should have sent fever patients to the hospital. Dr. McDougall said he was not paid to attend paupers at the hospital. —Mr. Taylor and the Clerk said they had not heard of any misunderstanding.--The Clerk said it was the first time he had heard that Dr. McDougall had refused to attend patients at the hospital. How could Dr. McDougall distinguish between a case in a cottage and a case sent to the hospital, where there was every re- quisite. If he was medical officer for the district he was the medical officer for whatever there was in that dis- trict.—Mr Mclntyre moved that the Clerk be instructed to ask the Local Government Board whether it was the duty of the medical officer to visit patients at the Run- corn Fever hospital.—Mr. Parr seconded.—Mr. Lewis said Dr. McDougall ought to be instructed not to send any more fever patients to the Workhouse.--The Clerk said they had never had a direct refusal from Dr. McDougall to attend fever cases at the hospital, and he suggested that he should write to the doctor before ap- pAying to the Local Government Board. This was agreed to, and the Chairman remarked that there was no blame attached to the relieving officer.

div.head: AN ALLEGED NUISANCE.
div.p: AN ALLEGED NUISANCE.

Mr. El. S. ChaTMIT-;;T-Min--s—t.:-irodsham, wrote complaining that a nuisance was caused by carts con- veying bones to M. Heywood's Bone Works, and he threatened that if the Authority did not take the matter up, he should be forced to take proceedings againt the Authority. The stench, he said, was enough to make any- one ill.-rlnspector Farrington said he had visited the works add seen the particular load of bones spoken of, and he could not Smell anything offensive. It was more like the smell of a butchers' shop than anything.—Mr. Parr said he had met many a load and he never found anything' objectionable.—Mr. Aerial said he should be ashamed to write such a letter. The bones in question were cows heads and had they been in any butch er's shop in England- the Authority would have found no fault with them. There was no more smell than there was in that room. (Laughter.) There were heaps of other bones in the works and there was no smell percep- tible from them. He had been in bone works in England, ' Scotland, Ireland and Wales, and he never was in one so sweet and free from smell and as clean as Mr. Heywood's. He thought the letter should be .on the table and the writer be treated with contempt. (Mr. Parr, hear, hear.) —Mr. P. Hall said the bones were sheeted up, and if other people would do the same, the inhabitants would be spared the sight of the bones.—Mr. Heywood said all , the manufacturers in the district did so.—Mr. Stokes, who had inspected the works, said there was nothing to complain of.—The Inspector was instructed to acknow- ledge the letter.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of Prescot Board of Guardians was held at the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday after- noon, when there were present Mr. J. W. Wareing (chairman), Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. J. W. Lolly, U. Davies, Peover, Leatherbarrow, Middlehurst, Syder, Birehall, Johnson, Tyrer, Ranson, Ellison, Kenwright, P. Longton, Borrows, Mercer, Stapleton-Bretherton, and S. 11. Hartley (clerk.) INMATES.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 497 inmates this week, 485 last week, 509 in the corres- ponding week last year,and 70 vagrants had been relieved against 66 last year. OFFICERS' RATIONS.—The Clerk said it would be neces- sary for some member to give notice of motion that the sum of 2s. 6d. per week be paid to each officer in lieu of certain rations. It was decided that the matter should be referred to the House Committee for the presentation of a report in accordance with a wish expressed by the Local Government Board last year that, they should" be furnished with the observations of the Guardians as to how the system worked, at the end of twelve months. WOOLTON SCHOOL ATTENDANCE OFFICER.—Mr. Marsh had given notice that he would move appointment of a School Attendance and Inquiry Officer for the Wootton district, but in his absence the matter was left over until the next meeting. THE WIDNES BELIEF DISTRICT.—Mr. Davies, in accord- ance with notice given, moved that an assistant relieving officer or clerk be appointed for the Widnes district. He said the Widnes Guardians were not bringing the matter forward in the interests of the relieving officer, Mr. Treacoy, but simply in the interests of the ratepayers. In 1881 the population of the Widnes district was 30,617 and it was now estimated at 37,000 or upwards. The rateable value was £210,099, and he thought that in popu- lation and rateable value the Widnes district was far above any other district in the Union.—The Rev. Dean Finegan seconded the motion,and said an assistant reliev- ing officer was necessary if the work was to be efficiently carried out.—Mr. Mercer said he thought it would be best to increase Mr. Treacey's salary by £2O per year and he could then provide his own assistant. He moved an amendment to that effect.—Mr. Kenwright seconded the amendment.—Eight voted for the amend- ment and eight against, and the Chairman gave his cast- ing vote against the amendment.—Mr. Leatherbarrow then moved another amendment that the matter be al- lowed to stand over for a month, and that in the mean- time a revision of the outdoor list of the Union be ar- ranged. Mr. Mercer seconded this amendment, which was carried. This was the principal business.

div.head: WESLEYAN BAZAAR AT WIDNES.
div.p: WESLEYAN BAZAAR AT WIDNES.

Albert-road Wesleyan Chapel having become too small for the requirements of the neighbourhood in which it is placed, the trustees and officials recently purchased a handsome and Commodious iron chapel capable of seating 400 persons at a cost of £4BO. The land required cost a further £2OO, and with the object of clearing off the debt thus incurred, a bazaar was held in Lacey-st. School, on Thursday afternoon. The various stalls were admirably Franged,and the room presented a bright and attractive appearance. The Rev. T. Law, the superintendent minister, opened the proceed- ings by giving a short history of the circuit, which he said had just attained its majority, and was never in a more prosperous condition than at present. With regard to Albert-road Chapel, they had received subscriptions amounting to £lOO. thus reducing the debt to £589. Mr. Samuel Melling, J.P., of Wigan, then de- livered a brief speech, and declared the bazaar open. The following ladies had charge of the stalls :—Mes- dames Meek, S. Robinson, Gallimore, J. Hughes, Hew- son, Salt, Law, Barrow, Beard, Bowyer, Duckworth, Crosier, Hartley, Timmins, Lock, Fairhurst, J. Flewitt, T. Hughes, Hollins, J. Ormroyde, Wise, Blinston, Randle, Oakes, S. Sadler, Spencer, Loimes, B. Thompson, G. Davies, A. Loimes, Peet, and Guy. Messrs. Pardoe, A.A. Kirkham, M. Taylor, A. J. Blinston, Bridge, Gallimore, and Hughes. During the evening a series of entertain- ments were given, and were patronised by large audi- ences. The phrenological examinations of Professor Davies,a local gentleman who has made a name through- out the country, were features of special interest.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Mr. G. L. Davies and Mr. G. L. Wigg. DRUNKENNESS.—SamueI Cox, Joseph Taylor, and Win. Corcoran, were each fined ss. and costs for this offence. OBSTRUCTION.—James 13ibby, a young man, was fined

2s. 6d. and costs for obstructing the footpath in Green- way-road. AN OLD OFFENDER.—Harriet Baxter was sentenced to a month's imprisonment in default of paying a fine of 40s. for being guilty of disorderly conduct. KLISPIUXANIA.—John Harvey, of Castle Northwich, pleaded guilty to stealing a box of drawing instruments from the taproom of the Clevedon Hotel, on Saturday, the 11th inst., the property of Mr. John Coxhill. The prisoner said he did not remember taking the instru- ments, and Mr. Coxh ill said the young man did not ap- pear to be responsible for his actions ; in fact,he appeared to be suffering from kleptomania. The prisoner was lbound over in his own recognizances of IS to come up for judgment when called upon. ' SCHOOL BOARD CASES.—A number of parents were sum- moned by the School Board for not sending their children regularly to school, and the usual fine of ss. was imposed in each case. TUESDAY.—Before Major Hazlehurst and Mr. G. L. Wigg. William Brockleby, a man of no settled abode, was charged with having on the previous day wiliully broken a glass panel in the door of the Barley Mow Hotel, Church-st. The prisoner entered the house and was about to perform a conjuring feat, when the landlord Alex Davidson ordered him out. The prisoner left, but shortly afterwards returned and deliberately smashed the panel with his fist. The damage was• £2 10s.—The prisoner went to goal for a month in default of paying a fine of 10s, and costs—£2lss. lid. DRUNK.—Esther Tucker, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for being drunk. WEDNESDAY.—Before Major Hazlehurst DRUNK.—Susannah Beans, was fined ;2s. 6d. and costs for being drunk. THURSDAY.—Before Major Hazleburst and Mr. H. Reynolds. DRUNR.—For this offence Edward Gardiner, John Wil- son, and Joseph Smith, were each fined ss. and costs. A PROFESSIONAL.—John Sutton, described as a profes- sional tramp, was sentenced to seven days' hard labour for begging.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. F. H. Gossage and Colonel Gaskell.

SLEEPING Om—For this offence, •ThDmas Spencer, John Morris. and Patrick Walsh were each sentenced to seven days' hard labour. TRANSFERS.—The license of the Arch Hotel was trans- ferred to Alfred Machin, and of the Market Hotel to Charles Goodwin. SCHOOL BOARD CASTS.—A number of parents were sum- moned by the School Board for not sending their chil- dren regularly to school, and the usual fine of ss. was imposed in each case. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—MichaeI Molloy, George Neville, John O'Brien, Jno. McFee, and William Macliff, were each charged with Iseina drunk, and fined ss. and costs. For a similar offence Sarah Jervis was fined 10s. and costs.—Mary Moran and Mary Treacy were bound over to be of good behaviour for three months for creat- ing a breach of the peace. FURIOUS Druviso.—Patrick Charles O'Connor, was convicted of furiously driving a horse in Birchfield-road, and he was fined 10s. and costs. FIREWORKS IN THE STREET.—For discharging fireworks in Terrace-road, John James and James Nityl•r, boys, were ordered to pay 7s. 6d. costs. DOG AT LARGE.—H fine of is. and costs was imposed upon William Brooks for permitting his dog .to be at large, unmuzzled.
A LIBERAL CANDIDATE FOR WIDNES.
SELECTION OF MR. H. WADE DEACON.

On Tuesday evening, a meeting of the Widnes District Liberal Council was held in the Lacey-street Schools, Widnes, with respect to Mr. Henry Wade Deacon's can- didature for the Division at the next election. Mr. E. Carey, chairman of the Widnes District Council, presided and there was a crowded attendance. Among those present were Alderman Muspratt, Major Wareing, Messrs. D. Wright, J. Reach, F. J. Poole, and J. Mor- rison. The Chairman said they were met together that evening as the Widnes District Council to consider the recommendation which had been for- warded to them by the executive council, that the dis- trict councils of the association should adopt Mr. Henry Wade Deacon as the Liberal candidate at the next Par- liamentary election (cheers). Mr. Deacon having de- livered an able address, Alderman E. K.Muspratt moved that Mr. Henry Wade Deacon be adopted as the Liberal candidate for the representation of Widnes at the next Parliamentary election. The motion was seconded by Major Wareing, and supported by Dr. O'Keefe, Messrs. D. Wright, F. Hartland, J. Parkhurst. F. Lawrenson, and G. Davies, and carried unanimously.

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN „AT RUNCORN, &c. BY AN "OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT." That the church mission conaucted at Runcorn during the past week,was attended with a consider- able amount of success, and those interested hope that much good seed has been sown. The Wesleyan missionary services are fixed for a week hence and are expected to be accompanied with more than customary success. The central figure will be the Rev. James Lewis, whose person- ality is gaining him a prominent position in the Wesleyan society. That Mr. If. Wade Deacon is now the accepted Liberal candidate for the Widnes Division, and the speech he delivered on Tuesday evening was such a one as might have been expected from his calm, critical and thoughtful mind. That it intensely pleased the large number of delegates present, who feel sure that with such a candidate there is a great chance of wresting the seat from the grasp of the Tories. That the question of the sewerage of Weston and Weston Point is likely to prove a stumbling block to the progress of the Ship Canal, unle-s tne Coin- panv concede the demands of the Rural Sanitary Authority and make the necessary ptovision as de- sired. That as the Company are disturbing present arrangements and absorbing the foreshore of the Mersey for several miles, they ought to be prepared to provide for the complete drainage of the locality. That the substitution of collars for muzzles has caused great satisfaction in Runcorn, and the dogs in the street appear to enjoy their new found free- dom.

div.head: CHESHIRE N. MIDLAND COUNTIES.
div.p: CHESHIRE N. MIDLAND COUNTIES.

Football teams representative of these counties met on the ground of the Runcorn club on Wednesday afternoon in the presence of about 2,000 spectators. The Cheshire players had the best of the game throughout, and in the first half Jones, after a capital run, obtained a try, Houghton failing at the place. Minor points were con- ceeded very freely, and at half time the score was Cheshire, one try, six minors, Midland Counties, nil. In the second half Crompton scored a try for Cheshire and the same player failed to convert. Subsequently Badger ' for the Midland made a fine run and scored, Evershed's attempt at goal failing. Towards the finish a clever display of passing ended in Jones scoring near the posts after a dodgy ran, and Crompton kicked a goal. Cheshire won by one goal two tries and eight minors, to one try and two minors. The teams were as follows : Cheshire: H. Houghton (Runcorn), ull back ; F. P. Jones (New Brighton), P. H. Crompton (Ransom), and Cookson (Sale), three-quarter backs; S. Abrams (Run- corn) and R. S. Thorpe (Sale), half backs ; T. W. Lock- wood, P. H. Lockwood (Birkenhead Park), W. Faulkner (captain). P. Riley, R. Dolan (Runcorn), R. P. Eskrigge (New Brighton) ; Dr. Smith, D. Schofield (Stockport), and R. Morton (Altrincham), forwards. Midland Coon. ties: J. F. Moores (Old Edwardians), full back ; Badger, W. l'. Nicol. and W. Auster (Old Edwardian), three- quarter backs; A. "Coventry " and C. H. Stone (Coventry), halfbacks; T. Evershed (captain) and I. R. Degkin (Burton), NV. A. Marvies, W. D. Lidlow, J. Long (Old Edwardians), W. N. Mayne (Moseley), R. McAlpine, W. H. Sturgess (Leiester), A. Bennett (Staf- ford-on-Avon, forwards. Mr. A. N. Hornby was the referee. After the match the teams and several mem- bers of the County Committee, including Mr. Thorpe, the president, sat down to dinner at Wilson's Hotel and the style and quality of the catering of Mr. Cooper, the proprietor, gave great satisfaction.

div.head: KINGSLEY.
div.p: KINGSLEY.

TYPHOID FEVER.-4 case of reported typhoid fever has just had a fatal termination here. The deceased, a youth named James Wilding, aged 17, was taken ill some five weeks ago with what was at first thought a bad cold, but shortly a fter decided symptoms of the Malignant nature of the complaint became apparent, and in spite of all medical aid the condition of the patient grew rapidly worse until Saturday, the 17th inst., when death took

place. INQUEST.—On Monday an inquest was opened at Shaw's Inn, Kingsley, touching the death of Thomas Frodsham, labourer, aged 69 years, who was found dead in bed on Friday morning. From the evidence brought forward it seems that the deceased up to the time of his death had been in good health, and on the Thursday evening previous went to bed at his accustomed hour, but in the morning, as before stated, he was found lying on his side in bed quite dead. The Coroner expressed his belief that death had resulted from natural causes, arising from some organic disease of the heart. A ver- dict in accordance was returned.
