div.head: WARIUNCir' TON.
div.p: WARIUNCir' TON.

THE CATHOLIC BALL. There was a large attendance at the annual Catho- lic tea party and ball which was held in the Public Hall en Monday evening. The gathering was, taken altogether, a great success. Mr. Percy Randall's band was in attendance at the ball, and played an - .

div.head: admirable selection of dance music. _
div.p: admirable selection of dance music. _

- - - ST. PATJL'S HARVEST FESTIVAL. This harvest festival services were continued on Sunday, when there were large congregations, especially in the evening. The preacher in the morning was the Rev. Canon Penrhyn. rector of Winwick, and in the evening the Rev. G. D. Wray, vicar of Halton. An anthem was creditably sung at each service as well as harvest hymns.

WARRINGTON HARRIERS. The weekly run of the above mentioned harriers took place on Saturday afternoon, 16 members turn- ing out for a capital run, which comprised a dis- tance of eight miles. The route lay to Winwick by way.of Lovely-lane, and after reaching the church the return journey was made by way of Orford. J. Massey was first home, being closely pursued by 11. Smith, jun., Jefferson being third, whilst the re- mainder were close up. Messrs. T. Walsh and A. Podmore acted as hares, T. Allen as pace, and J. Water worth (captain) as whip. WESLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. The weekly meeting in connection with the above society was held in the schoolroom, Bold-st., on Monday evening, under the presidency of the Rev. Thomas Ross. There was an unusually large attendance of members to hear a lecture on "The Study of History," by the Rev. Alfred Freeman. The rev, gentleman treated his subject in a very in- teresting and instructive manner, and was accorded a hearty vote of thanks. Messrs. John Gandy, Sleigh, Horton, and the Chairman also spoke on the subject, an enjoyable meeting terminating with the Benediction.

EMMANUEL CHITRCH MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. At the weekly meeting of this society, on Monday a paper was read by Mr. 11. Gandy on " The Chris- tian's relation to social progress." The essayist re- garded true socialism as man working with man for the common good ; and the true relationship of the Christian to the world as the servant of Christ
and the brother of man. Therefore, whatever way the social revolutions through which we are passing affect our fellowmen injuriously, we are hound as Christians to face the evil and try to remedy it.

WYCLIFFE YOUNG PEOPLE' SOCIETY. The usual weekly meeting of this society was held on Monday evening, when a large number of members assembled to hear a paper by Miss llulme on " Woman's Influence." The essayist was warmly applauded upon its conclusion. A very interesting discussion afterwards took place, in which the Mises Brown, Wallington, Atherton, Smith, and Dick, and the chairman (Rev. J. Yonge), Messrs. Hordon, Wyllie, Jeffery, Beswick, Podmore, G. H. Yonge, and Lowe took part. Votes of thanks to the essayist and the Chairman followed. The meeting closed by the singing of the Doxology.

THE CHILDREN'S DAY. Sunday being what is generally known through- out English Methodism as "The Children's Day," special sermons were preached in the Bold-st. Wesleyan Chapel. The Rev. Alfred Freeman preached in the morning, and gave an earnest address. The Rev. Thomas Ross occupied the pul- pit in the evening. when he delivered a special ser- mon on "The Crises of Life," hounding his discourse upon the text "Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth." In the afternoon a special ser- vice lvvas held in the school, conducted by the Rev. Thomas Ross. A number of addresses were delivered by the teachers and others.

ANOTHER FIRE.—DESTRUCTION OF FOWLS AND PIGEONS. About midnight on Sunday a fire broke out in a I stable at the rear of the Crown Inn, Queen-st. kept by Mr. Alexander Baird. The Superintendent of the Fire Brigade (Mr. Frank Turner) and a number of firemen were soon on the spot, and having attached the hose to the hydrant they commenced to play on the burning building, with the result that the flames were extinguished in good time. In addition to the damage done to the stable, some 70 to 80 fowls and a number of pigeons were burned. Fortunately, a horse which had been kept in the stable had recently been removed. The property is not insured.

COCKHEDGE MISSION CONCERTS. On Saturday evening another concert was held in Uockhedge Mission. There was again a large atten- dance, and a very pleasant evening was spent. The proceedings were opened with an address by Mr. B. Farrar, who took the chair. The following pro- gramme was afterwards rendered :—Violin solo, Mr. P. Taylor ; recitation, Mr. B. Farrar: comic song, Mr. T. Pilling ; song, Mr. 11. Bennett ; piano duet, Misses Sykes; song, Mr. G. Barnes ; song, Miss His- lop ; song, Miss M. E. Gallop; song, Mr. Johnson ; clarionet solo, Mr. A. Adcroft ; recitation, Mr. Wm. Wright ; sow; Mr. G. Barnes ; song, Miss Hislop ; reading, Mr. song, Farrar; comic song, Mr. Pilling; violin solo, Mr. P. Taylor. Mr. William Jackson was the conductor. CO-oPERATIvE SOCIETY QUARTERLY MEETING. A quarterly meeting of the members of the War- rington Co-operative Society was held in the Co- operative Hall, Sankey-st., on Monday evening. The president (Mr. T. Birchall) occupied the chair, and there was a moderate attendance. The balance sheet, which was adopted, showed that the sales for the last quarter were £18,364 ss. 6d.. viz : Sankey-st. grocery department, £10,397 13s, 3d.; boots and shoes, £534155. ; drapery, £1,23765.; Winwick-st. grocery department, .£5,571 14s. 9d. ; drapery, £6:12 16s. 6d. It was proposed that a dividend of of 3s 11 should be paid on members, and this was adopted. A suggestion having been made that a gratuity should be made the members of the Committee, after some discussion a resolution was carried that £BO should be handed to the eight members of the Committee for distribution amongst themselves. This was all the busineas before the meeting. WORKINGMEN'S SATURDAY EVENING CONCERT. The Committee which promotes these concerts commenced their season's work on Saturday night under the most favourable auspices. It was ap- parent that the impression made on the public , mind last season had not died away, for long before the time announced for commencing all the seats in the Buttermarket-st. School were occupied, and additional ones had to be sought. An excellent pro- gramme was provided, the chair being taken by his Worship the Mayor (Mr. R. W. Francomb). The following took part :—Duet, Miss Clara Hedgcock and Mr. J. Horton: recitation, Mr. Lawrence Gem- son, of Liverpool ; song, "The Midshidmite," Mr. C. 11. Kerry ; violin solo, "Oh, how delightful," Miss Florence Iledgcock ; reading, "King Bolmer and Elsie," by Miss Bessie Dutton ; song, " Twickenham Ferry," Miss Clara Hodgcock ,• recitation, Mr. Lawrence Gemson ; song, " Daddy," Miss K"ITV cornet solo, Mr. Thomas Lane; song," From rock to rock," Mr. C. H. Kerry; reading. " Mrs. Poyser has her say out," Miss Bessie Dutton ; song, "The Miller and the Maid," Miss C. Hedgcock ; accompanist, Miss Etty Toft. The whole of the pieces were ren- dered in an excellent manner encores being de- manded in most cases. A vote of thanks to the Chairman and all who had assisted proposed, by Mr. Stringer and seconded by Mr. Nicholson, brought a very enjoyable evening to a close. FRIENDLY SOCIETIES CHURCH PARADE. A meeting of the district officers of the various Friendly Societies in Warrington assembled at the Roebuck Inn, Bridge-street, on Friday evening, at 8.0. p.m. The following societies were represented by those members whose names are attached : Independent Order of Oddfellows, Manchester, Unity.—C. ilorrabin, G.M. ; Gilbert Riley, D.G.M. ; John Emson, G.S. Warrington District Society of Druids.—Thomas Eden, D.G.31.; James Sinicock, D.D.G.31. ; Thomas Roberts, D.C.S. 'Ancient Order of Foresters.—J. Chrimes, C.R. ; William Lightfoot, C.R,; Llewellyn Davies, D.S. Ancient Order of Shepherds, Ashton Unity.—Samuell Dunn, P.C.S. ; Peter Kirkham, D.P.C.S. ; Abel Henry Mather, Pro. I Cor, secretary. Grand United Order of Otidfellows,_ !M. Massey, D.G.M. ;J. Callon, D.D.G.M. National Independent Order of Oddfellows.-11. Rathmill, G.M.; J. Bramhall, D.G.M. The following were appointed officers: president, Mr. John Emson ; vice-president, Mr. Samuel Dunn, and secretary, Mr. Thomas Roberts. It was resolved that there be a church parade of the members of the various friendly societies on the third Sunday in November, viz., the 16th, and that the members assemble in the Bank Park at two o'clock, to form the procession. Also that they accept the services of the Volunteer Band for the occasion, and that the officers of the various friendly societies head the p.ocession and wear the regalia of their office, and that the pro- cession be formed of members without any distinc- tion as to society to which they may belong. The officers are to form the Committee to make the necessary arrangements, and to wait upon the Rector, Mayor, &c.
COMIING EVENTS.

To-morrow (Sunday) evening, the Rev. John Yonge will preach a sermon in Wycliffe Church on, "Woman's work for the world, as suggested by the life of the late Mrs. Booth, of the Salvation Army." The Rev. J. Warnock. MA., BD., will preach to- morrow evening in St. John's PresVterian Church on "The Mountain and the Sea, or the Two voices of Liberty."

div.head: 11017 NT SCHOOL.
div.p: 11017 NT SCHOOL.

Yesterday, Miss Slater, who has been connected with this school, for five years, was presented with a dressing case as a token of esteem. Miss Slater shortly leaves Warrington for Liverpool, where she has secured an appointment at the Park Hill Higher Grade School.

div.head: TRIDIC UNIONISM.
div.p: TRIDIC UNIONISM.

In connection with the National Union of Gas Workers and General Labourers of Great Britain and Ireland, a public meeting was held in the League Hall last night, when Mr. P. Connor (of Manchester), delivered an address on "Trade Unionism." There was only a moderate attendance. TREAT TO RAGGED CHILDREN.

On Saturday afternoon, the Rector and Mrs. Willis entertained a large number of ragged chil- dren of the town to an excellent tea:in the Drill Hall. Afterwards a magic lantern exhibition was given and much enjoyed by the children, who, as they lett, gave three cheers for Mr. and Mrs. Willis for their kindness.

div.head: BREARING INTO A. CHAPIM.
div.p: BREARING INTO A. CHAPIM.

We understand that some night in the early part of the week some person or persons broke into the Baptist Chapel, Wash-lane, Latchford, and carried off some money and a bottle of sacramental wine. Fortunately there was not much money left in the place. The police, are, of course, using every en- deavour to find the culprits.

div.head: PRESENTATION TO A WORKMAN.
div.p: PRESENTATION TO A WORKMAN.

Mr. John Worley, for many years hoop roller at Bewsey Forge, haying recently left the works a number of his fellow workmen presented him on Saturday, at the Eagle and Child Inn, with a valu- able pipe, cigar holder, silver match box, and a tobacco pouch. A very enjoyable evening was sp,nt, songs and recitations being given with good effect.

div.head: BRICK-ST., ScHoomoom.
div.p: BRICK-ST., ScHoomoom.

A fruit banquet and entertainment was given on Monday in the above schoolroom under the chair- manship of Mr. James Gandy. The following ladies and gentlemen took part in the programme ;—Miss M. Sherlock, Mr. N. Cook, Mr. IV. Wright, and Mr. Walter Bellian ; pianists, Messrs. J. Critchley and W. Woods. The entertainment was brought to a close by an amusing dialogue entitled " Mixem's matrimonial* mart," in which the following took part: Miss A. J. Barton, Miss A. Warburton, Mr. C. Furness, B.Warburton, R. llazeldine, and W. Barton. FARM STEA.DING FIRE AT WINWICK. At four o'clock on Thursday afternoon, a fire was observed in the stack yard of Mr. Gilbert Marsh, Rough Rouse Farm, Winwick. When the fire brigade arrived the fire had taken hold of three bays and one stack of hay and a bay of oats. It was at once seen that these were doomed, and the attention of the firemen was directed towards saving the adjoining row of stacks. The stacks continued to burn through- out the night, a number of firemen remaining to pre- yent the flames from spreading. The loss, which is considerable, is fully covered by insurance. The cause of the fire is unknown.

REV. G. S. REANRY AT Sr. PAUL'S CHURCH. Last evening the last of the harvest festival services was held. The church was packed from end to end, the principal cause for this undoubtedly being the presence of the Rev. G. S. Bewley, formerly minister of the Wycliffe Congregational church. The service throughout was very hearty; and an anthem was effectively rendered by the choir. The Rev. G. S. Reaney preached the sermon basing his remarks on the 35th verse, 4th chapter of St. John. Ile briefly referred to his present work in Warring- ton as showing that all classes of people had hearts .to be reached. He also touched on his recent work in the East of London. At the conclusion of the service a collection was made in aid of the Renova- tion Fund.

ST. PAUL'S MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY. The annual conversazione in connection with St. Paul's Mutual Improvement Society was held in the Girls' School, Heath-side, on Mon- day evening, among those present being the vicar of the parish (the Rev. S. Wilkinson), who is also president of the society; Mrs. Wilkinson, the Rev. T. Emmott, curate; Mr. Alfred Jolley, vice- president; and Mr. James Knowles, the secretary, who has done much to promote the interests of the society. After a short speech from the Vicar, danc- ing was indulged in to the music supplied by Miss Sykes and Mr. John Parkinson. Songs were also rendered, and during the evening refreshments, consisting of tea, coffee, &c., were partaken of; and an enjoyable evening was brought to a close about eleven o'clock. WORKINGMEN'S TOTAL ABSTINENCE MISSIONS. The weekly meetings in connection with the above mission were held on the enclosed ground, off Bewsey-st., on Sunday. The afternoon meeting was conducted by Mr. T. Frain, who was supported by Messrs. W. Davis (Manchester), G. Hunter (Leigh), and J. Drury, who gave very interesting addresses. ' Another meeting was held in the evening, when Mr. T. Frain again presided, and Messrs. J. Drury, J. O'Reilly, J. Price, and W. Davis (Manchester) gave addresses on the evils of intemperance. There was a meeting in the evening at the Ragged School, Bewsey-st., Mr. P. Storey in the chair, when ad- dresses were given by Messrs. W. Roberts, J. Price, and C. H. Mills. Mrs. Sheath sang a sacred solo; Several persons took the total abstinence pledge There was a large attendance at each meeting.

ARRINGToN AND DISTRICT TRICHBRS' ASSOCIATION. A meeting of the above association was held on last evening week. There was a good attendance. Several new members were elected. Amongst other teachers present were Messrs. Wallace (presi- dent), Jordan, Glover, Singleton, and Stansfield (secretary), Misses Burrows, Finney,Rigby, Bz,c. The chief business before the meeting was that relating to school attendance. Particulars regarding the at- tendance at the elementary schools in the associa- tion's district were required by the Executive of the National Union of Teachers, and the secretary was ordered to obtain and forward these particulars to the general secretary of the Union. The associa- tion also suggested various ways of improving the attendance in elementary schools. A letter was read from Mr. Heller (general secretary of the N.U.T.) promising to address the teachers of Warrington and district some time in November. As Mr. Heller is so widely known amongst teachers, a very large attendance is expected.- Messrs. Wallace and Stans- field were deputed to make all necessary arrange- ments for the visit. ODDERLLOWS ALERTING AT WARRINGTON. The twenty-ninth anniversary of the Loyal Gari- baldi Lodge, National Independent Order of Odd- fellows, was celebrated on Saturday by a dinner at Host Wm. Warburton's, Little Horse-shoe Inn, when 56 members and friends attended. After dinner. P. G. John Hughes was appointed chairman, and P. P.G.M. James Smith. vice-chairman. The chairman proposed the usual loyal and patriotic toasts and "Success to the National Independent Oider. of Oddfellows." P.P.G.M. Jos. Hands responded, and Bro. T. Dickenson, jun., enlivened the proceedings with a song. The Vice-Chairman gave " Success to the Loyal Garibaldi Lodge." Secretary E.Kenwright responded, and said the lodge was in a prosperous condition, being worth over .£4 per head for every member. They had invested with the Corporation £3OO, and had a banking account of .£124 last June, in addition to a share in the District Funeral Fund. To give an insight of the good done with regard to sick and dectased members and members' wives, he stated that they had received for sick and funeral fund alone since January, 1880, over £l,lOO. They had paid to sick members £7OO, and for the funeral allowance of deceased members and members' wives £2OO, besides paying for general management and helping to assist distressed members. It was the wish of the officers of the lodge to impress up- on the members the fact that the more they in- creased in numbers the greater would be the in- crease of the funds. Two new members had been made, and there were ten propositions for new members. The Chairman next gave 'The Juvenile Society," and said he hoped that every member would try to make it a success. P.G. J. T. Wilson proposed "Kindred Societies," and said he hoped that all societies were working for the good of the community. The rest of the evening was spent in an enjoyable manner.

An errand boy named William Williams, thirteen years of age, committed suicide at Chester, on Wednesday, by hanging himself to a beam. At Manchester, on Wednesday, Ellen Evans, wife of a. machinist, was remanded on a charge of attempting to murder her child by tying a tape round its neck. Two Welsh ladies are reported to have recently been the victims of an extraordinary outrage at the hands of Italian soldiers while sojourning for a night at the Mount St. Bernard Monastery.

div.head: ROMANCE OF NORTH DEVON.
div.p: A ROMANCE OF NORTH DEVON.

From the Bideford Gaeette. " A prosoic world,"" an unromantic age"—these and similar expressions are frequently heard to fall from the lips of many a mortal who goes lazily and comfortably through life, with eyes that see not, and ears that hear not. But to those whose faculties of observation are on the qui rive, this world and even this age—prosaic though they may be in some respects—provide inlinite variety and occasionally disclose what may be properly termed a romance. Such an experience befel the repre- sentative of this paper (and writer of this article) a few weeks ago. The occasion was the relating of a narrative, at once strange almost beyond belief and yet true beyond

question. But to tell the tale. About midway between historic Bideford and unique, picturesque Clovelly, the traveller passes through the little village of Horn's Cross. One of the residents is a young man named John Brownscombe Clements, a mason by trade, and known to all the country round. He was the speaker, and this is what he said "Up to September, 1887, I had always been in good health. About that time, however, after working in some water, I took a cold. This developed into inflam- mation of the right lung, and was accompanied with an attack of pleurisy. This laid me up for over,a fortnight, but I got out again as soon as I could—too soon, in fact, for I caught another cold, and had a relapse. After that I gradually grew worse. I continued in bed for sometime, and the doctor began to treat me for con- sumption. I took cod liver oil and other things; but I got worse and worse. At the end of six months—dur- ing part of which time three doctors had been attending me—my water was examined and I was found to be suffering from Bright's Disease. The doctors had given me up, saying na more medicine could be of any avail. But I had read in your paper, the Bideford Gazette, about wonderful things having been done by Warner's 'SATE' Cure. I was desperate; there was but one chance between me and the grave. I spoke to my sister, and she walked into Bideford and bought a bottle of Warner's 'SATE' Cure. I commenced taking it, and felt rather worse, being in more pain for a little while. But I stuck to it, and before finishing the -first bottle I was, to my great joy, considerably re- lieved. For three months I took Warner's • SAEB Cure regularly, and before the end of that period I was not only able to go out, but was actually able to resume my work again. I have taken in all twenty-seven bottles, and it is now eighteen months since I loft off. I have been in good health and constant work all that time, and am to-day strong and well. I consider I owe my escape from death, and restoration to health, solely to Warner's SATE' Cure." There is no need to add anything to Mr. Clements' story, beyond that it was told voluntarily, intelligently, simply, and with the utmost sincerity. Anyone whose curiosity or interest is aroused by the foregoing state- ments is perfectly at liberty to go to Mr. Clements or write to him, and he will tell them all, and probably more, than is recited here, for he is genuinely grateful for all that thismedicine has done for him, and is evi- dently eager that others may be benefitted by the same means.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
ASSAULT BY A_ HUSBAND.

On Wednesday, at the Warrington Police Court, William Gleave was charged with assaulting his wife on the 20th inst. Complainant stated that on Monday night defendant went,home and asked for his working clothes. Witness told him he should have them when he was sober. Defendant replied he would have them there and then or he would knock her through the wall; and, so saying, he made a rush at witness, and struck her on the face and head twice. Witness had once had a separation order, but,as defendant promised to be better, she allowed him to live with her again. Prisoner was bound over to keep the peace for six months towards his wife on one surety of £5.

div.head: THEFT OF A ROLL OF CLOTH.
div.p: THEFT OF A ROLL OF CLOTH.

James Gleeson, labourer, of no settled abode, and Daniel O'Lochlin, were charged at the Warrington Police Court, on Wednesday, with stealing a roll of cloth, of the value of 345. 4d. on Tuesday, the property of George Ross, draper, Winwick-st. Mr. Hunt said on Tuesday evening the two prisoners went to the house of Gleeson's parents in Rodney-st., in a drunken condition, and Glee- son entered the house and offered the cloth to his father for 65., remarking that he had bought it for 9s. The father, disbelieving his son's statement went for the police, and ultimaFely, the prisoners were arrested and taken into custody. Gleeson had nothing to say in an- swer to the charge, but -O'Lochin denied that he h had anything to. do with the theft; and said that merely took Gleeson home. Gleesion was sent to pri for 14 days with hard labour, and, there being a doubt in the case ot O'Lochlin he was discharged.

div.head: AN UNFOUNDED CHARGE.
div.p: AN UNFOUNDED CHARGE.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, Rose Thomas, was brought up on reinantl charged on sus- picion with stealing a silver watch and chain.—The Chief-Constable said the woman was brought before the Bench, along with a man on Friday last under very sus- picious circumstances. It appeared they travelled together from Liverpool where they slept the previous night, and,when near Warrington, she handed the man a watch to pledge for her. Constables Evans and Monog- han received some information of the transaction and Evans stopped them in the street and asked for the watch. The man replied that he had not got one; but at the Police Station he gave up the watch and both he and the woman were remanded for further enquiries.— Nothing was known of them at Manchester; but from Liverpool he had received a message which was confirma- tory of the woman's statement. The man had since been liberated, and he (Mr. Hunt) now asked the Bench to bind the prisoner over to come up when called upon, but he wculd certainly detain the watch.—Prisoner, who said she had the watch presented to her, wa.4 accordingly bound over.

AN INTERESTING PRISONER.—POLICE COURT ORATORY. A man named Michael Hennessey was charged at the • police court, on Monday, with having been drunk and disorderly at Townhill, on the I.2thinst. The case having been proved, the prisoner, in a statement to the Bench, said he listened very attentively to a very able and i practical lecture on temperance n the League Hall on Sunday, with the result that he had made up his mind to join the league. He had been per•al servitude, and had done his utmost to get an honest living since he came into the town. He quite agreed with genial Recorder Hopwood, of Liverpool,that penal servitude lowered and contaminated the mind, and that evil communications corrupted good matiners.—The Mayor: You have missed your calling, my man, you should have been a statesman, for you are quite an orator this morning. (Laughter.) Prisoner continued that he had determined never to take any more intoricating liqours ; and, after the Mayor had given him a little good acivice,the prisoner was discharged. On leaving the dock defendant said he was very thankful to the magistrates for their kind verdict, and by it he found them to be true gentlemen, of honour and principle. (Renewed laughter.)

div.head: ALLEGED THErr OF A WATCH AND CHAIN. – – – – -•
div.p: ALLEGED THErr OF A WATCH AND CHAIN. - - - - -•

A case which set forth the precaution which policemen should exercise as to whom they take into custody, and the desirability of their being able to produce corrobor- ative evidence, was heard at the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, when a woman, named Martha Smith, was charged with stealing a silver watch and chain of the value of £3 from the person of Wm. Foster on Saturday night. P.C. 40 deposed that on the day in question he was on duty in Sankey-st., when he re- ceived certain information respecting the prisoner and Forster. He proceeded down the street and found the prisoner and the man together. Foster charged the woman with stealing a sovereign; and witness noticed prisoner was in possession of a watch. In answer to his questions defendant said the watch belonged to her hus- band and that she would do what she liked with it.

Witness suspected that it was not her husbands and I took her into custody. Defendant said She had previous- ly co-habited with the man; but had been separated from him for some weeks and incidentally met him on Saturday night. She also strongly asserted that she never handled the watch.—Wm. Forster stated that it was true that at one time she co-habited with the pri- soner, but he had not seen her for about a month until Saturday, when she insisted upon staying with him. They had drink together, but he could not say that prisoner extracted the watch from his pocket. He never saw her attempt to take it, though she might have done. The woman had always been honest to his knowledge. —Mr. Hunt said there was no charge against the pri- soner at all, and he could not see that there was any foundation for making one.—Prisoner was accordingly discharged.
PROCURINO ALMS UNDER FALSE PRETENCES.

Mary Rowan was charged at the Warrington Police ,Court, on Wednesday, with having unlawfully collected alms on the 17th inst. The Chief Constalsle said the complainant in this case was the wife of James Martin, who was a dealer in fried fish and chip potatoes, in Bewsey-et. The defendant, who was the wife of a labturer. and who lived at Lee's-yard, lladdock-st., on the day in question went to the complainant's shop, and knocked at the side door. Mrs. Martin answered, whereupon prisoner said to her "I've a little child scalded to death, and I've called to see if you will give me anything towards burying it. My husband has been out of work five weeks, and I should be obliged for a little." Mrs. Martin, thinking the story true, gave the woman sixpence. Defendant then went away and left the door, after grasping the sixpence, very quick ly. Com- plainant noticed this, and also stsof aefendant laugh to herself, and this aroused her suspicions. Defendant told complainant that she lived at Glasshouse-yard but on inquiring at this place Mrs. Martin was told there had been no child scalded to death, neither was there a person, known of the name and description of the prisoner. Thi Monday last, between 10 and 11 o'clock, the defendant was seen to come from Messrs. Jackson's pawnshop by Mrs. Martin, who noticed that defendant carried some- thing under her arm. Defendant was then taken beck to the pawnshop and ultimately taken into custody by the police, who were sent for by complainant. Be (Mr. Hunt) was told that defendant also received alms from a woman named Mrs. Daly on the 11th ult. under similar circumstances. Prisoner was committed to prison for 14 days with hard labour.

THEFT FROM A SHOP DOOR. Arthur Longshaw, and his wife, Elizabeth Longshaw, I were charged with stealing a cardigan jacket, value 7s. 6d. from the shop door of Messrs. Unsworth, Arthur- st. on Tuesday night. The male prisoner was seen to walk past the shop several times within a short space of time, and when one of the assistants went to the door he missed the jacket, and his attention was directed to the male prisoner who was proceeding up the street, and who was carrying the jacket. About seven o'clock the same evening the woman presented the stolen article for pledge at Mr. Jackson's pawnshop, and Mr. Jackson, thinking the jacket was in all details in accordance with the description given by the police, sent for A constable, and the woman was taken into custody, and the male prisoner was arrested in Buttermarket-st. The man was committed to prison for a month and his wife for 14 days, each with hard labour
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE _COURT.
Mo;M-TY-.—Before Alderman Francomb Mayor (presid-

ing), Alderman Davies, and Alderman Harrison: DRIINEENNESS.—The following persons were charged with this offence :—Lydia Fowler, in Market Place, on Saturday night.—Discharged. William Foster, in San- key-st., Saturday night. Fined ss. or seven days. Eliza Ann Duffy, in Winwick-st., on the same day. Fined ss. and costs or seven days. James Rooney, in Bridge-st. on Saturday night, Fined ss. and costs or seven days. CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—Annie Miller was summoned for unlawfully setting fire to a chimney in her dwelling house. Ordered to pay the costs. PROTECTION OF A STEPMOTHER. Podmore was bound over on his own recognisance of .E 5 to be of good behaviour towards his stepmother for six months, and ordered to pay ss. and costs for drunkenness in Lord Nelson-st. on the 11th inst. _ . . .

AN UNDESIRABLE VlSlTOR.—Michael Hannon' who said 114 hailed from the country, was charged with drunken- ness and indnently exposing himself at Bridge Foot on Saturday. He was fined ss. and costs or seven days. BEGGING IN THE STRENTS.—JOhII %men was charged with drunkenness and begging in orsemarket-st on Saturday night. On promising to leave the town at once he was discharged. SLEEPING OUT.—John Johnson and Catherine Bowden were chargedwith sleeping in Mrs. Monk's shed at Arpley on Sunday morning at four o'clock. They were each fined ss. or the alternative of seven days imprisonment. MAINTENANCE ORDERS.—AIfrea Birchall and Richard Ridgway were each ordered to pay Is. 6d. per week to- wards the support of their sons who are on the ship Clio. AN OVERCROWDED HOUSE.—Edward Hart was sum- moned to show cause why he should not abate a nuisance caused by the overcrowding of his house. It was stated by Nuisance Inspector Norman that the defendant occupied a house which had only one room uptairs and one room downstairs. He had three children, whose ages ranged from three to fifteen years, and instead of them being able to properly accommodate themselves, they were causing a nuisance.—An order was made for the abate- ment of the nuisance within 14 days, and, in addition de- fendant was fined ss. and costs. _ . _

AN UNREGISTERED LODGING-HOUSE.—Joseph Boedell was summoned for keeping lodgers without being regis- tered on the 14th inst.—lnspector Church said on this date he visited the defendant's house and found it occu- pied by five persons—three of the family, and twe lodgers. The house was not a registered lodging-holise.—Defend- ant was fined ss. including costs, and told that he must get rid of his lodgers, which he promised he would do. PITCH AND Toss.--James Woods, for playing pitch and toss at Friar's Green, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.
TUESDAY.—Before Councillor Platt (in the chair) and Mr.
R. Garnett.

TRAVELLING ON THE RAILWAY WITHOUT A TICKET.— Sarah Standish was charged with riding on the Cheshire , Lines Railway from Manchester to Warrington, on Mon- day, without a ticket. Mr. F. Simpson, superintendent of the police department,appeared to prosecute. The pris- oner was seen to get out of the train at Warrington, and when asked for her ticket, she replied that she had torn it up, but afterwards stated that she had not purchased one. She further remarked that she had been in service Manchester, and that she was proceeding to her home at Widnes. The case was adjourned until Wednesday, in order that Mr. Simpson might make inquiries respecting the prisoner's parents. The prisoner was brought up again on Wednesday, when the Chief Constable said she 'had admitted that she travelled without procuring a ticket. The mother of the girl, who said she could not account for her conduct, proffered to pay the fare and costs, and the prisoner was discharged. DRUNKENNESS.—A man named Theophelus Issacs was fined ss. and costs, or seven days, for having been drunk and disorderly in Bold-st., on Monday evening. . - .

SCHOOL SO./LBO CASES.—The foll Owing persons were summoned for neglecting to send their children regularly to school :—Mary Miller, Silver-square, fined 2s. 6d. ; Thomas Rushton' indiarubber maker. Admiral-street, fined 55.; Patrick Downey, forgeman, Erwood-st., fined 2s. 6d.; James Travis, forgeinan, Haydock-st., fined 2s. 6d. ; Walter Stowell, wiredrawer, Old-road, fined 55.; Thomas Rowland, toolmaker, Baet.ersby-lane, fined 2s. 6d. ; Edward Hart, labourer' Old-road, fined 2s. 6d.; John Graham, tanner, Ship-yard, fined ss. ; Braide, signalman, Bewsey-road, fined 5s ; Alfred Birchall, forgeman, Silver-square, fined 55., and the case of William Moran was adjourned fr a fortnight. WEDNESDAY.— Befoie Alderman Holmes (in the chair), Captain Nicholson and Mr. J. Fairclough.

Thomas Cook. was charged with stealing 's padlock and key, value 6d., the property of John Pinston. The prisoner was seen to take the lock from off a shed 'door by complainant's sorvant. Fined ss. and costs or seven days. DRUNKENNESS AND ASSAULT. John Bagaley, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-st., on Tuesday afternoon, and also with assaulting P.C. Clough. Prisoner admitted having been drunk, but denied the assault. The constable stated that when taking the prisoner into custody he was very vio- lent, and kicked him on the left leg.—Mr. Hunt said it was a long time since he had had anything to say to the magistrates against the prisoner, but ot late he had become worse and worse, and on Tuesday it took five men to put him into the cell, he being so rough. Pri- soner was committed to prison for one month-with hard. labour.

DRUNKENNESS AND DISORDERLY CONDUCT.—Winifred Burke. who has been before the court 15 times pre- viously, was fined 10s, and' costs or 14 days, for this offence. Elizabeth Ellen Fleming was charged with a similar offence, and also with breaking a window, value 55., at the White Bear beerhouse,-on Tuesday evening. She was ordered to pay the damage to the window, or in default seven days' imprisonment, and for being drunk was fined 108. and costs or 14 days. Bridget Rooney,. against whom a charge of drunkenness and disorderly conduct in Butttermarket-st., was preferred, was fined ss. and costs or seven days. James Sauce who has a terrible black list of convictions against him, was again sent to goal for a month, for a similar offence in Butter- market-st., on Tuesday night, and a fine of 55. and i costs or seven days was mppied upon Elizabeth Pearse and Alice Thomas, the former for being inebriated in Knutsford-road, on Tuesday night, and the latter in Lord Nelson-st., on the same evening. TRURSDAY.—Before Major Litton (in the chair) and Major Pickmere. DRUNKENNESS.—Catherine Higgins of Mount-st., St. Helens, was charged with having been drunk and dis- orderly in Market-place, on Wednesday night. On pro- mising to leave the town at once she was discharged. DRUNKENNESS AND ASSAULT,—George Hopkins, lab- ourer, of Hardy-st., was charged with drunkenness and disorderly conduct in Market-place, on Tuesday evening, also with assaulting Catherine Higgins. The case hav- ing been proved by Constable Bell, tha prisoner was fined 10s. and costs or 14 day's imprisonment. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (in the chair) and
Alderman Sutton:

DRUNKENNESS.—Jannes Doyle was charged with having been drunk in Golborne-st. on Thursday night. On promising to pay Is., the lock-up costs, and leave the town, he was discharged. Mary France for a similar offence in Buttermarket-st., the same evening, was told to leave the town at once, and wasdischarged. William Morris was fined is. and told to leave the town at once for a similar offence in Bridge-st. DRUNKENNESS AND DISORDERLY CONDUCT. Anna Holmes and Mary Ellen Fairhrother were charged with having been drunk and disorderly in 13uttermarket-st. on Thursday evening. They were each fined ss. and costs or seven days' imprisonment. ALLEGED ASSAULT.—John Hickey was charged by a I servant girl, named Annie Lee, who was lately in the I employ of Mr. Craddock, clothier, with an assault, which was, according to the evidence, of an indecent char- acter. The case was dismissed, Nit.. Harrison remarking that he did npt consider it proved. MAINTENANCE ORDER.—An order for 7s. 6d. a week was made against E. Jarvis towards the maintenance of his wife who is in the Warrington Union. SHOCKING ASSAULT.— A man named Dutton was charged by his stepmother' Sarah Dutton for assault on the 18th inst. It appeared from the evidence that on the day in question defendant went into his father's house and demanded a cup, which bore his name. The com- plainant refused to let him have it unless he got the con- sent of his father to take it. Defendant then became rough, and squeezed complainant against a door and struck her on the arm so violently that he discoloured it. Defendant was fined 10s. and costs or in default 14 day's imprisonment. AWKWARD POSITION OF A FUSTIAN CUTTER.—Edwin. Mills, fustian cutter, claimed 20s. from Ann McGuire for neglect of her work. Defendant's husband said he pre- vented his wife from going to work. Mr. Harrison said the complainant could do nothing with defendant as she was a married woman, and, after a little further advice, complainant consented to withdraw the summons ; as he did also in the case of a similar nature which was next heard.

ASSAULT WITHOUT PROVOCATION.—Thos. Grady was Inithrnoned by Mary Walsh, for assault on the 22nd inst Complainant was leaving her work at this date when the defendantsaw her. Heat once rushed towards her and assaulted her, giving her a black eye and hurting her arm. A tine ot 20s. and costs was imposed, or in default 14 day's imprisonment.
OCCASIONAL COURT. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. Peter Stubs. A SERIES OF ALLEGED TIIEFTS.—Thomas Rothwell, of Go!borne, was charged with stealing from the Victoria

Hotel, Golborne, on the 9th inst., a metal coffee pot, valued 55., the property of Richard Dalton; also with stealing from a dwelling-house in School-lane, Golborne, a gun and a brass pan, valued at £1 10s., on the 13th inst., the property of Ralph Allan ; also with stealing from a dwelling-house in Lawton-road, Golborne, on the 9th inst., a silk handkerchief, valued at is. 6d., belong- ing to John Beckinsale. Prisoner was remanded until to-day (Saturday), no evidence being taken. Morinev.—Before Mr. Edward Greenall MxsaittLANsons.—John Riding,who was described as a "bird of passage," was charged with begging at Latch- ford, on Sunday, and on the evidence of P.C. Milling- ton, was committed to prison for seven days without the option of a fine.—A navvy, named Thomas Collin, was charged with damaging a number of cabbages and cauli- flowers growing in a field belonging to Mr. Isaac Turner, of Latchford. It appeared from the evidence that the prisoner was caught by P.C. Millington in the act of stealing cabbages and cauliflowers, 26 of which he had pulled up. He was fined 20s. including costs.
prisone:

got to work, however, and repulsing an attack of the enemy, some passing amongst the backs carried play to the Tuebrook end. Bayley with a kick stayed off the threatening danger, and the visiting forwards, who were playing splendidly together, quickly worked the ball to the opposite end, where some fast and exciting play was witnessed. Ultimately Mather, Cragan, and Isherwood regained the lost ground by a ground dribble,causing the game to flutter about midfield. Some rough and tumble tussles': between the combatants raised the excitement of

the isle elap-se—cl I could gain anything like an advantage. A slight stop- ' page was caused about this time, owing to Sampson receiving a nasty knack, and, though considerably dazed, he manfully stuck to his work, and the fray proceeded as keenly as ever. Loose play followed, in which Knowles, Eyres,-Catterall, and Russell distinguished themselves, and while the leather was worked nearer the

visitors' goal the excitement of the crowd visibly in- creased, and when the oval was forced over and dropped upon by Bate, the pent-up enthusiasm of the home sup- porters broke forth. Following the drop out, a find kick by Lawless was mulled; but Bleasdale, Wootton, and Pearson, with a mighty ruth transferred to neutral territory, where a lot of little exciting events occurred, Notwithstanding the close attentions of his oppo- nents, Bate at length got the ball smartly away to Mather, the quarter flag being reached, and a perfect roar was raised when at was seen that Bayley had mulled the oval, allowing the Warring- thnians to get close to the posts. A strong run by Davies followed a relief by Bleasdale, and from another mull, the home team almost scored. Eccles kicking dead in the nick of time. Succeeding this, Webster, who had been merely a spectator, got a splendid pass from Bate, and scattered several opponents before being pulled down at the 25. This was neutralized by a splendid dodgy run by Morris, a grand tackle by Eyres flooring him. Then the ball was gradually worked by Molyneaux, Hackett, Russell, and Knowles, to the visitors' lines. Eccles cleared the danger, and took warfare to his antagonists' quarters. Some fine passing by Tuebrook enabled Morris to make another grand effort until stopped by Moly- neaux, but directly afterwards Wootten literally forced himself over, and secured an equalizing try. Tuebrook now attacked strongly, and the close attentions they con- tinually paid to the home goal posts made the supporters wonder when this thing would end, but half-time arrived with no further score. Resuming at midfield, Hackett was early prominent with a run and pass, causing the battle to wage at the visitors' 25, and from a pass by Barnes, Lawless ran over. From the kick out Webster by a strong rush got well into his opponents' territory before being pulled up. but the advantage was soon lost, as Tuebrook by a dribble nullified. Tall kicking between the backs followed, and the visitors were gradually forced back. It was not for long' for a determined rush by the Liverpool men sent the leather to the opposite end. ,Bate then passed splendidly to Barnes, and a grand chance was lost by an ill-judged pass. This Was followed by a splendid dribble by Pearson right to the line, but Davies temporarily relieved by a dashing run. Directly afterwards from a free kick Pearson ran under the posts, and Eccles had no difficulty in placing a goal. Restart- ing, Isherwood charged Eccles' return kick, and Webster by a long punt gained ground. The-position was further enhanced by Bayley making a free kick dead near the post, from which mishap the visitors never recovered. On one occasion Bate was almost over, and completely foiled his opponents, but a few minutes afterwards a tremendous shout announced the fact that Lawless had scored from a pass by Barnes, and the applause was deafening when Barnes converted. Finally Warrington retired winners of a most stubbornly-contested'game by 1-2-3 to 1-1-0. Teams :—Warrington: Sampson, back; Webster, Baraes, and Lawless, three-quarter backs; Bate and Mather, half backs ; Molyneaux, Isherwood, Cragan, Davies, Eyres. Catered, Russell, Hackett, and Knowles, forwards. Tuebrook: Bayley, back; Morris, Eccles, and Ellams, three-quarter backs; Bleasdale and Vickiss, half backs ; Wootton, Roberts, E. Pearson, A. , Pearson, H. Pearson, R. Pearson, Stuart, Hewitt, and . Timmins.

wards. Stripes: R. Lewis (Askam), back; Sudlow (St. Helens), Gwynne (Oldham), and Winterbottom (Swinton), three-quarter backs ; Cross (St. Helens), and .1. Berry (Tyldesley), half backs ; J. Jolley (Warrington). Jowett (Failsworth), Cameron (Manchester), Hallam (Swinton), Pollard (Manchester Rangers), Gould (Old Boys). Squire (Broughton), Williamson (Walkden), Blomley (Oldham), and Pike (St. Helens Recreation), forwards.

ASSOCIATION. The Football League seems to have dealt with Sunder- land with undue severity at their meeting•On Friday night. For playing Doig, their new goalkeeper, when he was but a day short of the usual qualification, the Northerners were fined £25 and deprived of two paints. According to the evidence of the Sunderland secretary, he posted his registration of Doig in time to reach the League secretary on the Saturday, but it was not re- ceived until the day following, which made all thediffer- ence. It is certainly a hard case. The result is that Sunderland are now at the very bottom of the League table.

Everton are again at the top. But it took them all their time to beat the Bolton Wanderers at Anfield road by two goals, so that the latter have evidently improved since their first match last month. The Wanderers in- tended playing their new half-back, Gardiner, late of Renton, but Sunderland had also secured his signature and would not consent to his traesfer. The League clubs are very jealous of each other. Blackburn Rovers made small fry of Burnley, vanquishing them at Turf Moor by six goals to one. The Burnley team are rapidly going to pieces, and were twice defeated during the week.

Wolverhampton Wanderers collapsed wofully at Pres- ton, where the champions scored five goals to one. The North End forwards were vastly superior to those on the opposing side. The Accrington team added another draw to their list at Sunderland, and have still to win their first League encounter. Notts continue to hold a good position, and Derby County gained ' a couple of points by overthrowing Aston Villa.

The failure of Stoke at Birmingham has left Notts Forest at the head of the Alliance clubs. The best per- formauce in connection with this tournament was the splendid win of Darwen over Sunderland Albion by the pronounced margin of five points to one. Newton Heath sent Grimsby Town home defeated, after having much the best of the game.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

"4,* Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY.

WARRINGTON RANGERS 2ND V. TnELWALL HORNETS IST. —The above match was played at Thelwall,on Saturday, and after an evenly-contested game, resulted in a draw of 1 goal 1 minor each. Taylor secured the tries for the Hornets, one of which Hamlet converted into a goal, whilst the Rangers' score was made up by a grandly dropped goal by Clare, and an equally clever try by Fleming. WIGAN T. WIDNES ("A " TEAMS.)—Played at Wigan On Saturday, in fine weather, before 200 spectators. Widnes won the toss, two thirties being agreed upon. Wigan kicked off at four o'clock. Wigan pressed, and Murray I made his mark, Atkinson making a good attempt at goal. Murray again made his mark, and Atkinson this time kicked a grand goal. Wallwork was particularly prominent for the home side during this half. Score at half time—Wigan, 1 goal; Widnes, nil. Final result— Wigan A, 1 goal ; Widnes A, 1 try and 1 minor.

. . , WARRINGTON RANGERS V. PENBERTON SOUTH END.— This match was played at Warrington, on Saturday,and owing to the late arrival of the visitors, a game of two twenties was played. Pemberton kicked off, and no re- turn being made, the visitors at once attacked, only to be repelled by the combined play of the home team,who quickly made tracks for their opponents' line, where from a combined dribble Longshaw secured a good try • for the Rangers. From the drop eut fine passing be- tween the home team severely harassed the visitors' de- fence, the ball eventually falling into the hands of Potts, who kicked across, and following up quickly put his men on side, which resulted in Savage scoring a swond try for the home team, half time being called the score reading Rangers 2 tries, 3 minors; Pemberton nil. A re- start being made, the home team again pressed, but ow- ing to the strong defence of the visitors, nothing titit minors were scored, the final result being—Rangers, 2 tries, 4 minors Pemberton 1 minor. RUNCORN V. LIVERPOOL OLD BOYS, A TRANS.—These A. teams met at Liverpool on Saturday. Runcorn won the toss, and Bell kicked off for the Old Boys. Play was for some time time confined to theyisiting quarters, but a grand run and some splendid passing by the visitors transferred the play into the home 25, where Russell re- lieved with a good kick, and immediately afterwards the Boys were spoiled of an almost certain try by good tackling on the part of G. Robinson. The" All Whites" were awarded a free kick for off-side play by the Run- corn men, but the ball was kicked outside. , The home fortress was now placed in danger by a series of scrim- mages which took place Almost on the touch line, but Russell averted the danger, and the ball was taken into midfield, where play continued until from some magni- ficent passing by the visiting forwards Barker received and passed to Cawley, who scored a good try, which was not converted into a goal. The visitors kept up the pressure, and a few minutes later J. Robinson scored another try, but again the major point was not made. Final result :—Buncorn A. 1 goal, 4 tries, 3 minors ; Old _ .
Boys A,nil. WIDNBS • . WIG/VC—Considerable interest was shown

in the match between these two clubs, which was played on the ground of the former, before about 4,000 specta- tors, on Saturday afternoon. Widnes won the toss, and elected to play with their backs to the sun. After the kick off by Atkinson, play settled in the home quarter. where a kick from Plumpton was charged down, and Wigan following up the advantage, compelled Widnes to concede a minor. From the drop out, Wigan continued to press, but Brennan transferred play to. the visitors' half, where several scrimmages took place. McGurl at half back showed a disposition to feec4he three-quarters, but twice in succession within a few minutes, Brennan retained possession and played the ball, when Plump- ton had an easy chance of getting through. The visitors were now conspicuous with some good passing, and from a throw in, in the home quarter, the ball was car- ried over the horne line, where Bullough dropped unon it, and scored a try which Widnes might easily have pre- vented, had they played up on the ball, instead of wait- ing its return out of danger. Anderton, however, made a poor attempt at goal. In some rather rough play which followed, Tickle had to retire from the field, he having sustainee a fracture of his shoulder blade. This caused very ,great weakness in the home for- wards; but, notwithstanding this, they played up well, and gave the visitors, considerable trouble by the safe defence of their/ own line. A free kick fell to Widnes in a good position, hut Plumpton's kick went just outside the posts. Brennan next made his mark, but the free kick did not avail
Widnes much, as they were soon called upon to defend. This Plumpton did grandly, and played the ball after losing possession when collared. Drummond and Smith

were next conspicuous with some sharp play, which re- pulsed the visitors, and Anderton cleared. After another invasion into home territory, the whistle blew for half- time, when the score was—Wigan, one try two minors ; Widnes, nil. On changing ends, the ball was carried rapidly into the Widnes quarter, where another minor was conceded. Wigan continued the attack, and a few minutes later, Seddon for Wigan scored the second try, but Anderton again failed at goal. Three wore minors followed in rapid succession to Wigan, and a splendid run by Slevin from quarter to quarters just before the close of the game, was only prevented from being fruitful by some exceedingly goad play on the part of Plumpton, who brought him down within a few yards of the line. The game ended in a win for Wigan by two tries, six minors, to Widnes nil. The following e.omprised the Widnes team :—Hartles, back ; Clarke, Brennan, and Plumpton, threequarter backs; McGurl and Drummond, half-backs; Smith Gordon, Hewitt, Farmer, Pearson, Laws, Whelan, Tickle, and Carroll, forwards. Minoru,' v. OLD RoYS.—This popular fixture was brought to an issue on Saturday at Runcorn. With the exception of Davies the Runcornians had their full strength. Goold stood out of the Old Boy's ranks. Teams: Runcorn—Houghton, back; Gayter, Crompton, and Pendlebury, three-quarter backs; H. Hughes, and S. Abrams, half-backs; Faulkner, Broady, Riley, May, Dolan, Hancock, Rigby, Bower, and J. Davies, forwards. Old Boys—W. Hilton, back; Atkinson, Legge, and H. D. Wood, three-quarter backs; O'Dwyer and Harrison, half-backs; Wilson, Wood, Bullen, Rowe, Littlewood, Armourer, J. Harrison, C. Allen, and M"rurk forwards. Faulkner opened the play on behalf of the home team, and the Old Boys getting well down forced a minor point. Riley was to the fore with a capital dribbling movement, which Woods checked, play for the next few minutes settling down in the centre. Some smart half-back play was followed by a couple of ex- changes between Legge and Houghton but it was not until a free kick was awarded the home team that they obtained a dangerous footing. The forwards re- lieved, and another strong raid was made upon the home defence, but by splendid combination among their backs danger as averted. Abrams put in a neat sprint, and at the other end Atkinson looked like getting in, but Peddlebury was in readiness. A loose movement led on I by Faulkner carried the play well within the Boys' half; but a capital movement, initiated by ~O'Dwyer, was instrumental in again repelling their opponents. At half time the score stood—Old Boys, 2 minors; Runcorn, nil. O'Dwyer having restarted, the visitors established themselves in the home half until Crompton, with a grand run, raced to the other end, but failed to pass Atkinson. Lining out, the home lot got well down, and Bowyer crossed the line, but the place kick failed. Shortly afterwards Crompton scored a second from a pass by Faulkner, and Riley finished lip with a third, neither points being improved upon, the Old Boys meeting with their first reverse by 3 tries to nil. The game was splendidly contested, and abounded in clever incidents and smart play. In the first half the Old Boys had distinctly the greater share of the play, and Legge and Atkinson were collared four or five times when within five yards of the line. In the second half, however, the extra weight and the better training of the wearers of the green became apparent, and some very good passing and quick following up was the means of gaining three tries. For the Old Boys, Wood played very cleverly in the centre, but passed after he was col- lared in a very wild manner. Harrison and O'Dwyer played capitally at half, and the former did more and better work than any one on the field. Legge played a good game, but kicked somewhat feebly, when a little determination might have resulted in a try. Armourer, 11. C. Wood, and Bullen played well forward,and M.Turk was often prominent by his energetic following up. For Runcorn, Houghton was very reliable, and at three- quarters Crompton played one of his best games. The halves were very successful, but the forwards won the match by their very resolute play in the second . Riley was the best forward, bat all played a good com- bined game. A noticeable feature in the first portion of the game was a beautiful passing movement among the whole of the Runcornians, while in the last minute of the game the tackling of Crompton by Hilton was cleverly accomplished. WARRINGTON A v. TITEBROOK.—A great amount of interest was centred in this match, which was played on the Wilderspool ground on Saturday, before a large num- ber of spectators. Warrington lost choice of ends, and in consequence had to face the sun, a mull being made straight away from the kick off. The home team soon
half.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

The first stage of a notable feat in bicycle riding has been completed by the arrival in London of Lieutenant George Martos, of the Imperial Russian Artillery, who on Saturday visited the Lord Mayor at the Mansion House previous to his departure on a bicycle tour to Scotland: With only an old-fashioned roadster of about 60 lbs. weight, this young rider, who is in his twenty- third year. has covered the 2,000 odd miles which divided London from St. Petersburg in thirty-two days. Lieuten- ant Martos is of medium height, and slightly built, his weight being under ten stone. Nevertheless his well- knit frame shows plenty of power. He is unable to speak English and has an indifferent knowlodge of French.

Naturally enough, in the first flush of enthusiasm, the bicyclist made rapid headway at the outset. He had soon passed into Germany. There unpleasant experiences awaited him. Once,in Garfield,he was attacked by a dog, and the encounter resulted in the dog being left a victim to the knife. In Witten, the lieutenant had similiarly to defend himself, and passed on, leaving some unknown' burgher to bemoan the loss of his dog. However, the inhabit Ants were much more friendly and he never wanted for hospitality. France received him with much kindness. His appearance in Vervins extorted a banquet. This was given by the Mayor, who had travelled in Russia. Paris rained congratulations upon him, the Russian Ambassador and 51. de Freycinet, the Minister of War, complimenting him upon the feat and displaying keen interest in his experiences. Interest still more acute was shown by cables from America, which bid eagerly for his bicycle for exhibition in dime museums and shows. As much as £5OO was offered in one instance.

In a few days Lieutenant Martos, who habitually wears the cyclist's uniform, will set out upon his run round these islands. He will then return to London, and, after a short rest, will make for his home in Cronstadt. Altogether, his journey will furnish an extraordinary achievement of speed and endurance on the part of a young rider.

The one hundred • /lines safety bicycle and tandem tricycle records were beaten on Saturday. T. A. Edge, on a safety, and S. F. Edge and J. E. L. Bates on a tandem, started two miles south of Lincoln, at the 130th milestone from London, and rode to the fourthimilestone, where the safety rider arrived in 5h 27min. 38sec. from the start, while the tandem riders finished in 5h 30min. 31sec. The riders had a strong northerly breeze with them all the way.
LACROSSE.

The Warrington Lacrosse club commences the seas on to-day with a match at home against the famous Owen's College team, and we wish our local exponents of the game every success. The Owen's College men will be under the captaincy of Mr. Norman Welland—" Eng- land's only captain"—certainly the finest defence player in England to-day—and a gentleman to whom the lacrosse world owes a vast amount for making a thorough study of the game and doing much to popularize it. Warring- ton as yet is not fully alive to the pleasures of this inter- esting game which possesses all the qualities of football, on a more scientific scale and without its dangers—more scientific because it is so difficult to keep the ball well balanced in your crosse when running and dodging an opponent. Lacrosse brings into full use a man's running capabilities and affords in passingsplenclid opportunities for unselfishness, a fact not always sufficiently appreci- ated, for as a combined team the game must be won and not by the superhuman efforts of one man. ,

The list of fixtures arranged by the secretary Mr. C. Spinks, 80, Sankey-t., and Committee, includes home and home matches with such first class teams as Liver- . Prestwich,. Blackley, Sze., Liver- pool, Birkenhead, Southport and we hope that such an ambitious programme may be backed up throughout the season with that help which the team need in their plucky efiterprise. A better ground and accommodation than that which the War- rington Cricket Club possesses could not be wished for and it is here that the matches are played.

Mr. R. E. Garnett will captain the team, with Mr. W. Kiernan, as vice-captain and new members will be wel- comed, as it is intended to arrange A team fixtures if sufficient join. Amongst an admirable list of Vice- Presidents we notice the name of Mr. Sydney Crosfiold, the popular captain of the Cricket Club, and an nll round sportsman, whose support will no doubt prove in- valuable to the game, as it is just now with the club in its infancy so to speak that help is needed. We heartily wish the club all the success it deserves for providing a splendid winter sport, in which any gentleman may par- ticipate.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. KENDAL HORNETS.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. KENDAL HORNETS.

"A splendid game !" was the opinion of the two thou, sand enttfusiasts who assembled at the Mint's Feet Ground, Kendal, the home of, Rugby football in West- morland, on Saturday, when the above mentioned clubs I met in the first of their annual fixtures. This opinion I was fully borne out by every player who participated in the match, one and all affirming that a more enjoyable game it has rarely been their lot to take part in. Throughout the game, which was of seventy minutes' duration, the issue was in doubt. Fine passing, running dribbling, and tackling were shown at their best, and the spectators were not slow at the close of hostilities to accord both teams a hearty cheer for the creditable man- ner in which they had acquitted themselves. The War- ringtonians were only indifferently represented, but ex- cellent substitutes were provided. Turner kicked off, and the opening movements of the match found play at the Hornets' quarter flag. Some sterling play by T. Jolley, Evans, Ashton, and Turner found Hine responding in brilliant style, and, although he got the oval back to neutral territory, T. Jolley, by the aid of a couple of powerful kicks, again placed the Warringtonians on the aggressive. Passing by Kendal was frustrated by the clever tackling of Evans and Bate. Hall eventually cleared, and the hopes of Kendal ratched a high pitch when Armstrong darted along touch and took play in close proximity to the visiting goal. The hope of bringing downfall to the Warrington citadel was but a faint one, for a capital combined movement, Sri which Holmes Dillon, and Berry were the shining lights, changed the venue to more desirable quarters. The game so far had been of a fast description, and neither side could, claim a distinct advantage. Succes- sive raids were made on the Kendal goat, all with a futile result, the defence being admirable. A kick by Allen forced Warrington to defend, but Boscow and Evans were equal to the pressure, and a capital save by the visiting custodian met with due appreciation. The Brothers Jolley now exhibited some rare form, and then a short passing movement by the Warringtonians ended in Evans punting to touch near the home quarter flag. Some dribbling tactics of Kendal were frustrated by Evans, who again compelled a retreat. From a scrim- mage Bate stole away from a palk and ran to the line, ulti- mately throwing wide to J. Jolleyobut the pass being de- fective the chance wa4 lost. Turner tackled Hine near the posts, and T. Jolley having the oval passed to him from the succeeding scrimmage he had a splendid opening, but preferred to drop, a minor only accruing. The Hornets went away with commendable dash on the drip out, but they lacked combination at a critical moment, and a passing movement by Ashton, Jolley, Thorniley, and Evans again found Warrington in the ascendancy. So the game continued to be of a give-and-take though interesting nature, and R. Wilson putting in a huge punt, Bosons,/ adopted the saving clause. Bandies put in a grand run from the drop out, but he was hauled down when he reached Hine. Berry. tackled Hall when the latter was endeavouring to clear, and another fine move- ment of the visiting forwards, in which Ashton, Turner, and Povey were foremisst, again forced the game at the Kendal end. Evans was now htkrt and retired, Holmes being drafted to fill the vacancy' in the back division. The homesters gallantly responded, and a second minor was credited to them, Some fine passing by Warrington was again witnessed, and at the call of half-time the oval was under the Kendal posts,the homesters then lead- ing by two minor tto one. Ashton showed up on the re- start with a useful dribble to the home quarter flag, but his progress was stayed when Allan picked cleverly up. and a passing movement was promptly nipped in the bud by T. Jolley. The latter then passed to his brother after Bate and Antrobus had given a sterling display of short passing, but the oval unfortunately rolled into touch. The Warringtonians were now having a deal the be of it, the forwards playing splendidly. Holmes put in a judicious kick, Povey supplemented this effort with a useful dribble. Antrobus next dashed away, and ran to within a yard from the lino, but a wild pass was takenby Beard (Kendal) and the chance lost. Boscow now showed of what value he is as a custodian by some remarkably cool clay, repeatedly punting back to the Kendal quar- ters when surrounded by a host of his opponents. A huge kick by T. Jolley was next productive of a minor. No sooner had the oval been dropped out than the War- rington forwards again broke away, and the ball being beautifully worked through the opposing defence, Ashton scored a try, which proved to be the winning point of one of the most enjoyable games evgr witnessed between the clubs. Fair Turner failed at goal, and the remaining portion of the game being in the home quarters, only a minor was added to the score. The final result reading— Warrington, 0-1-3 ; Kendal Hornets, 0-0-2. Teams :--Warrington :S. Boscow, back; T. Jolley, 3: Jollev, and J. W. Evans, three-quarter backs; J. T. Bate, and W. Antrobus (captain), half backs; Fair Turner, E. Dillon, W. Povey, J. Holmes, B. Berry, W. Bandies, A. Barnes, H. Ashton, and J. T. Thorniley, forwards. Kendal Hornets : T. Hine, back; J. Armstrong, J. Allan, and C. Braithwaite, three-quarter backs; W. Hall, and E. Braithwaite, halfbacks; R. C. Beard (captain), E. Wilson, W. Wilson, R. Wilson, W. Parsons, F. Heap, C. Exton, J. H. Thompson, and R. Simm, forwards.

div.head: WARRINGTON ELECTIONS.
div.p: WARRINGTON ELECTIONS.

MR. ALFRED WOODS' MEETING. There was not much of an attendance at the meeting held in St. Barnabas' Schools, on Tueaday evening, in support of Mr. Alfred Woods, the Tory candidate for Whitecross Ward. The candidate was well supported by outsiders ; but at the time the meeting began there was a poor display of voters of the ward, though later on a moderate number looked in. Amongst those present, be- sides the candidate, was Mr. Robert .Pierpoint, who pre- sided, Dr. Carmen, Mr. W. Spinks, Mr. H. J. Longton (the Tory nominee for Fairfield Ward), Councillor Bolton, Councillor Muir, Dr. Spinks Mr. James Smethurst, Mr. W. W. Westwell,Mr. H. W. C:ookson,Mr. R. T. Smith,Mr. Woollacott, and others. The Chairman opened the pro- ceedings with a referenceto the entrance of party poli- tics into municipal elections. All he had to say with re- gard to that was,that politics had entered into those ques- tions, and they had to acknowledge the fact. They were there, and they were bound to do the best they could for their candidates. Mr. R. T. Smith next moved the usual

" fit and proper" resOliTiaJr;,—S;nl;;;;;C;Ze'd;;;; briefly by Mr. Binks. Mr. W. Spinks, in speaking in sup- port of the resolution approved of Mr. Woods' "plank" in favour of better baths. With regard to the sanitation of the town, he said the Sanitary Committee claimed to have reduced the death-rate, but he held that the Paving and Sewerage Committee' and the Street Improvement ' and Lighting Committee deserved some of the credit as well as the Sanitary Committee. He considered the pail and tub system was not a success, as was shown by the fact that out of 49 towns which sent their sewage into the Mersey or its tributaries only 10 had adopted the systeni, while only two out of the ten adopted the method of manufacture practiced at Longford. Mr. H. .1. Longton argued that Mr. Woods could not be said to

be opposing an-old representative as that was an entirely new ward, and consequently he and Mr. Roberts were on precisely the same grounds in that respect. There had been something said in last Saturday's" Examiner" with regard to a small contract with the Corporation held by Mr. Woods' firm, and it had been suggested that through this Mr. Woods' might be ineligible for a seat in the Town Council. But, speaking as a lawyer, he (Mr. Longton) assured them they would not be called upon to vote for a man who was likely to be disqualified. He thought this objection was a little bit ungracious con- sidering that the firm with which Mr. Roberts was con- nected had had so much larger contracts with the Corpor- ation. Mr. Woods, in his speech, said he was tackling one of the most" amateur-professional" politicians they had in Warrington. With regard to what had been said about the contract with thee Corporation, he was not going to say anything against the " Examiner." He knew he should receive fair play from the " Exam- iner" though he might not receive fair play from some of those who supplied matter to put in it. He had assigned the contract to a friend, and intimated the fact to the Town Clerk to be laid before the General Pur- poses Committee. Mr. Roberts was on that Committee —though he had no right to be on it—and what did they think he did? He actually prostituted his position as ti member of the Committee to go to it and propose that Mr. Wood's assignment be not accepted, and he drummed up all the Radicals he could to help him. When it was proposed that the assignment should be accepted, Mr. Roberts cried out " It's a job," but it was carried by the casting vote of the Chairman. Mr. Woods also re- ferred to the fact that the Warrington Slate Company held contracts with the Corporation, and he went on to speak in favour of better baths, and to condemn the • elegant circus vans " which perambulate Warrington streets and give off disagreeable odours. Councillor Bolton was the next speaker and he spoke against the sanitary system of the town, and especially the Long- ford" experiments." Dr. Cannell said that if they were not careful there would be another sum of from eO,OOO to £60,000 spent on the Longford scheme. Councillor Muir also spoke after which the meeting concluded.

div.head: MEETING IN SUPPORT OF COUNCILLOR H. ROBERTS.
div.p: MEETING IN SUPPORT OF COUNCILLOR H. ROBERTS.

There was a. successful meeting in St Barnabas' School on Thursday evening in support of Mr. Roberts's candida- ture for Whitecross Ward. There was a large attendance of electors and the proceedings were markedly unani- mous and enthusiastic. The chair was taken by Mr. G. Legge, and amongst others present besides the candidate, were Councillors W. Pierpoint, J. 11. Fleming, J. Shaw- Green, T. Flood, Messrs. T. Morris, J. Walker, I. Hay- ward, J. Hayward, J. Fieldhouse, J. Titchett, J. Salt, and S. Dunbobbin. The CHAIRMAN said lie should like them to give an opinion as to which candidate was the best to represent that ward. Mr. Roberts had already had. six years municipal experience but Mr. Alfred Wood had bad no experience except at—winding watches up. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Mr. T. MORRIS spoke strongly in favour of M. Roberts as being a tried and experienced representative and one who had already done a great deal in promotion of the baths question. Mr. FIELDMOUSE moved' a resolution pledging the meeting to use every legitimate effort to secure Mr. Roberts' election. In speaking to this resolution, Mr. Fieldhouse said he had been very much astonished at the way the Town Council at its last meeting treated a repre- sentative of the working-men. When this representative brought forward a motion of which he had given notice there was a regular stampede of the members of the.. Council, which was disgraceful to those who took part in it. (Hear, hear.) It was not only an insult to the repre- sentative himself but to thoss who sent him. (Hear, hear.) He had been reading Alderman Chandley's remarks at the Mayor's dinner, that working-men were not fit to have a seat in the Town Council, but surely if workhig-men were fit to have seats in the House of Com- mons they were fit to have seats in Warrington Town Council. (Applause.) All this was insulting to working- men, but they had the remedy in their own hands—they could return men who would show a different feeling to that. (Applause.) Mr. I. HATWARD seconded the motion in a humourous speech, in which he criticised the Tory speeches at their meeting on Tuesday night. He had gone to that meeting expecting to hear a fellow working. man speak, but he found a. squire in the chair, and after him came the can- did , ate next a lawyer, then a brewer, and last of all the , doctor. (Laughter.) Councillor ROBERTS met with a very cordial reception on rising to speak. He first (if all expressed his gratitude to the managers of the schools for their kindness to him and the party he represented in allowing them to meet there that night. Coining to election matters, he said Mr. Woods told them in hit address that he was his father's son. Mr. Roberts did net think anybody in that room would venture to dispute the fact, but whether that little matter of geneological history was of any interest to any- body except to the noble family of Woods, he did not know. (Laughter.) He (Mr. Roberts) could not boast that he was the son of a man who had been twenty years in the Town • Council, but he could say he was the son of a man who had lived an honour- able and a clean life, and nobody could claim a better record than that. (Applause.) With regard to the alleged disqualification of Mr. Woods through his firm holding a contract with the Corporation, Mr. Roberts claimed that he had a perfect right if he could to beat his opponent whether it was at the poll or before the poll. Did they not think that Mr. Woods, if he had an oppor- tunity of disqualifying him, would not use it? If they did they had a different opinion of Mr. Woods from what he had. Having mentioned that during the last year he had attended something like 90 meetings of the Town Council and its Committees, Councillor Roberts went on to say that exception 'had been taken to the fact that his firm held contracts with the Corporation. He was not going to shirk any allegation. About three years ago they would remember that there was a serious and gross scandal in Salford in connec- ion with the gas contracts. At that time he was a member of the Warrington Corporation and he found that a great deal of the ratepayers' money was being spent outside of Warrington upon 'materials and labour, without those who lived in the town and found the means having the slightest oppor- tunity of tendering for the supply of those materials or for doing the work. He held it was a fair principle that the ratepayers of Warrington should have the same opportunity of supplying their own Corporation with materials as those outside the town, and that being the case he moved a resolution in the Council requiring that all contracts over £2O should be advertised for. Some of the Committees did not Rke his resolution and some of them do not like it to-day, but he held over them the threat of the position in Salford, and he said it was their duty to put themselves above suspicion, and that if they were doing what was right and fair they had nothing to be afraid 'of. From that time public tenders had been sent in for different matters, and with regard to his own firm he could say that they had not obtained a single contract from the Warrington Corpor- , ration, except in such case as they had been the party ' tendering lowest for the supply of the materials. He invited examination of the Corporation records, and if any one could bring forward a single case where the Warrington Corporation had given his firm an unjust preference at the expense of a single farthing to the ratepayers he would give £lOO to the Infirmary. (Ap- plause.) He wished every member of the Corporation could say the same that day. (Hear, hear.) He had been asked to join the Paving and Sewerage Committee but becase his own firm were sending in tenders and be- cause he thought his presence at the Committee meet- ings considering those tenders might act prejudicially on the other parties present, he declined to join the Committee. (Applause.) If the people who brought for- ward these things would only look at the constitution of the Paving and Sewerage Committee they would find there membeis who were not actuated with the same feelings as he had been, and not only this if he dare— which he dare not—he could open their eyes in regard to the action of a certain member of that Committee only last week. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Roberts next re- ferred to his action in opposing the proposed payment of £lOO a year to Mr. Patterson on his retirenaent from the post of gas manager, and also to the action he had taken for several years past in promotion of improved baths. He alluded to a statement in the local Tory paper that he had done nothing on the baths question until the present election. He did not want to say anything un- kind about that newspaper. He knew the editor, or rather he used to know him when he (the editor) ' wore a coat of rather a different political colour than he did to- day. What the motive was for changing that colour
