div.p: that editor and he knew pretty well. He was Aot at liberty to reveal secrets, but if he did perhaps he would astonish some of them. (Laughter.) After touching upon the work of the Sanitary Committee, Mr. Roberts referred to the treatment dealt out to ex-P..0. Shaw during the last few weeks. If there was one thal more than another that Englishman liked it was fair play, and he contended the treatment Mr. Shaw had received was the reverse of fair play. (Hear, hear.) Sergeant Shaw had offended the powers that be at head- quarters and he had to go. That was not the worst, fur he was not allowed to have back any part of what he had paid to the superanuation fund. There had been two similar cases in which allowances had been made from the superannuation fund—that of P.C. Hitchmough Nali o got £2O in 1888, and that of P.C. Fern who got £lO la 1889. Why could not Sergeant Shaw be allowed a VI" tion of the money he had contributed during the len years hehad been in the force to the superannuation fund? It would have been done if the Chief Constable had ventured to make a recommendation. Why had be not done so ? If he had a good reason by all means, apd in justiceto himself, let them know it. If he did not give any reasonthey could only assume that he had no reason to give, and that would bear the light of day. (Hear' hear, and loud applause.) The resolution in support of Mr. Roberts was then put to the meeting, and carried unanimously by acciaraa.

tion. Mr. JOHN WALKER, in moving a vote of thanks to the Chairman' said he had heard that the reason why thet Chief Co nstable did not make the recornmendationie the case of ex-Sergeant Shaw was that he would have 0? certify that Mr. Shaw was not in a physical/ or mentsi condition to follow his employment. He did think, however, that Sergeant Shaw bad been very hardli treated. (Hear, hear and applause.) Councillor FLooirseronded the vote of thanks, whicil was passed, and the meeting terminated.

'GENERAL BOOTH'S SCHEME.

div.head: "IN DARKEST ENGLAND AND THE WAY
div.p: "IN DARKEST ENGLAND AND THE WAY
OUT."

General Booth's much-talked-of, book is out to- Y. In Darkest England and the Way Out" is a ook of about 300 pages, and is accompanied by a Pamphlet of 14 or 15 pages, which summarises it— I 1 innovation for which busy men or the hasty editors will be grateful. The book is prefaced with It lithograph of the picture, and which gives a good Idea of the scheme at a glance, In the lower part is ragritig sea in which thousands of shipwrecked 'wretches are struggling in waves labelled "beg- Y,"" starvation," "unemployed," and the like. he Salvationists, who are high and dry on the eky shore, lend a helping hand, and carry away 'Lie saved to a "City Colony" formed of "night !heifers," "cheap lodging-houses," and "rescue naonaes." Beyond these, again, is the "Farm ,s'ionv,". with its sections of allotments and co- perative • farms; and its pleasure city named Whitecbapel-by-the-Sea." A remote perspective represents "The Colony across the Sea," to which all the abler hands are drafted for their final Chances of a new career. General Booth startles Fpnifortable, self-satisfied people who consider that ‘Le existing agencies to which they give a yearly fillbscription do all for the outcast that can fairly be ;Xpected, by saying he only intends to do as much O 5 the fallen as is done for

- - _ THE LONDON CAR HORSE. 'The cab horse has its charter with two points, work !s found for it, with food and lodging sufficient to enable nto get through its daily task—that is the first; the Second is that when it falls down, whether it be by its Zwn fault, or by mischance, or by the fault of others, it helped up again—all questions as to who was respon- sible for its fall being deferred until it is set upon its feet again!, General Booth estimates—and, in view of other cal- culations which have been made, he does not exaggerate "-that one-tenth of the population of England, Scotland and Wales, or roundly three millions of people, belong to 'ue black battalions of the lapsed masses. This " sub- Illerffed tenth" includes, however, a certain proportion %rim an all-wise Government has taken under wing, to Wit, the occupants of prisons, workhouses, and lunatic as, ylums. "Get at those classes by all means," says ?,eneral Booth, "and I shall do so; but it is urgency and 'kouble urgency, for those unaffected by public funds or Private charities, the homeless, the out-of-workers, the drunkards, the harlots." For assistance, in civilising tugland's savages, the General "appeals neither to Ysterical emotionalists nor headlong enthusiasts." "I Put forth my proposals," he says, with the view of 46eilring the support and co-operation of the sober, serious, practical men and women, who constitute the ving strength and moral backbone of the country." Lie General turns away from Utopian ideals—from the 6themes of those who propose to bring in a new heaven 4ad a new earth by a more scientific distribution of the I)leces of gold and silver in the trouser's pockets of_man- lund, "They may be good or they may not," he says. I intensely sympathise with-the aspirations that lie behind all these Socialist dreams. But lam a practical Alan." , THIS IS HIS PRACTICAL PUN as sketched in the summary of his book. The scheme is tbreefoldiconsisting of— (1) The'City Colony; (2) The Farm Colony ; and (3) The Colony over sea. Elia first step is to take that hungry, workless wight and give him some food for his telly and a shelter for ?c, night. This he proposes to do by the extension of , is food and shelter depots, some five of which have been 1,11 operation for the last two years in various parts of cudon. With or without fourpence, General Booth sllroPo.ses to take him into his shelter ; but if he has no :°drpence he must not go out therefro until he has done °llrpennyworth of work to pay for his bed and board. ..'rus work General Booth proposes to find for him in the :Ira instance by the establishmOnt of labour-yards or 'actories in connection with the shelters, where the pen- less unemployed will be engaged on such rough and licnple industry as chopping wood , for firewood, making laats; sewing sacks, Sm. Their work will be duly mea- anted, and when they have done their fourpenny-worth 2f work they will be free to go and seek work elsewhere. 'tePs have also being taken to pave the way for the or- Fanisation of the sandwich men, and the result so far been fairly satisfactory. What General Booth pro- ses is simply to generalise and multiply a hundredfold he kind of work that is being done by the Social Wing ,Iluder the direction of Commissioner Smith. The next uevelopment of the General's scheme, is novel. He pro- to organise out of the unemployed what he calls he Household Salvage Corps, or the -

WASTE NOT, WANT NOT BRIGADE, the members of which, in uniform, numbered and under strict discipline, would undertake the collection from house to house of broken victuals, old clothes, old news- LPaPers, and such-like exuviEe of the household. From Zue waste food and waste clothes of the working popu- lation General Booth maintains that he will be able to 2ed and clothe and house all the workers. The Refuge, tae Shelter, the Labor Factory, the Household Salvage 'zigade, and the Labor Bureau constitute what General tooth calls the City Colony. Even when they are all set agoing, however useful they may be, they are only palli- atives. It is necessary to provide a way out, and that ljay is only possible in one direction, namely, by plant- g the people upon the land. Wast Labor to Waste 'dad is General Booth's watchword. Here he would Fetablish his second stage of remedial operations, which tke calls

THE FARM COLONY. Ile would treat the estate as a training ground for emi- grants as well as a great market garden for the supply of the rations with which he undertakes to provide the Chat-of-Works of the city. The picked workers from the ftivation Factory or Labor-yard seat down from the estate would have to put up their own shanties and L.kfterwards make their own bricks to make their own 'nuses. They would be supplied with spades and seeds a„nd moth with which to grow their own vegetables. Ihe salvage of the households of London will be con- 'Peyed in barges drifting downwards with the tide to the 'Wharves of the Farm Colony, there to be utilised in a th.ousand different ways. Broken victuals. endless store 13t old crusts, will be capable of being served up when Steamed and dressed as human food. Other crusts Zill serve to diet the horses, and what the , orsJs will not eat will be passed on to the Innumerable clutches of poultry with which tile estate will be goaded, and what the poultry will not eat will come to the pig as the residuary legatee. The ~4.iony Piggery will be the largest in the land. Round the eggery will spring up an industrial community to feed, ~.et kill, to cure, to work up, the invaluable porker. Ilacon factories, brush works, saddlery of all kinds, will illove to be created and run by the Army. Old clothes join another material from which will spring many Industries. The deft fingers of the women will be tinployed in patching and repairing. A colony of .obblers, technically known as translators, will be I, ormed for the purpose of renovating the damaged shoe- teather of the citizens. Cheap second-hand clothing i 13stablishmentS will be created n order to provide the no, lonists who are working for lodging and rations with ;he uniform proper in their colony. The old bones of London will lead to the establishment of button works and manure works. The grease, fat, and kitchen stuff ill afford the material for a soap works. The waste paper of London and the otherwise unusable rags will able the Army to manufacture all its own paper, and - 't Present it uses 30 tons a week. And so forth, and so forth. Thus the Farm Colony includes not only the I tarm colonists proper, but also an industrial village. -"Nit farms will be established, cottages with allotments, and every kind' of experiment will be tried with co- °Peration. There will be no public-house, but attend- ance at the Salvation Army meeting will be quite optional. For this colony General Booth's idea is to °lotain possession of 500 or 1,000 acres of freehold land at a reasonable distance from London, and within the Thames estuary, but secluded as much as possible from towns or villages. TRU COLONY OVER SEA is the next step. General Booth condemns emigration as usually conducted, and insists that if emigration is to Bocceed the land must be prepared for the people, and the people prepared for the land. His idea is to take estates in the colonies, by preference in South Africa, and have them laid out and made ready for the advent °f the colonists. He would fill a sailing ship with a eel-Aly of men and women who had passed the probation t3f the Farm Colony and had proved themselves to be cap- able and willing workers. The colonists would be debited with the cost of their transport and the capital ;value expended in providing them with a house, stock, 'andi and food for a few months. General Booth does toot think that the expense of transportation would be a real difficulty, nor that the foundation of a colony vould be objected to by people already in the land that nt ight be chosen. Once founded in the Over-Sea Colony 1 he would, he reasons, develop, as other batches of men :3,1 far countries have grown into great communities. Of he regulations which he would establish for his colonists 't is hardly necessary to speak, beyond the statement that for repeated offences of drunkenness, dishonesty, °,r falsehood, colOniSts would be expelled or handed over to the police. At the best, and even under his scheme, general Booth admits that there is a certain residum for ;Which nothing could be done, unless indeed it were to Inck- them up for life as moral lunatics. If so it must be, L'ave some kind of Broadmoors to which these utterly sent"Peless ones, lost beyond hope of recovery, might be I

OTHER THINGS SUGGESTED g roe a prison gate brigade, cheap inebriate asylums, and r those not sunk so low, which cannot be more than Inentioned, improved lodgings a model village in the tUburbs, and the establishment of a cheap seaside Zf_atering-place, which the General calls Whitechapel-by- ue-Sea, and which he proposes to be brought within tdange of a shilling return ticket of London. He would velop the co-operative system, superadding the prin- e2Ples of discipline and authority. He throws out in a rrY tentative fashion the suggestion that a matrimonial 0 urea la might be a very desirable adjunct of modern

• civilisation. But the chief suggestions in this chapter are those which deal with the establishment of a Poor Man's Bank and a Poor Man's Lawyer. WHAT WILL IT COST? is the question last, but not least, to be considered. The General says that no one can say what expenditure will be necessary to deal with lall the sunken tenths of all, nations, but in Britain he is prepared to grapple with I the question if he has £lOO,OOO down, and an assured income of 430,000 per annum. That is to say, General Booth's scheme demands for its effective application in this country a million sterling--one-tenth down, and the rest as an endowment, realising £30,000 per annum,, This, he says, may seem a large sum, but John Bull,who I spent nine millions in the expedition to rescue two pri- soners from King Theodore of Abyssinia, will not grudge a pound a head for the rescue of the million men women, and children who were at present the hopeless victims of vice. crime, and destitution. Onithis point the "Daily Chronicle" makes a suggestive obser- vation. If, it says, the bishops and deans and opulent pluralists of the State Church would only sacrifice half their enormous emoluments, and consent to live like cul- tured gentlemen in the modest and dignified simplicity not uncommon among our professional classes, they could soon supply General Booth with the money he wants to carry out his vast and far-reaching polidy of social salvage. -
LORD SALISBURY AND MR. OSBORNE
I.IORGAN.

A letter having been published, in which Lord Salis- bury, through his private secretary, characterized a pas- sage in Mr. Osborne Morgan's speech at Eccles, as reported in the Manchester papers, as" a pure inven- tion," Mr. Morgan replied as follows : The language which I attributed to Lord Salisbury was used by him, though the report of what I said was necessarily very much condensed. I now repeat my assertions—(l) That in one of his speeches, I think at Liverpool, Lord Salisbury compared the Irish Nation- alists to " Hottentots." -(2) That he stated thatit would take "twenty years of resolute Government" to reduce the Irish party •to submission, or used words to that effect. (3) That, on another occasion, he endeavoured to throw ridicule and discredit on one of the most elo- quent and distinguished of his Indian fellow subjects—a "political opponent "—by contemptuously calling him a " black man." I noted down all these expressions at the time, and lam certain that I have given them cor- rectly. They are substantially what I said at Eccles, and anyone who has access to the back files of the daily newspapers may verify them for himself. G. OSBORNE MORGAN. Oct. 20th, 1880.

div.head: MANCHESTER AND LIVERPOOL AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.
div.p: THE MANCHESTER AND LIVERPOOL AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.
MEETING AT WARRINGTON.

The annual general meeting of the members of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool and North Lancashire' Agricultural Sciciety was held at the -Lion Hotel, Bridge-st., Warrington, on Monday afternoon, under the presidency of Lord Egerton of Tatton. The attendance was mummify large, a great deal of in- terest being intparted to the proceedings by the fact that one portion of the business was the election of a new secretary to succeed Mr. Thomas Rigby who has, after holding the office for 21 years resigned, and who was made the recipient, during the after- noon, of a very handsome testimonial.

div.head: REPORT.
div.p: THE REPORT.

The Secretary (Mr. Rigby) opened the proceedings by reading the annual report, which stated that" the list of members has been increased this year from 634 to 711. 140 new members have been added, while 63 have resigned, or have died during the year. The show of next year will be held in the borough of Bury, in Lan- cashire, as has been announced, and your. council anti- cipates a large show, and a large attendance of visitors. They have the promise of the liberal assistance and co- operation from the Corporation and residents of Bury, and they will exert themselves to make the first visit of the Society to this populous district a great success." The adoption of the report was proposed by Mr. G. C. Hale (Knowsley), and 'seconded by Mr. T. Egerton Tatton. The Chairman, before pUtting the proposition, referred to a paragraph in the report which suggested the alteration of the rules, and said that the committee who drew up the rules seemed to have thought that it was within their power to recommend an alteration of the title of the Society. He held, as president, that that was entirely beyond their powers—they could not do it with- out the consent of the patron, her Majesty the Queen, and the consent of the president. The report was adopted.

PRESENTATION TO TIM SECRETARY. The noble Chairman said he now had the pleasant duty, as the representative of the Society, to present a testimonial to the Secretary on his retirement. He was sure all those who had been connected with the Society for a number of years could not have failed to have noticed the activity and energy which Mr. Rigby had always displayed. He had raised the Society into a foremost pcsition among agricultural societies, and had been the cause of increasing the size of their Society. A secretary of a Society like theirs, must have many qualifications—he must be courteous energetic, constantly alive to the wants ' and requirements of agriculturists, regular in his attendance, and endeav- our to carry out, under the orders of the council, the operations of the Society with economy, and with due regard to the interests of the Society. For 21 years he was sure Mr. Rigby had done all this, and now, owing , to failing health, he had thought it best to retire from the 'active duties of secretary. He had in his hand an ad- dress to Mr. Rigby, and,accompanying it, they presented a clock, a quantity of plate, and a purse containing 90 sovereigns. (Applause.) In a few complimentary re- marks Mr. G. C. Hale said, having been Chairman of the council for a number of years he had had intimate con- nection with Mr. Rigby. He had seen the diligent manner in which he had conducted the affairs of that great Society, and he had fully borne out the character which had been given to him. He trusted Mr. Rigby would live many years to enjoy, in his social capacity, the presents which had been presented to him, and hoped that they might be to him a memorial of many happy, yet arduous days--Mr. Robert Lansdale, who said he had the honour of proposing Mr Rigby as secretary to the Society 21 years ago, also made a few appropriate remarks, as also did Mr. White (Warrington).—On rising to reply, Mr. Rigby was loudly applauded. He said he felt much at a loss for words—indeed he could not iind them—to express his thanks to them for the handsome gift, and for the spontaneous way in which it was given to him. He thanked them one and all, and he would take the gift as a testimony of their kind estimation of the services which he had tried to render. He knew he had made many mistakes ; and he knew too, that in dis- charging his duties, he had very often felt they were very imperfectly and inadequately rendered; but he could only say, however, that he had endeavoured to do his best, and had done his utmost to promote the interests of the Society. Whilst acting as secretary he had made many friends, though a good many of them had passed away. But he still retained the good opinion and the kindly friendship of many of the gentlemen connected with that Society who remained. (Applause).

THE NEW SECRETARY. The election of a new secretary was then proceeded with, Lord Egerton remarking that he thought no candi- date should be over 40 years of age.--Mr. Beck, of Wigan, protested against any remarks as to the qualifica- tions of a candidate from the chair; and he moved" that a vote be taken without remarks, and that the remarks already made be erased." (Loud applause.)—Lord Egerton to the mover of the resolution: I must ask you to withdraw the last part of the proposition, or I must leave the chair. (Cries of "No, leave it in.")—Lord Egerton, said he liked to see business matters conducted in a buiiness like way, and he, as chairman, was per- fectly in order, he considered, to make a few observa- tions. (Cries of" No, no," and 'yes.")—Mr. Beck, who was again requested by the noble Chairman to withdraw the latter portion of his' motion, moved an amended proposition to the effect that a vote be taken without further remarks ; and he was proceeding to say a few words, when, amid an outburst of laughter, the Chair- man rcse and reminded him that he himself objected to any remarks, whereupon Mr. Beck desisted.—Mr. Hugh Cawley seconded the motion, which, on being put to the meeting, was carried.nnanimously. The candidates, five id number, were then individu- ally introduced to the members lay the chairman, and after a vote had been taken, it was seen that Mr. William Wrennall had a large majority of votes over the others, and he was, therefore, duly elected as Secretary to the I Society. Mr. Wrennall, is a Liverpool surveyor and valuer, and is stated to have had 25 years' experience in agriculture and kindred matters in Lancashire and Cheshire. For several years he had the, management of the Leyland Hundred Agricultural and Horticultural Society, and tlie secretarial work a the old Manchester and Liverpool Agricultural Society. For the past 16 years, also, he has laid out and planned the showyard arrangements of the Society of which he has been elected secretary. MISCELLANEOUS BUSINESS. The Earl of Derby was unanimously appointed pre- sident of the Society for the ensuing year. It was also decided that the show next _year should be held on the 23rd, 24th, and 25th days of July, and a discussion fol- lowed on the question in which division the show of 1892 should be held. The northern and western divi- sions were proposed and put to the meeting, which se- lected the latter, and the selection of tthe town at which the show should be held was left ove for consideration at an adjourned meeting. Twenty four members were next elected to serve on the Council; after which Mr. J. White brought forward the subject of the new rules drawn up and approved by the special committee ap- pointed at the last meeting. The first alteration was the one referred to by the Chairman when proposing the adoption of the annual report, and it read—" This Society to be called the Royal Lancathire Agricultural Society, and that its district is not confined to any lim- its." Some conversation took place with regard to this proposal, and ultimately the whole subject was deferred, the meeting adjourning for a fortnight.

- - - " THE CRUEL LAW OF DISTRAINT:"

-- Sir,—Your generous columns being always open to discuss subjects of vital interest to the working class, permit me to solicit the opinions of your readers upon the following points. (1.) That the law of distraint affords to landlords over other creditors a preference which is both unjust and inexpedient, and is, in nine cases out of ten, a sudden and most violent " Law of ejectment "against which honest but unfortunate tenants sorely need pro- tection. (2.) That the power of distraint, although pecuniarily almost worthless to landlords, can yet be used as a merciless coercive weapon against unfortunate tenants who, if allowed reasonable time, would be able to satisfy all just demands. "Cruel eviction scenes" are of daily occurrence in London and other large towns, under the name of distraint, but the victims are too poor and de- jected to make their woes publicly known. (3.) That it would be far more equitable to abolish the law of distraint, and confer upon the landlords the same right to refuse prolonged credit as is possessed by tradesmen—subject to a length of ,notice to the tenant beyond the time of default, corresponding to the periods at which the rent is agreed to be paid. 'Under such a law of ejectment the self-interest of the landlord would invariably work favourably to the honest ten3nt—caus- ing the landlord to give reasonable time for the payment of arrears, rather than lose such tenant, and be put to the expense of" doing up "the house for a new tenant, who would be no less liable to misfortune than the present

one. (4.) The "Workingmen's Home-Union "is founded solely on the basis of a thoroughly just relation between landlord and tenant. There is no fee or payment re- quired. Membership forms will be forwarded, post free, to working-men in London or in any other part of Eng- land on written application to me at International College, Hampstead, London.—Your obedient servant. JAMES BATSMAN (President of the Union.

div.head: STANDING TO •CLERGY.
div.p: STANDING TO •CLERGY.

--- Sir,—ln your valuable issue ,of Saturday last " False Teaching" refers to the almost universal practice (not only in churches which have the reputation of being " High " but churches otherwise) of standing when clergy and choir" proceed to and from the holy of holies," but more especially as carried on in the Runcorn Parish Church. I take it that "False Teaching" attends the Parish Church (though he does not say so) because of his knowing or thinking (which?) that this practice" is causing some unpleasantness:" I may say I attend regularly the church services and classes, and this is the first intimation I have received (excepting from a man who lives a little distance from Runcorn and wise has not the slightest interest in the work of the church, but to cause disturbances and opposition to rescuing souls from sin) that unpleasantness is caused. Assuming this is so, why was it that when csir beloved Canon was appointed to Runcorn the congregation stood of their own free will ? They were notagired to do it, nor have they once been asked to do so by any of the curates. How is it that in the Parish Church out of the whole congregation not three persons remain seated? How is it that the worshippers themselves have not made .complaints? I feel sure your numerous readers who attend the Runcorn Parish Church can bear me out in what I say. What person, I wonder, in this or other churches .of the Church of England stand up from fear of the clergy ? I have asked about twenty persons whether they object to this, and not one of them said they did. lam under the impression that your correspondent is one e those maar persons alas! who prefer to go to church to hear a good preacher, to sit down if they dare during the singing of anthems, psalms, hymns, &c., rather than go to confess; their sins to God, and when suehpersons do this (whether , the right spirit or not) the matority of them take their ease—by sitting down_ Two months ago I attended a Church near Runcorn. I had the misfortune to be put into a pew between a young " lady "and two young men. When the choir proceeded to the Chancel, the younger of these men said in a tone which was heard by the Vicar, that he turned round—" I'm not going to stand up to worship an old i canting fool like—,(meaning the Vicar) and a lot of drunken squarking choir men." While the Psalms were being sung, the other young man read them. During the j prayers this same young man wrote notes to the young lady who was the other side of me, and threw them along the pew to her. Then they began to laugh, and she showed me the paper and it bad on it a drawing .of this Vicar with a mitre on. I never spent in ray whole life a more uneasy and worthless time in the house of prayer. Is this 'Protestantism" is this Bibtlical, if the ‘ta.nding up is not ? Away with such narrow prejudices. lam not encouraging Romish ritual, but I think no ob- jection can be made against decency and order. I con- sider it unnecessary to deal with the other parts of your correspondent's epistle ; it had already, I think, been dealt with at some length. My view of the matter is this —stand up if the others do, sit down if the others do ; but at any rate try to dispense with so much bigotry, and let us endeavour to have one common object in go- ing to Church, to learn to think, to pray, and to thank "Him who to the Maker of us all."—Yours, &c., A CHURCHMAN,
UMorn, October 21,1890.
PENKETH.
GAS AND WATER COMPANY.

Steps are being taken for the promotion of a "Penketh and Sankey Gas and Water Company, Limited" for the purpose of supplying gas and water to the Penketh and Sankey district. The capital of the Company is .£lO,OOO divided into 1,000 shares of £lO each. On the other hand the Gas Committee of the Warrington Corporation are inviting applications from Penketh and Sankey for the supply of gas from the Warrington Gas Works.

div.head: CHILDREN'S DAY AT THE WESLEYAN CHAPEL.
div.p: CHILDREN'S DAY AT THE WESLEYAN CHAPEL.

Last Sunday being known as '• Children's Day,' special reference was made to the young at Penketh Wesleyan Chapel. At the morning service, the pulpit was occupied by Mr. James Summersgill, who preached an appropriate sermon. Mr. Summersgill spoke of the efforts now being made in the direction of the education of the young, and remarked that since compulsory education had been adopted juvenile crime had considerably diminished. More vigorous and successful efforts were now being made than ever in the interests of the children, and it was also a praiseworthy fact that the waifs and strays of our large towns and cities are better looked after. In the afternoon a children's service, which was at- tended by many adults, was held in the school. The usual Sunday school work was abandoned, and appro- priate and interesting addresses were given by the teachers, and were listened to with much interest.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

MR.CONINGSBY DISRAE LT.—The members of the Lymin Conservative Club have been presented with an excel- lent portrait of their own candidate, Mr. Coning,sby Disraeli. The likeness is a faithful one, and the picture is elegantly framed. CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH.—The pastor of the above church (Rev. Charles Clay), delivered the second of a series of special discourses on the life of St. Peter, in the above church, on Sunday evening. There was a crowded congregation.. SUNDAY SCHOOL CONFERENCE.—The Rev. Wm. Evans, of Lymm, presided over a conference of Snnday School workers held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Altrinc- ham, on Monday afternoon, when a paper was read by the Rev. J. Dudley, of Golborne, on "How to interest and retain our young people." An interesting discussion follovred,and subsequently a tea and public meeting were held. . .

AN AGED AND HELPLESS WAYFARER.—At midnight on Monday, as P.C.'s Griffiths and Buchanan were going their rounds at Thelwall, they came across an old woman who was lying in a helpless condition near the railway station. They took her to Lymm Police Station, and having restored her to consciousness, she stated that she was named Mary Durgan, of no settled abode. She was 79 years of age, and had fallen in the road and could not get up. On Tuesday morning she was removed by Mr. W. C. Moore, relieving officer, to the Workhouse at Knutsford. WESLEYAN BAND OF HOPE.—In connection with the above society, a public meeting and entertainment took place in the schoolroom at Rush Green, on Monday evening. There was a large attendance, Mr. Joseph Thorp presiding. A miscellaneous programme, of an enjoyable character, was well rendered by the members and friends. The Chairman and Mr. Moore (of the Thelwall Ship Canal Mission) delivered addresses in ad- vocacy of temperance principles. Masters Elliot and Miss Ross took part in a dialogue, and several other children recited. Messrs. Shakeshaft, violin, and H. Brown, piano, contributed an instrumental duet in an effoctive manner, whilst Mr. Moore contributed a couple of humourous songs. A collection was taken at the close.

div.head: PARISH CHURCH.-TEA MEETING AND ENTERTAINMENT.
div.p: PARISH CHURCH.-TEA MEETING AND ENTERTAINMENT.

The congregation and friends of this church spent a most enjoyable evening in the Public Hall, on Thursday, the occasion being the annual tea and entertainment. Tea was provided at six o'clock, to which a very large number sat down, and the latter portion of the evening was devoted to addresses, songs, and recitations; concluding with the farce, "The Area Belle." The cloths having been cleared, the Rector (the Rev. P. Willis) delivered the first address, during which he said he wished to make a public acknowledgment of the kindness and court- esy which he had received at the hands of the clergymen of the town. Of the clergy of his own ' parish he could say that no rector could have a more able or energetic set. (Applause.) The , reverend gentleman then said he was glad to- see St. Peter's Church was rapidly approaching completion. Towards the building fund of this Church they had £3,500, and he hoped that the remaining £1,500, which was needed to wipe off the debt, would be realised by the projected bazaar. The Rev. C. E. Jack- son next gave a humerous address, after which the Rev. D. S. Hodgson briefly touched upon the work of the mission room in Bank-st. The speeches were interspersed with songs and recitations, the contributors being Miss Slater, and Mr. W. H. Hope, both of whom were much appreciated. The farce, as stated above, created con- stant merriment, and it was performed in a very credita- ble manner. those taking part in it being Miss Schofield, Mrs. Kewley, Messrs. A. Woods, W. H. Cookson, and A. Browne. Mr. A. Woods and Mr. H. W. Cookson, en whose shoulders rested the major responsibility, are to be congratulated for upon satisfactory manner in which they had arranged the programme. The proceeds were devoted to the church and parochial expenses.

div.head: CHOKED BY A PIECE OF MEAT.
div.p: CHOKED BY A PIECE OF MEAT.
SAD AFFAIR AT NEWTON.

On Saturday night last a man named Samuel Turner who lived in Kirkgate, Leith, arrived at Newton from Edinburgh for the purpose of effecting some repairs to machinery at Messrs. Gillespie's Paper Mills. Ile reached Newton about ten o'clock at night. and went to his lodgings in Mill-lane about 10.15. Mrs. Pilling his landlady, prepared supper for him and about 10.30 whilst eating the meat, Mr. Pilling observed him gasp and stagger. He caught him as he was falling, and laid him on two chairs, and sent for medical assistance, but before this arrived the man was dead. The facts were reported to the coroner who ordered a post-mortem examination to be made. Dr. H. E. Watkins of Newton conducted the examination, and found that the man had died through being:choked with a piece of meat.
THE INQUEST.

An inquest on the body of Samuel Turner was held by Mr. W. T. Husband, at the Millstone Inn, Newton, on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. R. Barton was present and watched the enquiry on behalf of Messrs. Gillespie, Messrs. Bertram and Co., and the relatives. The first witness was John btewart who said he was an engineer in the employ of Messrs. Bertram and Co., Sciennes, Edinburgh, and resided at Edinburgh, but at present lodged in Mill-lane, Newton. The deceased, Samuel Turner, was about 55 years of age, and resided with his wife in Kirk,gate, Leith, near Edinburgh. He was also an engineer in the employ of the same firm as witness. On Saturday the 18th inst., the deceased and eight others were sent by their firm to de some repairs to machinery at Newton-le-Willows paper mill. They all, with the exception of deceased, got to the railway station at Edinburgh, in time for the 10.25 a.m, train, and when the train was moving out of the station, he saw deceased ceme on to the platform, and he was left behind. He came on by a later train, arriving at about 11 o'clock the same night, and went to lodge ' with John Pilling. He had known deceased for the last 20 years and he always enjoyed good health. John Pilling a bookbinder living at kEill-lane, Newton, said the deceased came to lodge with him on Saturday night last about 10.15. He commenced to get his sup- per. He had a cup of tea, bread and beef, and a drop of whiskey which he had in a bottle. He was not sober. He took a little drop of tea, and a bit of beef off the plate. After chewing it a little hethrew it away.—He sat chat- ting and talking, and took another piece of beef, and commenced eating. He then sent witness's wife for a drop more whiskey., and while she was away he gave a sort of stagger, and witness tried to save him, but he fell right over, witness asked his wife to bring a chair, as he could not holdhim, and witness then let him go down on the chairs. Be did not seem to be choking. He sent for Dr. Watkins but the man was dead when he arrived. Dr. H. E. Watkins, of Newton, said on Satur- day night, the 18th inst., he saw the deceased dead in the house of John Pilling, and he had since made a post o dem examination of the body. When he was first called to the'deceased, he could not assign the c arise of death, as the man was already dead, and the statements of Pilling and his wife made then, did not quite agree. On the 20th inst he received instructions to make a post- ' mortem examination, which he proceeded to do at once. Part of the examination was made in the presence of his father, Dr. Watkins. The brain and other organs were intensely congested, and on examining the throat he found a piece of meat 21 inches long / inch broad, sin, " Ito sin. thick, impacted in the throat, and filling up the wholeof the upper part of the gullett. The cause of death was obviously from the impaction of a piece of beef in the throat, and the intensely congested state of the organs. A verdict of " Accidental death from chok- ing," was returned.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.

AN ALL-ROUND CONTEST. As was anticipated last week, the nominations reveal that there will be contests in every ward in the town, excepting Bewsey Ward. There the Liberals are so strong that it was felt by the Con- servative party that it would be hopeless to attempt to obtain the seat, which is at present held by Conn-

cillor Shaw Green. So far, the liveliest struggle has been in VV hitecross Ward, where Councillor Henry Roberts (L) is being opposed by Hr. Alfred Woods (C). A meeting of Mr. Wood's supporters was held on Tuesday evening, and Mr. Robert Piei- point, who is chairman of the Conservative Associa- tion, said they recognised the fact that party politics entered into these municipal elections. The Liberals, accepting the challenge, have nominated candidates for every ward in the town; and it is now left to the electors to determine, on Saturday next, who shall represent them. Councillor Henry Roberts held a meeting in Whitecross Ward on Thursday evening, and delivered a vigorous address in criticism of the Tory meeting, at the same time giving a full account of his own stewardship. There was a good attend- ance; the proceedings were enthusiastic, and there is every reason to believe that Mr. Roberts will be returned with a substantial majority. In Town Hall Ward, Councillor Fleming (L) is opposed by Councillor J. Fairclough (C.) Councillor Fleming's address will be found in our advertising columns, and it will be seen that he stands on the same plat- form as other Liberal candidates in being pledged to getting rid of the nuisance of the intercepting depots, and being in favour of new baths, and the freeing of the library. He is anxious, too, that the Public Health Amendment Act should be enforced

with the object of removing property that is untit for habitation, and getting rid at the same time, of the black spots of Warrington. Mr. James Walker (L), who is well-known by his connection with Chandos Foundry, and as a large employer of laboui, is the Liberal candidate for Orford Ward, in opposi- tion to Lieutenant Colonel Bolton (C) who is the nominee of the Tory party. Mr. Walker is anxious to aid industry by keeping down the rates, and will support the rest of the Liberals in freeing the library, providing new baths, and abolishing the nuisance of the depots. His familiarity with the electors of the ward will certainly stand him in good stead. Councillor Blackhurst (L) who sits for St. John's Ward, is to be opposed by Mr. James Hill (C) who is not regarded as a formidable oppon- ent. The latter has taken the place of Mr. John Roberts, who is prevented, by indisposition, from , entering into the contest. After casting about some time, the Conservatives have found a candidate , for Fairfield Ward in the person of Mr. 11. J. Long- ton, solicitor, lie will be opposed by ex-Councillor Dixon, who stands as an Independent candidate, and is confident that he will be supported by Liberal electors and by no small number of Conservative working-men. Councillor Percival (C) offers him- self for Howley Ward, but he will be opposed by Mr. Arthur Browne, solicitor, who has con- sented to contest the seat at the unanimous and pressing request of a large body of electors, who are not quite satisfied with their present representative. Mr. Browne's address to the electors will be found on our front page. In Latchford Ward the seat is at present occupied by Councillor Ashton (C). It has been felt for some time that it was no advan- tage to the ward that two of the three of its repre- sentatives should be publicans, and it has been been determined by the Liberals that an effort should be made to improve the representation. Mr. S. B. Stringer is nominated on this occasion to oppose Councillor Ashton. Mr. Stringer is an active, intelligent man of independent means. He is well-known for the successful way in which he has organised the Saturday night Penny Concerts in the Buttermarket-street Wesleyan Mission-room; and, if fitness and ability are taken into account, he will leave " the silent member" a long way behind on the day of the polling. Councillor Hepperd (C) will be opposed in St. Austin's Ward by Mr. Joseph Titchett (L), who con- tested the ward some months ago. Since then, the ward has been extended under the Improvement Bill ; and, as Mr. Titchett is a man of ability and high character he will win the seat if supported by .the active and unceasing exertions of the ward committee. His address, along with the addresses ot other candidates will be found in our advertising columns. It will also be seen that there are to be two Liberal Meetings in Latchford Ward, and one in St. Austin's Ward; and a Conservative meeting in St. John's Ward. div.head: WARRINGTON UNITED TRADES' COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON UNITED TRADES' COUNCIL.

A special meeting of the above Council was held on Monday to take into consideration the resolu- tions to submit to the candidates for election iii the different Wards in the Borough. The following questions were passed unanimously ;—Will you, if elected member for this Ward promise to vote (Ist) That all Corporation work and contracts be given only to those firms who pay the recognised rate of wages to their workmen, and will you vote that the workmen in the employ of our Corporation shall receive the recognised tate of wages? (2nd), Will you vote for an advance of wages to all able- bodied Corporation workmen who receive less than 20s. per week? (3rd), Will you record your vote in favour of the workmen of the Corporation being allowed holidays every year, and receive wages for the same, the number of holidays to be the same as allowed to the higher officials of the Corporation? The attention of the Council being drawn to a speech delivered at the Mayor's dinner by Alderman Chandley, it was considered to be a serious reflection upon the abilities and character of the working-men of Warrington; and the Council had in consider- ation to call a meeting of working-men upon the slanders uttered by a gentleman who has been placed in the position he now holds by the vote ot the working-men. It was decided to let the question rest with the decision of the working-men at the forthcoming municipal election. A discussion arose upon the motion Councillor Flood was about to bring forward at the last Town Council meeting when the unseeml3 sight was witnessed, of members of the Town Council retiring as the motion was about to be brought forward. The Warrington Trades Council representing (with a late addition) 1,300 Trades Unionists of Warrington unanimously passed a vote of censure upon Town Councillors who left the Council Chamber rather than listen to a motion that hits been passed by the highest Council Chamber there is, namely, the London County Council.

div.head: WAR RINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WAR RINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
A meeting of this Council will be held on Tues- day to complete the business of the municipal year. The following are some of the matters that will come before the meeting.
_ THE ERIDEWELL.-STAGE PLAYS.

-- --- The Watch Committee will propose as follows That the allowance of £2O per annum granted to Inspec- tor Soinks for cleaning, &c., at the Bridewell be increased to £3O per annum; that a license be granted to Mr. Edward Greenall, junr., for the performance of stage :plays at the Latchford Parish Rooms for 12 months from this date, subject to the usual conditions upon which such licenses were formally granted by the Justices; also, that a stand for four carriages be appointed in Cairo-st., opposite the Unitarian Chapel. THE GYMNASISM IN THE PARK. The Town Hall, &c.. Committee will propose that the Borough Surveyor be instructed to erect a wood parti- tion across the centre of the gymnasium so as to separ- ate the part used by boys from that used by girls; and that the gymnasium be enclosed with an unclimbable iron palisade. THE PROPOSED BRIDGE AT LOWER WALTON. The Rivers Committee's minutes contain the follow- ing :—That the Borough Surveyor laid before the Com- mittee a plan submitted by the Manchester Ship Canal Co., of the bridge proposed to be constructed over the river at Walton. After carefully considering the same, it was resolved that Councillors R. T. Fairclough and Heaton, and the Borough Surveyor be requested to see Mr. Leader Williams with the view of obtaining a head- way of at least 28 feet above low water, and ascertain the width and position of the locks to be constructed in the river at Walton. THE INFIRMARY EXTENSION. With regard to this subject the following letter has been received by the Corporation from the Assistant Sec- retary of the Local Government Board :—" I am di- rected by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 3rd instant, with refer- ence to the application of the Town Council of Warring- ton, for approval of the grant of a plot of land to the Trustees of the Warring,ton Infirmary and Dispensary. The Board direct mete refer to the interview which Mr. Alderman Davies had with one of the officials of the Board upon this subject on the 9th instant, and to the memorandum left by him, in which the Board observe that it is stated that the Trustees of the Infirmary would he prepared to purchase the land for such a sum as might he deemed to be reasonable ; and to state that the Board would not object to consider a proposal on the part of the Corporation to sell the piece of land in question. Should the Town Council propose to adopt this course the proposal should be embodied in a memorial under the seal of the Corporation which should be accompanied by a valuation of the land proposed to be sold,by a valuer independent of the Corporation." The Committee has passed the following resolution :—That Mr. Percy Sil- cock, A.R.1.8.A., he called in to make tho valuation ; also, that the Town Clerk be instructed to prepare and forward a memorial under the seal of the Corporation to the Local Government Board to carry out the proposal contained in the above communication.

HARVEST FESTIVAL AT ST. MICHAEL'S CHURCH. Special thanksgiving services for the ingathering of the harvest were held in St Michael's Church, Burtonwood, on Sunday. The interior of the church was tastefully decorated with fruit, flowers, and vegetables, by the choir, with the assistance of Mrs. Sanderson. Over tho chancel was the text " The harvest is the end of the world, and the reapers are the angels," while facing it, on the gallery was the text" And thou crownest the year with thy good- ness," the letters being of gold and silver. The corn and vegetables were very kindly given by Messrs. G:eave. Welsdy, Hewitt, Fairclough, Heyes, and W. Hewitt, the fruit being given by Messrs. A. Kilshall and W. Fairclough, the grapes being sup- plied by members of the choir. Appropriate ser- mons were preached at the morning and evening services by the Rev. C. Jackson, curate of Warring- ton Church, and in the afternoon by the Rev. W. Michael, of Manchester. Special hymns and an- thems were sung by the choir, under the conduc- torship of Mr. W. Sepliton. There were large congregations throughout the day, and the collec- tions, which were in aid of the choir fund, amounted to £l2. FINEST KIEL BUTTER. one shilling per pound.—lmperial Tea Co.—Advt. div.head: MR. PEARSON'S CONCERT.
div.p: MR. PEARSON'S CONCERT.

On Wednesday evening the second annual concert provided by Mr. R. H. Pearson, was given in the Public Hall, before a large and fashionable audience. Great pains had been taken with the orchestra, and the front of the orchestra, in the way of adornment and decoration. A large number of shrubs and , flowering plants had been obtained and very taste- fully arranged under the direction of Mrs. Pearson, and the effect, heightened by a number of coloured lamps,was altogether pleasing. Every reserve seat. it should be stated, was engaged,and the other parts of the hall were crowded. The Vocalists were : Madame Alwina Valleria, Miss Louise Bourne, Mr. Braxton Smith, and Signor Poll ; and the instru- mentalists :—Madame Annette Essipoff, pianist, Mons. Johannes Wolff, violinist, and Herr Julius Klengel, violoncello. The programme was as follows :

Signor Foli was,as at the concert last year," the bright particular star" of the evening, and he received a capital reception when he presented himself to sing Gounod's "She alone charmeth my sadness." He was in splendid voice, and, as he rendered the air with fine dramatic effect, it is a matter of course to say that he was enthusias- tically recalled. He sought to escape an encore at this point, but the audience were not to be denied, so he com- plied by rendering a new song by Battison Haynes with the title " Off to Philadelphia." Signor Foli is always successful with an Irish air, but he was never more suc- cessful than he was with " Off to Philadelphia." It was a powerful rendering alike in its humour and pathos, and brought down the house. In the second part, he sang two songs in succession" Deep in the valley," and "Say but the word." Neither of them was of the highest quality, either as to words or music ; but they were well sung and loudly applauded. Signor Foli was three times recalled, but he was firm in refusing to add another contribution. Madame Valleria suffered from a cold when she was last here, but she was under no such disadvantage on Wednesday night, and delighted her admirers, in the old style, by her rendering of "Halloween," and " Widmun,g." She was most effective, however, in "A lark's flight," which she sang with much power and sweetness of expression, and, being recalled, she responded with the " Hazel Dell," accompanying herselt on the piano. Miss Louise Bourne acquitted herself very satisfactorily, without making any special impression. She has a good contralto voice, and she sings with skill and care and it was due rather to the songs than their rendering care, no encore was insisted upon. Pretty much the same criticism applies to Mr. Braxton Smith. As a tenor his voice is sweet, and it is not wanting in power and range; but it was not to his advantage that he came before the audience in the first instance with an Italian air. He was recalled, however, and, being encored later on in the " Song of Love," he gave a rendering of the " Anchor's weighed," which left nothing to be desired, and won him loud applause. The pianoforte solos by Madame Essipoff were brilliantly executed. Her delicacy of touch is such as may be said to merit the Shakesperian epithet of" flower-soft hands," and every thing she did was wholly satisfactory. Herr Klengel was compelled to substitute the :Chopin-Sarsate nocturn for a composi- tion of his own, which was down on the programme, in consequence of a hurt to his hand. But the accident seemed to be no disadvantage to him in other selections as lie played throughout with such brilliance, sympathy, and high finish as to rouse, at the close of every perfor- mance, the enthusiasm of the audience. Recalled after the nocturn he played Popper's Gavotte. We had occasion to comment on the high qualities which Mons. Wolff displayed as violinist when he was last in Warrington. His performances on Wednesday evening showed that he had lost none of his extraordinrry skill. He was encored after the "Romance," (his own compo- sition), and it was owing solely to the lateness of the evening that he was not again encored in the " Fantasie Caprice." Mons. Sieveking showed himself in every respect capable as musical director and accompanist. The concert was brought to a close at quarter past ten. Mr. Pearson is to be congratulated upon its success, alike from a musical and from a financial point of view. Ho does not go beyond one concert a year, but it is due to him to say that he makes that concert,by the number high artistes which he engage.s,the concert of the season.

div.head: GOLBORNE.
div.p: GOLBORNE.

SERMONS.—On Sunday two sermons were preached in the Congregational Chapel, Golborne, by the Rev. A. N. Gilmour, of Prescot. Collectionswere made in aid of the church fund. FRUIT BANQUFT.—On Monday evening a fruit banquet was held in the Bridge-st. Primitive Methodist Chapel, when there was a good attendance. The chair was oc- cupied by Mr. E. Parr, Golborne, and a programme of songs, recitations, and addresses was gone through in good style. Fruit was distributed at intervals, and a gLECTRIC was spent. WIRES QUESTION.—This very pleasant pleraßsaonptoseEvDeniEn question, which has caused much discussion among the members of the Golborne Parochial Committee, came before a special meeting for the purpose of considering the application which had been made by Messrs. R. Evans and Company, Limited, to erect electric wires from their collieries to Golborne Park, the residence of Mr. T. D, Grimke. The members present were—Messrs. W. Mitchell (chairman), W. H. Arnott, J.P. C.C., W. Garton, J. Robinson, S. S. Brown, C.C., J. Dobb, R. Yates, W. Glover. J. Unsworth, jun., J. Wakefield, J. Fearns, and the Surveyor (Mr. C. S. Bennie). The Sur- veyor reported that in accordance with instructions re- ceived at the monthly meeting, he had, in conjunction with the chairman, taken legal advice as to their position in the matter, and consulted Messrs. White and Son, solicitors, of Warrington, who had forwarded a reply stating that " the Committee will be justified in with- holding their consent until the company have agreed to take such precautions for the safety of the public as re- gards the whole of the elactric lines, whether on public or private property, as the Committee think necessary. If the Committee think the safety of the public requires a license to be obtained from the Board of Trade, they may reasonably grant their consent, expressly subject to such license being obtained, and require the company to undertake to proceed to obtain such license. If, as we understand, the Committee was formed by the Leigh Rural Sanitary Authority, under sec. 1 and 2 of the Public Health Act, 1857, it may be advisable in case of difficulty to bring the matter before the Sanitary Auth- ority before giving any consent, as the Committee are considered the agents of the Authority. Some corres-. pondence was now read as to the custom in other towns A plan was submitted by Mr. Robinson of the intended route, and also a model of the scheme. After he had explained the model, he said that Messrs. R. Evans and company were desirous of satisfying the Committee as far as possible, and were also prepared to satisfy the public as to their safety. After some discussion, a reso- lution was passed by three votes to none giving the re- quired permission on condition of the laying of the wires underground where,they passed through the public streets and footpaths, suah stipulations to be in writing. The route which it is proposed to take the electric wire IS as follows :—From the collieries across the fields to Heath-st., thence across the fields past Messrs. Mitchell, Arnett, and Co.'s works, and forward crossing Park-rd., near Brook Villa, and on to Golborne Park.

div.head: MARKETS.
div.p: MARKETS.

MANCHESTER TRADE. FRIDAY.—There is not more than a moderate trade doing in any department. Cotton has de- veloped increased activity, the estimate of sales haying been raised from 8,000 to 10,000 bales, without material change in prices. Yarns are not vigorous. Twists of good makes are generally well under contracts, and spinners show a good deal of steadiness, but manufacturers are not eager operators, and not many lines ofereat weight are being secured. Wefts are perhaps stiffer than:twists, and here and there some little buying is being done for quick delivery. undies are not in great request. Cloth is rather slow.

Middlesbrough buyers 47s cash and 47s 3d one month ; sellers lid more. Hematite done at 56s lid to 57s cash ; buyers 57s cash and 57s 3d one month ; sellers lid more. LIVERPOOL PROVISIONS, FDlDAY.—Holders of beef are stiff on fine parcels. In pork the tone is steady, with a moderate trade passing. There is no change In the oacon market to day, which continues firm, and all cuts are held for previous full prices, short rib middles being exceptionally firm through scarcity. Short cut hams continue to meet a good inquiry at hardening prices, but long cuts rule steady and unchanged. Cheese is firm but quiet. Butter shows no alteration. Lard closes firm. -

MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS, 1890. TO THE BURGESSES OF TOWN HALL WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN.-AB the term for which I Wall elected a Member of theWarrington Town Council is about to expire, I offer myself as a candidate for your Ward at the pressing request of an influential body of ratepayers. During the six years I have had a seat in the Council, I have made it my duty to promote those meaaures whish had for their object the economical and better government of the town. If again returned I need hardly say that it will stil be my object to faithfully serve the ratepayers as a whole. I trust that the Public Health Arniendment Act, which has just been adopted, will be drought into operation, and thus be the means of improving or removing insanitary pro- perty, while ridding us at the same time of the Black Spots of Warrington. I am in favour of an immediate inquiry being instituted es to the effect of the Intercepting Depots upon the health and comfort of the inhabitants, and shall vote for their being closed, or removed, if they cannot be made inoffensive. Having supported the movement for freeing the Library, I shall vote, if returned, for the Lending Department being made free to the public as soon as it can be done in the , coming year. I think the time has arrived when new baths should be provided, and every facility offered for boys to learn to swim. These and other matters shall receive my careful consideration if you return me to the Town Council. Hoping to have your support on the day of election, I remain, Ladles and Gentleman. Your obedient Servant, JOHN H. FLEMING. Winmarleigh Lodge, October 24th, 1890.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION. TOWN HALL WARD. TO THE BURGESSES OF THE WARD. LADIE4 AND GENTLEMEN.—After having served you in the Town Council for eighteen months, I have consented, at the request of a large and influential body of Ratepayers of the Ward, to be again nominated for election as the Representa- tive of your Ward. Being a resident in the town, and a large employer of labour, it is my interest equally with yours to secure due economy and efficiency in all the affairs of the Borough, and, should you honour me lby electing me to be your repre- sentative, my constant endeavour will be directed to that end. lam in favour of the extension of the Public Baths, and any well-considered scheme for the utilisation of the ground in front of the Town Hall for the benefit of the people will receive my cordial support. As I am well known in the town, I feel that I may confi• dently appeal to you for support on the Polling day. I am. Ladies and Gentlemen, Your Obedient Servant, JAMES FAIRCLOUGH. 5, Wilson-Patten Street, Warrington, 24th October. 1890

TO THE ELECTORS OF TIIE WHITECROSS WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—I beg respectfully to request the honour of your support at the ensuing Municipal Election. Having had six years experience of corporation work, I trust this fact and the character of my conduct during that period are such as will justify a renewal of the coalidence I am now seeking. I am, your obedent Servant, HENRY ROBERTS. Rose Cottage, Latchford, October 17th, 1890.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION. WHITECROSS WARD. 110 THE BURGESSES OF THE WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—The decision of the Commissioner appointed for the purpose of re-arranging the Wards of the Borough, having constituted your district a separate Ward—l have much pleasure, at the invitation of a large and influential bqy of ratepayers, in offering myself for election as your representative on the Ist of November. I have, as many of you know, for a a last ten years taken lan active interest in all matters calculated to benefit the rate- payers generally and to improve our town. I am a resident in your Ward, and will therefore give attention to all matters promoted to improve the better sewer- tog, lighting and sanitation of the Ward. I am most favourably disposed towards large and commodious Baths being erected as soon as possible, and being free on certain days to all School Children under control of their Teachera ; also that the prices charged shall be as low as possible, consistent with Efficiency and Economy in the work- ing of the establishment. I pledge myself, if returned,to support all schemes that may be brought forward from time to time, for the benefit and welfare of all. I am a native of Warrington (as was my Father, who had the honour of being a member of the Town Council for over 20 years) and as all my interests are centred in the town, you may rely upon me doing my duty faithfully. Jam, your Obedient Servant. ALFRED WOODS. 98, Bewsey-road, Warrington, October 14th, 1890.

TO THE BURGESSES OF BEWSEY WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEIC,,—I beg sincerely to thank you for the honour conferred upon me by my unopposed re-election for your Ward. During the past three years, I have considered my position a trust and a duty and I have spared neither time nor labour —whilst taking an interest in all—to make the departments in which I was especially interested as effective as possible. In the coming year, in addition to our present engage- ments, most important matters will demand our attention— finance, the Water Works, the freeing the Library, the new baths, &c., to all of which, if spared, I shall devote most earnest consideration. Yours obediently, J. SHAW-GREEN. 24th October, 1890.

MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS, 1890. To T" BIJEciESSES OF THE ORFORD WARD. I LADIES IND GENTLEMEN.—I have been waited upon by a deputation asking my consent to contest your Ward as a Candidate for the Town Council. After giving the matter very careful consideration, I have decided to place my services at your disposal. As a large employer of labour in the town, I shall at all times endeavour to keep down the Borough expenditure, and so lessen the rates, in order to induce other manufacturers to open out new industries in our midst. The question of a Free Library (which is practically settled) and the proposed new Baths will have my hearty support. With regard to the Intercepting Depots, I regret that serious complaints are made as to the nuisance arising from them. I shall do my utmost to secure the abatement of this nuisance, and. if that is impracticable. I shall be prepared to vote for the closing of the Depots rather than inflict upon my friends and neighbours anything which interferes with their health and the comfort of their homes. All other matters of local interest, which may come before the Council shall have my best attention, and, should you honour me by election, rely lupon it,. I shall do my best to deserve your confidence and approval. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, JAMES WALKER. Banana-lane Foundry, Warrington, October 24th. 1890.

BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. MUNICIPAL ELECTION. ORFORD WARD. TO THE BURGESSES OF THE WARD LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,- At the urgent request of a large and influential body of Ratepayers of the Ward. I have consented to be nominated for the vacant seat in the Town Council as your representa- tive. I am in favour of the Intercepting Depot, which is such a nuisance to many of you, being removed entirely from the neighbourhood, and, if you do me the honour to elect me, I shall do my utmost to have it done. It will be my study to see that all matters affecting the health and happiness of the inhabitants of the Ward. such as good sanitary arrangements for workingmen's houses, proper paving and lighting of streets, good gas at as low a charge as possible, and the provision of suitable Baths for the use of the people are attended to by the Council. As there is no retiring candidate for your Ward, I am opposing no old representative. My Glass Manufactory being Situate in your Ward, I feel sure you will see that my interests in its welfare, either as Ratepayer or Occupier, are the same as yours, and I have therefore much confidence in asking for your votes at the polling booth on the First of November next. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, GEORGE YATES BOLTON. Orford-lane Glassworks, October 25th, 1890.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION. ST. JOHN'S WARD. TO THE BURGESSES OF THE WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN.—At the request of a large and influential body of the Ratepayers of the Ward; I have much pleasure in offering myself as a candidate for election on the Ist November next, as your representative in the Town Council. Should you do me the honour to elect me, my constant object in the Council will be to do all in my power for the Improvement of the Town and its Trade, so as to create Labour and Wages for the Working Classes, and Business for the Shopkeepers and Commercial Interest. My best attention will be given to the Improvement of your Streets, Workingmen's Houses, the supply of good Gas at as low a rate as possible, the Improvement of the Sanitary Arrangements of the Town, and to full efficiency with due economy in all matters connected with the Ward and Borough. As regards the Intercepting Depot so cruelly planted in your midst. I shall do all in my power to have it swept away and entirely removed. I am also strongly in favour of the nightsoil being removed during the night, and thus do away with the nuisance of having to meet bad smelling carts in the streets at all hours of the day. I am a la sident in your Ward. your interests and mine are Identical, and I shall at all times be at hand and ready to bear the grievance of any Burgess. and so far as it lies in my power I shall endeavour to have such grievance remedied. Waving lived amongst you for many years and being well known to a very large number of you. I feel that I may with great confidence ask your votes and active support on the: Pol- ling Day. I am, Ladlesaud Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, JAMES HILL. 24, Ashton-street, October 23rd, 1890.

TO THE BURGESSES OF TIIE FAIRFIELD WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—I beg to offer myself as Candidate for a seat in the Town Council, as your representa- tive, and, if elected, the work of the Sanitary Committee shall have my attention, which at the moment is so very un- satisfactory. The Gas Committee has not reduced the price of the gas. It will be one of the things which shall have my immediate attention, and the quality shall not be overlooked. I hope the voters will be good enough to register their votes in my favour, and so give me a majority to secure the seat. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours truly, FRANCIS DIXON.

PTO THE ELECTORS OF THE HOWLEY 1 WARD OF TUB BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,—I have been asked by a large number of the ratepayers of your Ward to come forward as a candidate for the vacancy in the Town Council In the Howley Ward on the Ist November next, and, as I understand I have been nominated, I have consented to place my serviceg at your disposal. I have lived all my life in Warrington, and am doubtless known to most of you. There are several questions that require the earnest con- sideration of our Town Council, and the most important is the nuisance caused by the Intercepting Depot in your midst. As I have personal experiences almost daily of this nuisance, I shall, If elected by you, support any resolution for prevent- ing the nuisance, and, if it is found impor.sible to remedy it, I shall certainly vote for the abolition of such Depot. With regard to the proposed New Baths, I am strongly in favor of having them free, at least once a week, for all youths under sixteen years of age. There are other questions which require immediate atten- tion by our Town Council, and, if elected. I shall use my best endeavours not only to do my duty to you with regard to them, but also to try *td ingeasetl prmerity of our Town. I at, Ladles and Gentlemen, Your Obedient Servant, ARTHUR BROWNE. 1, Cloth Hall Yard, Warrington.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION. HOWLEY WARD. TO THE BURGESSES OF THE WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN.—My term of office having expired as your representative in the Town Council, and hav- ing been requested by a large body of ratepayers •to serve again, I have consented. If re-elected I shall endeavour to serve you in the future as in the past. As a large ratepayer and property owner in the town, it will be my study to keep down all unnecessary ex- penditure. My attention will be given to the Intercepting Depots and Howley Brook—so often complained of—to have them reme- died, and all other nuisances that may arise; also to have the sanitation of the town placed on a first-class footing; with other improvements, such as proper dock accommodation in connection with the Ship Canal, new Public Baths, &c. After my ten years service in the Town Council, I have every confidence in again seeking your suffrages. I am, Ladies and Gentleman, Yours obediently, NATHAN BROWN PERCIVAL. 14, Buttermarket Street, Warrington, October 24th. 1890.

MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS, TO THE ELECTORS OF LATCHFORD WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN.—Thera has been no contest in your Ward for the last ten years, and I have every reason to believe that you are far from satisfied in being given no choice in representation. At the urgent request of a number of ratepayers, I have decided to offer myself as a candidate for your suffrages on the first of November. I have observed with satisfaction that the Water Works will soon be in the hands:of the Corporation, as is the case with the Gas Works. lam in favour of New Baths ;of the Library being made free; and of the removal of the Black Spots of Warrington by the enforcement of the Public Health Act. There are great complaints against the Intercepting Depots, and if they cannot be mended I think they should be ended. lam of opinion that no person In the liquor trade should have a seat on the Watch Committee ; and, further, that "the trade" Is over-represented in the Town Council, and especially in Latchford. If you return me to the Council, I shall regard It as my duty to further your interests and the interests of the town by supporting the views which I have here set forth, and which will be further explained at public meetings In your ward. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient servant, SAMUEL B. STRINGER. Gordon Villas, Wilderspool Road, October 24th, 1891

WARRINGTON MUNICIPAL ELECTION. rpo THE BURGESSES OF LATCHFORD WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,-My term of office having expired, I again offer myself to the Electors of Latchford Ward, and seek their suffrages for re-election. My line of action in the past, extending over 22 years, has been faithfully devoted to the interest of the ratepayers in general, performing my duties on the various committees fearlessly and conscientiously to the best of my judgment and ability. I can only add, should you again place your confi- dence in me, that nothing shall be wanting on my part to serve you as earnestly in the future as in the past. I remain, Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours faithfully, ' JOSEPH ASHTON: Bridge Inn, Wilderspool Causeway, October 24th, 1890.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION, NOVEMBER IST, 1890, TO THE BURGESSES OF ST. AUSTIN'S WARD LADIES AND GENTLENIEN,-At the urgent request of a large body of ratepayers in the Ward, I have decided to again offer myself as a Candidate for the representation of your Ward in the Town Council. As it is my intention to avail myself of an early opportunity of addressing you upon various matters of local interest and importance, I shall not deai with them in this address, but will content myself with assuring you that, should you honour me by electing me as your representative, my earnest endeavours will be, by diligent and devotet labours in your behalf, to merit your confidence and approval. I am, Ladies and Gentleman, Your obedient Servant, JOSEPH TITCHETT. Whitecross House, Liverpool Road, October 21st, 1890.

TO TIIE ELECTORS OF WARRINGTON AND DISTRICT. LADIES IND GENTLEMEN,—Not " having been solicited 1)37 a large and influential section of the ratepayers of your ward to allow myself to be nominated for election," I come forward on my own account to solicit your patronage and support. I need hardly say that I shall endeavour to serve you, as I have always done, to the best of my ability. As some of you will be prepared to admit. I have " taken thp measure " of no small number of the electors ; and can say with confidence that I can" suit" you to a nicety. Unlike some representa- tives, I have net the least objection to " take orders " from you. Indeed, nothing pleases me better than knowing that while lam clothed with your authority, you are in return clothed by me. "Return's the word " ; and as my motto is " small profits, quick returns, and general satisfaction," I hope to have your "support and interest" on the Ist of November and ever afterwards. lain, Ladies and Gentlemen. Your obedient servant JOHN MAWSON. Messrs. Mawson & Co., Standard Tailors, 35, Sankey-4., Warrington.

In cases of Rheumatism, Gout, Sciatica and Lumbago, his Massage and other treatmenthas proved marvellously success- ful. For some years past he has made this treatment a spe- cial feature and study, and in the eases he has had under the sanction and supervision of Medical men, he has produced re- sults which even they admit have been singular and excep- tional. " REUBEN'S HYDRO," 49, Lord Street, Leigh, Lancashire, July 12th. DEAR SIR, It is with gratitude and love that I am writing to such a gentleman as you. Mr. Pearson, who has done so much for the benefit of my health. You will perhaps remember me coming to your establishment at Hale-road, in August. 1886, quite crippled in my hands and feet with the Rheumatic and Chalk Gout, and after staying for a few weeks with you, I returned home at the end of six weeks, and I have never felt anything of the Rheumatic or Gout since. I can both use my hands and can walk quite well. Thanks be to God for it, for I am sure if I had not come to you and received your treatment, I should never have been able to walk, but should have been a eripple for life; I had been under two eminent doctors for several months before I came to you, but I kept failing an going worse. I shall ever feel thankful and grateful to you. My wife joins me in kind regards to you for restoring me to 'lealth, and hoping by the help of God I may remain so. I tah Dear Sir, yours, JINIES COLLIER, Builder and Contractor, Leigh. REUTER'S ALTRINCItAM. EXTRA CHARGE AFTER 8 P.M.

GREAT LIBERAL VICTORY. The polling to fill the vacancy in the Eccles Division of Lancashire, caused by the death of the Hon. A. J. Eger- ton took place on Wednesday, and resulted in a great Liberal victory. The figures were declared about one o'clock on Thursday morning, as follows : Mr. Henry John Roby (L.) Hon. A. F. Egerton (C.) Liberal majority The subjoined figures show the results of the two previous elections: 1885. 1886. Hon.A.J.F. Egerton(C.) 4,559 Hon. A. J. Egerton (C.) 4,277 V. K. Armitage (L.) 4,312 E. D. Gosling (L ) 3,985 -- 247 I 292 It will be seen that the poll is the heaviest ever known in the constituency, 9,597 electors having recorded their vote as against 8,871 in 1885. As compared with 1885, the Liberal vote has increased by 589 and the Conserva- tive by only 137. As compared with the election of 1886, the Liberal vote has increased by 916. Immediately after the declaration of the poll Mr. Roby proposed, and Mr. Egerton seconded, ,the customary vote of thanks to the returning officer. The result was received with enthusiasm in the streets and square oppo- site the Town Hall. The political clubs in Mauchester were beseiged with enquiries anxious to learn who had succeeded. At the Manchester 'Reform Club triumphant speeches were made, and there was a large attendance at the Conserva- tive Club, but the demonstrations were less marked. There were 41 spoiled votes. Mr. Roby has received numerous telegrams of congrat- ulation. A Barrow Liberal wired that the victory shows that Balfour is being shadowed by the electorate of England. The seat at Eccles is the sixteenth which the Liberals have won since the general election, as compared with two won by the Conservatives. Apart from Ayr, where the Tories have recaptured the seat which the Liberals had wrested from them at a previous bye-election, the Liberals have a balance of 14 gains, counting 28 on a division. The secessions from the Dissentient Liberal party in the House number five, counting ten on a divi- sion, and the above gains, reducing the Ministerial major- ity by 38. That majority which, four years ago, was 118, is now 80. 40 - THE EX-PRESIDENT OF BUENOS AYRES. A telegram from Buenos Ayres, of Sunday's date, an- nounces that an immense meeting was held in that city to demand the impeachment of ex-President Juarez Cel- man and his partisans for various fraudulent practices. Perfect order prevailed.
